english: Those being murdered are released from such sluggishness by the Lord's command, which is symbolized by the donkey being loosed by the disciples toward the opposite village so that the Lord, sitting upon it, might release from bonds, irrationality, and sluggishness the beast-like men shown through it.

But camels are also in a human way men, who find it difficult to enter the kingdom of heaven, and they themselves are released by being freed from the harmful burdens of evil, which they happen to carry, according to the prophet Isaiah saying: 'There shields and flying aspides which carried upon donkeys and camels their wealth' (Isaiah 61:5). For it is clear that a shield or a lion has not possessed a perceptible wealth, but the evil powers, which are symbolically named shields and lions through tropology, have possessed that which is signified by tropology, which they do not deposit upon a rational animal or an ox capable of performing noble and useful work, but upon donkeys and camels, which happen to be crested and unclean. These therefore are led out from the master's hand by way of repentance, as it is said, with God presiding over this: for He does not desire the death of the sinner as His repentance (Ezekiel 18:23).

And God saw that it was good (Genesis 1:4). For it is good a transition from evil into virtue. And God has done these things, it must be said, training them so that the once wild beasts of ferocity might be transformed into gentleness. And just as, if I say that the potter makes the clay, I do not signify that he labors so that the clay might remain just as it is, but that, having taken the clay, an earthen vessel might become and no longer exist being broken, so did He make the beasts according to the allegory, not so that they might remain beasts, but so that they might be transformed from the ferocity of evil into the most gentle virtue. And since the characters of men are diverse, through the...

It is said in the plural, 'And God saw that it was good' (Gen 1:31). Since the character of men is signified through irrational animals, this is shown from the book of the Acts of the apostles, when certain foreigners came to the foremost of the apostles, calling him to preach the gospel to them, being foreigners. For when he had gone up to the rooftop to pray, there appeared a vessel like a veil set down with four corners from heaven to earth, in which were all the quadrupeds and the creeping things and the beasts of the earth, and a voice came from heaven to him saying, 'Rise, Peter, slaughter and eat' (Acts 10:13). But he said, 'By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean' (Acts 10:14). And a voice a second time came to him, saying, 'What God has cleansed, do not call common' (Acts 10:15). This is the vision of the animals appearing in the veil, which Peter himself explains when he came to those calling him, saying, 'God also showed me not to call any man common or unclean' (Acts 10:28), lifting up the appearing quadrupeds and beasts to men, having been cleansed by the casting away of impurity.

And this must be stated, that having said 'Bring it out,' he was not satisfied with the command but performed it; for God is not only inciting toward virtue but is already also joined together; for when the good is chosen by one, God also cooperates toward the good, so that, having resolved to obey the command, they may be able to bring the striving thing to its end. For even if someone uses a private impulse toward virtue, he happens to be aware of God, who grants the outcome and the good end of it. [Τὸν] κρυπτὸν οὖν τῆς 21 καρδίας ἄνθρωπον λέγει ὁ πρόκριτος 55 τῶν ἀποστόλων Πέτρος τὴν ψυχήν, καὶ Παῦλος ὁ μακά- ριος· "6Συνήδομαι γὰρ τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ κα<τὰ> τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον"6, του῀̣τ' ἔστιν κατὰ τὸν νοῦν, κατὰ τὴν ψυχήν. Οἱ δὲ μὴ βουλόμενοι ἕτερον εἶναι τὸ πνεῦμα παρὰ τὴν ψυχὴν λέγουσιν ὅτι τὴν γνώμην ση[μ]αίνει διὰ τοῦ πνεύμα- τος ἢ ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴν τὴν ψυχὴν τῇ προσηγορί[ᾳ] τοῦ 56 πνεύματος ἐδήλωσεν. Κατασκευαστικὸν δὲ τὸ ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος συνεστάναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον παράγουσιν τὸ ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ διαρρήδην λεγόμενον· "6Μὴ φοβεῖσθε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀποκτεννόντων τὸ σῶμα, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν μὴ δυνα- μένων ἀποκτεῖναι· φοβήθητε δὲ τὸν δυνάμενον καὶ ψυχὴν καὶ σῶμα ἀπολέσαι ἐν γεένν[ῃ]."6 Εἰ δὲ τὸ μὲν ἀποκτέν- νουσιν ἄνθρωποι, τὸ δὲ οὔ, δύο εἰσὶν τὸ σῶμα καὶ ἡ Ἐλέγομεν οὖν ἄνθρωπον καὶ τὸ σῶμα μόνον, ἀλλ' οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλ' ἔξω ἄνθρωπονμετὰ προσθήκης, καὶ μόνην τὴν ψυχὴν ἄνθρωπον οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, τὸν δὲ σύνθετον ἁπλῶς ἄνθρωπον μηδὲν προστιθέντες. Ζητείσθω οὖν ἐνταῦθα περὶ οὗ λέγεται πρὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων. "6Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοιώσιν ἡμετέραν."6 Οὐ κατὰ τὸν σύνθετον τοίνυν κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ ὁ ἄνθρωπος γέγονεν· οὐ γὰρ ἀνθρω- πόμορφος ὁ Θεός. english: [...of] the fish of the sea and the winged ones of the heaven and the beasts and all the earth and all the creeping things creeping upon the earth. And God made the man; according to the image of God He made him, male and female He made them. And God blessed them, saying: 'Increase and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and the winged ones of the heaven and all the beasts and all the earth and all the creeping things creeping upon the earth' (Gen 1:28).

The word 'man' signifies also the composite living thing which is composed of soul and body, and especially the soul. Therefore, the wise Peter the apostle calls the hidden part of the heart 'man', and the blessed Paul: 'For I consent according to the law of God according to the inner man' (Rom 7:22), that is, according to the mind, according to the soul. But when it is said: 'There was a certain man in the land of Assyria' (Gen 45:2), and: 'It happened when many men began to become' (Gen 6:9), it signifies the common [meaning]. If therefore we take the explicit [meaning], the composite man signifies the 'And God said: Let us make man' (Gen 1:26).

And not only regarding the composite, but even regarding the visible and perceptible, that is, the body, the blessed Paul intends to extend the name of man, saying: 'Even if our outward man is being destroyed, but the inward is being renewed day by day' (2 Cor 4:16). And according to a first imposition, each of us was composed of soul and body, but there are those who say that man is composed of three, of soul and body and spirit, which they construct by joining themselves to the apostolic saying which says: 'And the God of peace sanctify you completely, and your whole spirit and soul and body' (1 Thess 5:23), not following [the idea] that it must be said concerning the Holy Spirit in order to be whole, which is not even destined to come into weakness. Therefore, they produce another proof from a different saying having this: 'The Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit' (Rom 8:16); for they say our spirit is a different spirit from the Holy Spirit, being witnessed by the Holy Spirit when it is well. And that from Daniel: 'Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord' (Dan 4:35).

They think it is a mere assistant. But those who do not want there to be anything other than the spirit besides the soul say that it signifies the will through the spirit, or that he has shown even the soul by the designation of the spirit. But those renewing this argument say that, having used a connective conjunction, even in 'spirits and souls of the righteous' (cf. Heb 11:35), he shows the soul to be something other than the spirit.

And as a constructive argument for the composition of man from soul and body, they produce that which is said in the Gospel, broken out: 'Do not fear those who kill the body but are not able to kill the soul; but fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell' (Luke 12:4). And if it is the case that men kill one thing and not the other, then the body and the soul are two. We say, therefore, man and the body only, but not simply, but man with an addition; and the soul alone is man not simply, but man within; and the composite is man simply, without anything added.

Let it therefore be sought here concerning what is said regarding God of all things: 'Let us make man according to an image and in our likeness' (Gen 1:26). The man has not become according to an image of God in the composite sense; for God is not man-shaped. And the divine teaching confirms this; for it is said that God is spirit and light (1 John 1:5), and light and spirit do not have the form of man.

But the Scripture also discusses God having seven eyes, seeing all the earth (Rev 4:8), while man has two; so therefore the man will not be found to be according to the image of God in this way of our seeing. But these things we say not as if God has seven sensible eyes, but we are investigating how man is according to the image and likeness of God; for the Word has shown his perfect contemplative power through the seven, and through the virtues which the number seven has, as has already been foretold.

Again, God is said to have wings, just as the holy one says: 'In the shelter of your wings you will protect me' (Ps 17:8); but man is a wingless animal, and the wingless is not able to have the image and likeness of God, not through sensible things received by us, but through intuitions surpassing and carrying those who desire this upward. It must therefore be investigated how man is according to the image and likeness of God.

Ἑτέρως ἄρα δεῖ λαβεῖν τὸ κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν αὐτὸν γεγονέναι. Ἔστιν δὲ μάλιστα κατὰ προηγουμένην διάνοιαν ἐκλαβεῖν τὸ προκείμενον· προείρηται κυρίως ἄνθρωπος εἶναι ὁ νοῦς καὶ ἡ ψυχή· αὕτη μετέχουσα Θεοῦ ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς μετουσίας εἰκὼν αὐτοῦ γίνεται, καθὸ λέγομεν εἰκονίζ[ει]ν τὴν ἀρετὴν τὸν μετέχοντα αὐτῆς, ὅπερ ἐπιστάμεν[ος] καὶ ὁ ἐν Χριστῷ λαλῶν Παῦλός φησιν οἷς προτρέπεται κατὰ 58 Χριστὸν εἰκονισθῆναι· "6μέχρις οὗ μορφωθῇ Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν"6, διδάσκων ὅτι ἡ περὶ Χριστοῦ νόησις ἀληθὴς ἐγγινομένη ψυχῇ χαρακτηρίζει καὶ εἰκονίζει αὐτὴν κατ' αὐτόν. "6Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν"6· εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν ὁ Υἱὸς αὐτοῦ ὁ μονογενής· Παῦλος τοῦτο διδάσκει γράφων· "6Ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου"6, εἰκὼν δὲ οὐσιώδης καὶ ἀπαράλλακτος· "6Ὁ"6 γὰρ "6ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν Πατέρα."6 Ἐὰν οὖν εἴρηται πρὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ· "6Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν"6, οὐ δεῖ διαφόρους τὰς εἰκόνας λαμβάνειν· οὐ γὰρ ἄλλη Πατρὸς καὶ ἄλλη Υἱοῦ τυγχάνει· εἰ γὰρ ὁ ἑωρακὼς τὸν Υἱὸν εἶδεν καὶ τὸν Πατέρα καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ ὁ Υἱός ἐστιν κατὰ τὸν μακάριον Παῦλον, οὐ δεῖ ἑτέραν εἰκόνα ἐννοεῖν. Ὡσπεροῦν ἀρχὴ καὶ προοίμιον ὁμοιώσεως εἴη ἂν ἡ εἰκών. Πρῶτον οὖν δεῖ γενέσθαι αὐτὸν κατ' εἰκόνα, εἶτα καθ' ὁμοίωσιν, τὸ δὲ πρῶτον οὐ χρόνῳ δεῖ λαβεῖν καὶ μάλιστα ὅτε πρώτη ποίησις τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἦν, ἀλλὰ κατ' ἐπί- νοιαν. Καὶ ὅτι τοῦθ' οὕτως ἔχει, ἐπιφέρει τὸ συγγραφικὸν Πνεῦμα· "6Καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν"6. οὐκέτι προσθεὶς τὸ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν. Ὁ γὰρ ν[οῦς] προσελθὼν τῇ θεοσεβείᾳ τυποῦται μὲν κατὰ τὴν εἰκόνα τ[οῦ Θ]εοῦ, ὕστερον δὲ διὰ προκοπῆς τῆς 59 ἐπὶ τελειότητα καθ' ὁμοίωσιν Θεοῦ γίνεται ὅπερ <παρ>ι- στα`̣ς ὁ μακάριος Ἰωάννης φησίν· "6Ἀγαπητοί, νῦν τέκνα Θεοῦ ἐσμεν καὶ οὔπω ἐφανερώθη τί ἐσόμεθα· οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἐὰν φανερωθῇ ὅμοιοι αὐτῷ ἐσόμεθα."6 Ἤδη γὰρ κατ' εἰκόνα ὄντες ἐλπίζουσιν καθ' ὁμοίωσιν γενέσθαι. english: A man has become. For even the most wise Paul, using this name for man, says: 'For a man ought not to cover his head, being the image and glory of God' (1 Cor 11:7). It has been shown that being an image is not according to the composite; for the one is incorporeal and a spiritual essence, while the other is a body having been formed. Therefore, it is necessary in another way to take the image and the likeness to have become him.

For God, having made all things and being both ruler and leader of all—for as Creator he is thus both ruler and king—having made man so that he also rules over the beasts, cattle, and birds existing through him, shows that the man is an image according to his own ruling. That he has this in such a way is to be learned from the apostolic word: 'But I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man, and the man is the head of the woman' (1 Cor 11:3). Just as the man is ruled by Christ, so the woman is ruled by the man, having him as head.

For according to analogy, the likeness is to be taken, which does not have likeness in the same matters, as we say that the one who has a reason for a physician to produce health, the builder has a reason for constructing a house; for each is a maker of a certain work. Since therefore the man, having become a rational being, imitates God according to his ruling over the things subject to him, by this he is able to be according to the image and likeness of God.

But it is especially possible according to a previously mentioned thought to grasp what is set forth; it has been previously stated that the mind and the soul are man; this, participating in God through His communion, becomes His image, just as we say that the one participating in virtue images it, which even Paul, speaking in Christ, knows and exhorts to be imaged according to Christ: 'until Christ is formed in you' (Gal 4:19), teaching that the thought concerning Christ, being a true soul approaching, characterizes and images it according to Him. 'Let us make man according to our image and likeness' (Gen 1:26); the Son, His only-begotten, is the image of God. Paul teaches this, writing: 'Who is the image of the invisible God' (Col 1:15), an image substantial and unchangeable; 'for He' 'who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). If it is therefore said concerning God: 'Let...'

Let us make man in our image and likeness; we must not take different images, for there is not one image of the Father and another of the Son. For if he who has seen the Son has seen the Father, and the Son is the character of the subsistence of God according to the blessed Paul, we must not conceive of another image. For nothing of the created things images or characterizes God according to essence. Therefore it is not said: 'Let us make man an image,' but 'according to an image,' which means to be imaged from that image and to imitate it; for man was constructed to be capable of the image.

And it is necessary to understand that there are two things which God says he is making when saying: 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' (Gen 1:26); for I think that the surpassing similarity shows an unchangeable likeness, such that the likeness is an image beyond measure, but not necessarily the image being so precise as to have an unchangeable likeness. Nevertheless, the image would be the beginning and the prelude to the likeness. Therefore, first it is necessary to become according to an image, then according to a likeness; and the first must not be taken by time, especially since it was the first creation of man, but by intention. And that it is so, the written Spirit shows: 'And God made man, in the image of God He made him' (Gen 1:27), without adding 'according to a likeness.'

For the mind, having approached godliness, is first stamped according to the image of God, but later, through progress toward perfection, it becomes according to the likeness of God, as the blessed John says: 'Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be; we know that when He is revealed, we shall be like Him' (1 John 3:2). For already being according to an image, they hope to become according to a likeness. That this thought is strong, Paul also testifies, exhorting someone to make progress in virtue, saying: 'That you may become according to the image of the Creator,' even though they already are so according to the word of essence. What he therefore says is this: that every man, insofar as he is a creation of God, being receptive of the Word, exists according to an image, being capable, as we have said, of the image and having an aptitude for participation in it; if, however, he should receive this according to energy, just as the man created from the beginning [was].

source_text: ἔχει ἤδη ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἐνεργοῦν τὸ κατ' εἰκόνα. Καὶ ἔστω ἐπὶ παρα- δείγματος σαφὲς τὸ λεγόμενον. Ὁ ἄνθρωπος λογικός ἐστιν· καὶ αὕτη ἡ οὐσιώδης ἐπιτηδειότης ὑπάρχει καὶ τῷ βρέφει, τὸ δὲ λογικὸν οὔ· ἔχει οὖν καὶ τὸ βρέφος ταύτην τὴν δύναμιν· συμπληρωθέντος γοῦν τοῦ λόγου ἐπιδείκνυται ταῦτα, ἐὰν πρὸς παίδευσιν ῥέψῃ. Οὕτω καὶ τὸ κατ' εἰκόνα, ἕως μὲν οὐκ ἐπιχώννυται, φέρει τῆς πρώτης δημιουργίας τὴν ἀξίαν, ἐπὰν δὲ προσχωσθῇ κακία καὶ μοχθηρία, δεῖ δέξασθαι τὸ σάρον κατὰ τὰ ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ εἰρημένα, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ὁ τῆς μετανοίας λόγος, ἵν' ἀναπτύ- ξαντες τὴν ἐπικειμένην ἀχλὺν τοὺς τύπους τῆς εἰκόνος φανερώσωμ[εν]. Τὸ δὲ "6καὶ ἀρχέτωσαν τῶν ἰχθύων τῆς θαλάσσης καὶ τῶν πετεινῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ τῶν κτηνῶν καὶ πάσης τῆς γῆς [κα]ὶ πάντων τῶν ἑρπετῶν τῶν ἑρπόντων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"6 κατὰ [τὴν] προτέραν διήγησιν ἐμφαίνοι ἂν 60 τὸ ἀρχικὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατὰ τῶν ὑποτεταγμένων αὐτῷ ζῴων. Θαυμάσαι γὰρ ἄν τις πῶς τὰ πάνυ ὑπὲρ τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ τυγχάνοντα καὶ ἄγρια ἅμα καὶ βλάπτειν πεφυκότα καὶ προσέτι ὑπερμεγέθη πάγαις τισὶν καὶ δικτύοις ἀγρεύει· οὐκ ἂν δὲ τοῦτο οὕτως ἐγίνετο, εἰ μὴ ἀρχὴν κατ' αὐτῶν εἶχεν θεόθεν. Ἔσθ' ὅτε γὰρ καὶ ὑπὸ κομιδῇ παιδίου ἢ ἄλλως ἀνθρώπου ἀσθενοῦς ἀγέλαι πολυπληθεῖς διαφόρων ζῴων ἐλαύνονται, ὅπερ σαφῶς ἐπιδείκνυσιν θείαν τινὰ δύναμιν ἐνεῖναι τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ, καθ' ἣν αὐτῷ ταῦτα ὑποτέτακται. Ἀρχὴ δὲ οὐδὲν ἕτερόν ἐστι ἢ νόμιμος ἐπι- στασία. Οὐδὲν γοῦν τῶν ἄλλων ἄρχει τοῦ ὁμογενοῦς· κἄν ποτε δὲ ὁ καλούμενος κτίλος πρόβατον ἐξάρχῃ ἀγέλης κατὰ τὸ προηγεῖσθαι, οὐ λογισμῷ κατὰ τοῦς ποιμένας ἀνθρώπους, φύσει δὲ τοῦτο δρᾷ. Γέγονεν δὲ ἄνθρωπος κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν Θεοῦ, ἵνα ἄρχῃ τῶν εἰρημένων. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ καὶ κατ' ἄλλην διάνοιαν τὸν νοῦν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου λέγομεν εἶναι ἄνθρωπον, κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν Θεοῦ προσταχθέντα γενέσθαι, καταλλήλως λαμβάνομεν αὐτὸν ἄρχειν θηρίων ἐκείνων περὶ [ὧν] εὐχὴν ἀναπέμπων φησὶν ὁ ἅγιος· "6Μὴ παραδῷς τοῖς θηρίο[ις] ψυχὴν ἐξομο- λογουμένην σοι"6, ἅπερ εἶεν αἱ ἀντικείμεναι ἐ[νέρ]γειαι, ὧν ἔξω γενέσθαι τὴν ἐξομολογουμένην ψυχὴν εὔχεται, ἢ λογισμοὶ πονηροὶ παρ' αὐτῶν ὑποβαλλόμενοι. Πάλιν τῷ Ἰὼβ λέγεται· "6Ἰδοὺ θηρία παρὰ σοὶ χόρτον ἴσα βουσὶν ἐσθίει"6, οὐχ ὅτι τὰ κατὰ τὸ πρόχειρον θηρία παρὰ τῷ Ἰὼβ ἐξήλλακται τὴν φύσιν, ἀλλ' ὅτι τὸ ἀτίθασον τῶν ἐναντίων δυνάμεων ἐξημεροῦτο μὴ σθένον πρὸς τὸ μέγεθος τῆς ἀρετῆς τοῦ ἁγίου. Καὶ πολλὰ ἔστιν εὑρεῖν ἐν τῇ γραφ[ῇ] ζῷα μυστικῶς ἀναγόμενα. Καὶ γὰρ ἰχθύες εἰσὶν συμβο- λικῶς καλούμενοί τινες ἐν ἀνθρώποις, οὓς ἑλκεῖ ἡ βληθεῖσα βασιλεία τῶ[ν οὐρα]νῶν εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν. Ἀπὸ γὰρ παντὸς γένους, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἀ[πὸ] παντὸς ἤθους ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἔθνους ἄγει τὸ κήρυγμα τοῦ λόγου. Ἄρχει οὖν καὶ τῶν 61 ἰχθύων τούτων. Καὶ πετεινὰ δέ εἰσιν νοητά, τὰ μὲν ψεγόμενα, τὰ δὲ ἐπαινούμενα· "6Νεοσσοί"6 φησιν "6γυπῶν τὰ ὑψηλὰ πέτοντα"6, καὶ περὶ τοῦ καταλαλοῦντος πατρὸς ἢ μητρὸς εἴρηται· "6Ἐκκόψαισαν αὐτὸν κόρακες ἐκ τῶν φαράγγων καὶ καταφάγοισαν αὐτὸν νεοσσοὶ ἀετῶν"6, ἅπερ ἐπὶ ἱστορίας οὐκ ἂν εἴη, ἐπὶ παντὸς τόπου δυνατοῦ ὄντος εὑρίσκεσθαι κακολογοῦντα τοὺς γονεῖς, κοράκων πανταχόσε μὴ εὑρισκομένων· ἀλλὰ δῆλον ὡς τούτῳ τῷ σφάλματι ἐνεχόμενος ὑπὸ σκοτίων ἐνεργειῶν τρόπον τινὰ δαμάζεται καὶ κατεσθίεται, αἵτινες ταπειναὶ τυγχάνουσιν, φάραγξιν ἐνδιατρίβειν εἰωθυῖαι. Καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὁ φιλόκαλος εὑρήσει καὶ 24 ἐπαινετῶς καὶ ψεκτῶς ζῷα λαμβανόμενα. Ἄρχειν οὖν ὁ ἄνθρωπος τούτων ἁπάντων τέθειται, κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ γεγονώς. Οἱ ἀπόστολοι εἰς ταύτην τὴν κατάστασιν ἐληλυθότ[ε]ς ὥστε κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν Θεοῦ εἶναι ἦρχον τῶν ἰχθύων τ[ῆ]ς νοητῆς θαλάσσης, ἁλεεῖς ὑπὸ Χριστοῦ γεγενημένοι εἰπόντος πρὸς αὐτούς· "6∆εῦτε ὀπίσω μου, καὶ ποιήσω ὑμᾶς ἁλεεῖς ἀνθρώπων"6, ὡς καὶ τῷ Πέτρῳ· "6Ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν ἀνθρώπους ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν"6, τοὺς ἐν τῇ εἰρημένῃ δηλονότι θαλάσσῃ ἐννη- χομένους. Ὅτι δὲ καὶ θηρίων ἄρχοντες ἦσαν, ἐξουσίαν εἰλήφασιν πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἐχθροῦ. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ψαλμῷ δείκνυται ὡς παρὰ Θεοῦ ἐξουσία τῷ δικαίῳ κατὰ τῶν τοιούτων δέδοται, λέγοντος τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος πρὸς τὸν ἐνάρετον· "6Ἐπ' ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήσῃ καὶ καταπατήσεις λέοντα καὶ δράκοντα."6 ∆έδωκεν δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ τῶν πετεινῶ[ν] ἐξουσίαν τῶν ἁρπαζόντων τὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου πεμπόμενον
english: The image-nature is already active within him. Let the saying be clear by way of an example. Man is a rational being; and this essential capacity exists also in the infant, though the rationality does not. Thus the infant also has this power; for when the logos is fulfilled, these things are demonstrated, if he responds to instruction.

So also the image, until it is encroached upon, maintains the value of the first creation; but when evil and hardship are attached, it is necessary to receive the flesh according to what has been said in the Gospel, which is the word of repentance, so that having developed the lying-in-waitness lying upon him, we might make manifest the forms of the image.

And 'and let them rule the fish of the sea and the birds of the heaven and the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth' (Genesis 1:26), according to the previous discourse, would show the beginning [dominion] of man over the animals subjected to him. For one would marvel how all things, being beyond his power and being wild and having a nature to harm, are simultaneously caught by great fires and nets; yet this would not happen in this way, unless he had a beginning [dominion] over them from God. For even when large herds of various animals are driven by the gathering of a child or otherwise by a weak man, they clearly demonstrate that there must be a divine power in the rational animal, by which these things are subjected to him. And a beginning [dominion] is nothing other than a lawful standing. Nothing of the others rules the same-kind; and even if the so-called firstling of a flock is a sheep, it begins the herds according to the preceding way, not by reasoning according to men the shepherds, but it does this by nature. And man became according to the image and likeness of God, in order to rule the things mentioned.

And since we say that the mind of man is man according to another understanding, having been commanded to become according to the image and likeness of God, we appropriately receive that he rules those beasts about which the saint says he sends up a prayer, 'Do not deliver to the beasts a soul confessing to you' (Psalm 22:20), which were the opposing energies, outside of which he prays for the confessing soul to be, or evil thoughts being subjected by them. Again, to the I...

Regarding Job, it is said: 'Behold, beasts eat grass beside you like oxen' (Job 1:24), not that the immediate beasts were driven wild in nature by Job, but that the disorder of opposing powers was being made manifest because they lacked strength against the greatness of the saint's virtue. And many things are found in the Scripture where animals are mystically led.

For indeed, some are called fishes symbolically among men, whom the cast kingdom of the heavens draws into the sea. For from every kind, that is, from every character of men and nation, the proclamation of the Word draws. So it begins also with these fishes. And the winged ones are intellectual, some being slandered and others praised: 'Young vultures flying on high' is said, and concerning a father or mother being spoken ill of, it has been said: 'Ravens tore him from the cliffs and young eagles devoured him' (1 Kings 19:4), which would not be according to history, since slandering parents is found everywhere, while ravens are not found everywhere; but it is clear that, being held by this error under dark energies, he is in some way subdued and devoured, those which, being lowly, are accustomed to wear away a crevice.

And regarding the others, the lover of beauty will find animals taken both praiseworthily and slanderously. Thus the man has been set as ruler over all these, having been born in the image of God. The apostles, having come to this state so that they might be like God according to the image, were the rulers of the fishes of the intellectual sea, having become fishermen by Christ saying to them: 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men' (Matthew 4:19), as also to Peter: 'From now on you will be catching men' (Luke 5:10), those dwelling in the aforementioned sea.

And because they were also rulers of beasts, they received authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. But it is also shown in the Psalm how authority is given by God to the righteous against such things, the Holy Spirit saying to the virtuous one: 'He shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk; he shall trample the lion and the dragon' (Psalm 91:13). And He gave them also authority over the winged ones who snatch up the one being sent by the Word.

source_text: σπόρον, ἵνα θηρεύοντες αὐτὰ πόρρω αὐτοὺς ἀποπέμπωσιν, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τῶν κτηνωδεστέρων ἀνθρώπων, περὶ ὧν εἴρηται· "6Μὴ γίνεσθε [ὡ]ς ἵππος καὶ ἡμίονος, οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν σύνεσις"6, καί· "6Ἵπποι θηλυμαν[εῖ]ς ἐγενήθητε."6 Ἄρχουσι δὲ τούτων ἁπάντων 62 οἱ ἅγιοι μετατιθέντες αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν χειρόνων ἐπὶ κρείτ- τονα διὰ τοῦ λόγου. Ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἑρπετῶν ἐξουσίαν εἴληφεν ἄνθρωπος, ἅπερ εἰς τὰς ἡδονὰς καὶ τ[ὰ] πάθη ἀναφέρων οὐκ ἂν ἁμάρτοις, ἀπεχόμενος τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν ἐν τῷ κατεξανίστασθαι αὐτῶν καὶ νεκροῦν "6τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, πορνείαν, ἀκαθαρσίαν, πάθος, ἐπιθυμίαν, κακήν"6. Καλῶς δὲ κατὰ τῆς ἀνταποδόσεως ἔχει λεγούσης· "6Καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν."6 Τῆς γὰρ προστάξεως περιεχούσης, πρὸς τῷ "6κατ' εἰκόνα"6, "6καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν"6 αὐτὸν γενέσθαι, ἡ ἀνταπόδοσίς φησιν ὅτι "6κατ' εἰκόνα ἐποίησεν αὐτόν"6, οὐ προσθεῖσα τὸ "6καθ' ὁμοίωσιν"6, περὶ οὗ ἐν τοῖς ὀλίγῳ πρότερον διειλήφαμεν. Τὸ δὲ "6ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐ[τ]οὺς"6 ἐξεταστέον, πῶς, περὶ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου προστάξαντος τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἡ ἀνταπόδοσις λέγει· "6Ἐποίησεν αὐτούς."6 Καὶ εἴη ἂν κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν ἀπόδειξις αὕτη τοῦ ὁμοούσιον εἶναι τὴν γυναῖκα τῷ ἀνδρί, ὑπὸ ἓν εἶδος αὐτῶν ταττομένων καὶ διὰ τοῦτο εἰρημένου τοῦ "6ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον"6· τὸ δὲ "6ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ"6 παραστατικὸν τῶν τμημάτων <ὧν> τῆς διαδοχῆς ἕνεκεν ὁ Θεὸς ᾠκονόμησεν, ἐμφαῖνον ἅμα ὡς καὶ ἡ γυνὴ "6κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ"6 ἐστιν, τῶν αὐτῶν δεκτικοὶ ἀμφότεροι, μιμήσεώς τε τῆς πρὸς Θεὸν καὶ τῆς τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος μετουσίας καὶ ἀναλήμψεως ἀρετῆς. Καὶ ἐπεὶ ἐλέγομεν δηλοῦσθαι τὴν ἀνθρώπου π[ρο]σηγο- ρίαν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ νοῦ καὶ ψυχῆς, νοήσομεν κατ' ἀναγωγὴν οὕτω τὸ "6ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ"6, ὡς ὁ μὲν δυνάμενος διδα- σκ[α]λικὸς εἶναι, ὡς τὸν τοῦ λόγου σπόρον εἰσ̣ι̣έναι ταῖς παραδέξ[ασ]θαι δυναμέναις ψυχαῖς, οὕτως ἂν ἄρρην εἴη, 63 ἐκείνων συμβ[ολι]κῶς τὸν θήλεος ἐπεχόντων τόπον τῶν ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν μὲν τίκτειν οὐδὲν δυναμένων, τὰς δὲ παρ' ἑτέρων παιδεύσεις δεχομένων δίκην σπόρου. Καὶ ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ αἰσθητοῦ παρὰ Θεοῦ τὸ θῆλυ καὶ τὸ ἄρρεν γίνεται, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ νοητοῦ ἑαυτῷ τις καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἰδίας προαιρέσεως ἢ διδασκάλου χώραν ἐπέχει, ὅς ἐστιν ἄρρην καὶ τῶν ἀγαθῶν σπορεύς, ἢ μαθητὴς τὸν ἑτέρου σπόρον δεχόμενος καὶ θῆλυ κατὰ τοῦτο τυγχάνων. Καὶ οὕτω μὲν ἄν τις νοήσαι τὰ μείζονα πρὸς τὰ ὑποδεέστερα τῶν λογικῶν δεχόμενος. Εἰ δὲ ὡς πρὸς τὸν Λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ τις ἐκλαβεῖν βούλοιτο, πᾶσα ἡ λογικὴ φύσις θήλεος πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔχοι τάξιν. Νυμφίος ἐστὶν οὗτος τῆς λογικῆς οὐσίας· "6<Ὁ> ἔχων"6 γὰρ "6τὴν νύμφην νυμφί[ος ἐσ]τίν."6 Καὶ ἐν τῷ Ἄισματι δὲ τῶν ᾀσμάτων καὶ ἐπιθαλάμι[ος] ὕμνος ᾄδεται νύμφης πρὸς νυμφίον, τῆς ἐκκλησίας ν[ύ]μφης νοουμένης ἢ τῆς τελείας ψυχῆς τῆς ἤδη δυναμέ[νη]ς ἁρμοσθῆναι τῷ Λόγῳ, ὅστις σπορεὺς ὑπάρχει πάσης λογ[ι]κῆς οὐσίας, ταύτης δεχομένης τὴν παρ' αὐτοῦ 25 ὠφελίαν ἔν τε ἠθικοῖς καὶ τοῖς τῆς ἀληθείας δόγμασιν. Καὶ ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἐξαλλαγὴν γενέσθαι τῆς φύσεως ἀδύνατον, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν νοητῶν ὁ νῦν μαθήματα δεχόμενος καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐν τάξει θήλεος ὑπάρχων εἴη ἄν ποτε ἐκ προκοπῆς ἀνὴρ ὡς ἄλλων γενέσθαι διδάσκαλος, ὡς καὶ ἀνάπαλιν ἐκ ῥᾳθυμίας ἀποβαλεῖν τις δύναται τὸ διδάσκαλος εἶναι ὥστε μάλα μόγις δύνασθαι δέξασθαι παρ' ἄλλου ἃ αὐτὸς πρότερον τοὺς [ἄλλο]υς ἐπαίδευεν. Καὶ εἴη ἂν μαρτύ- ριον τῶν δεχομένων τὰς τοῦ Λόγου σπορὰς τὸ "6ἀπὸ τοῦ φόβου σου ἐν γαστρὶ ἐλάβο<με>ν καὶ ὠδινήσαμεν καὶ ἐτέκομεν πνεῦμα σωτηρίας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"6. ῾Ο̣ φόβος δὲ τὴν [ἁγί]αν ἐργάζεται σύλληψιν περὶ Θεοῦ· εἴρηται· "6Ὁ φόβος Κυρίου ἁγν[ός], διαμένων εἰς αἰῶνα αἰῶνος"6, 64 καί· "6Φόβος Κυρίου πάντα ὑπερέβαλεν"6, ὅντινα ἔχων τις καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ προκόπτων ὡς καὶ ἀνὴρ γενέσθαι γυναικὸς νοητῆς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο
english: A seed, so that having nourished them they might send them far away, and also of the most beast-like men, concerning whom it has been said: 'Become not like the horse and the mule, to whom there is no understanding' (Psalm 32:9), and: 'You have become female horses.' But the holy ones begin all these things, having transferred them from the hands to better things through the Word. But man has also received authority over the creeping things, which, when he carries them toward pleasures and passions, he would not sin, by abstaining from fleshly desires in the overcoming of them and killing 'the members upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, passion, desire, evil' (Colossians 3:5).

And rightly, according to the reciprocity, it is said: 'And God made the man, according to the image of God He made him' (Genesis 1:27). For the command containing, at the 'according to the image,' the making of him 'also according to likeness,' the reciprocity says that 'according to the image He made him,' without adding the 'according to likeness,' concerning which we discussed briefly before. And the 'male and female He made them' (Genesis 1:27) is to be examined: how, concerning one man commanded by God, the reciprocity says: 'He made them.' And this might be a demonstration according to the literal sense of the woman being consubstantial with the man, being categorized under one kind of them, and because of this the saying 'let us make man' (Genesis 1:26) was uttered; but the 'male and female' is a representation of the parts for the sake of the succession which God established, showing at once also that the woman is 'according to the image of God' (Genesis 1:27), both of them being recipients of the same, both of the imitation and of the participation in God and the taking up of virtue of the Holy Spirit.

And since we were saying that the approach of man is made manifest also in the intellect and soul, let us consider by anagogical ascent thus the 'male and female': just as the one, being able to be a capable teacher, as being able to receive the seed of the Word into the souls capable of receiving it, so if he were male,

They symbolically possess the place of the female, being unable to conceive anything of their own, but receiving instruction from others like the manner of sowing. In the sensible realm, the female and male are made by God; but in the intelligible realm, one possesses a place for himself through his own choice or a teacher, who is male and a sower of good things, or a disciple receiving the seed of another and thus becoming female.

Thus anyone might perceive the greater things through the lesser of the rational. If one wished to take it regarding the Word of God, every rational nature would have a female rank toward Him. This is a bridegroom of the rational essence; for 'he who has' is 'the bridegroom of the bride' (Song of Solomon 2:16). And in the Song of Songs, a bridal song is sung of a bride to a bridegroom, the church being understood as the bride, or the perfect soul already able to be joined to the Word, who is the sower of every rational essence, this essence receiving the benefit from Him both in moral and in the doctrines of truth.

Regarding the sensible, a change of nature is impossible; but regarding the intelligible, a man currently receiving lessons and therefore being in a female rank might at any time, through progress, become as others become a teacher, just as one might again, from sloth, fall away so that he is barely able to receive from another what he himself formerly instructed others. And a testimony of those receiving the seeds of the Word would be, 'From the fear of you we conceived in the womb and labored and brought forth a spirit of salvation upon the earth.' For fear works a holy apprehension concerning God; it has been said: 'The fear of the Lord is pure, remaining for an age of ages' (Psalm 111:10), and: 'The fear of the Lord surpassed all things' (Psalm 111:10), so that whoever possesses it and progresses in it, as a man becomes a rational woman and because of this...

english: To be called blessed, as the Psalmist says: 'Blessed are you, and good shall it be to you; your wife as a vine growing straight in the trellises of your house, your sons as young olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall be blessed the man who fears the Lord' (Psalm 128:1-4). This, according to history, is not without contradiction, for many who feared God remained childless, or remained so until old age, according to Abraham and the father of John, Zechariah. Therefore, what he says is this: the opinion and the faith which the blessed one received, a wife is living with him, able to give birth to works, words, and divine thoughts. For it is said: 'Wisdom gives understanding to a man' (Proverbs 8:22), and the wise man says concerning her: 'I became a lover of her beauty' (Proverbs 8:35), making the wisdom evident, and 'I led her to a union with myself' (Proverbs 8:26).

The one fearing the Lord therefore has this wisdom living with him, the faith, the virtue, from which he produces nothing female but all male; for he does not produce an action recognized as [weak/effeminate] or a shallow or reproached thought, but all things well-proportioned and strong. For it says, 'Your sons' (Psalm 128:3) 'as young olive shoots' (Psalm 128:3), which brings forth oil, the nourisher of light and the reliever of labors. For the spiritual person always progressing has an action like oil, poured out upon his own light, which also contributes to manliness and to the struggles against the opposing energy.

'Male' (Genesis 1:27) therefore 'and female' (Genesis 1:27), taking according to the aforementioned understanding, [is] the one teaching [things] male, and the one receiving from a teacher or from the Word [of God], conceiving them and shaping them and bringing them to completion as female, giving birth to the divine virtues, from which he also shall be led to a perfect man. And God blessed them, saying: 'Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and rule over it, and rule the fish of the sea and the birds of the heaven and all the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth' (Genesis 1:28). And God said: 'Behold, I have given you every herb-bearing seed-bearing plant upon all the earth, and every tree which has in itself the fruit of a seed-bearing plant shall be for your food and for all the beasts of the earth and for all the birds of the heaven' (Genesis 1:29-30).

english: It was said previously regarding certain cages, machines, and hooks for men. These things happen such that even the most fearsome, like the lion and the leopard, whose nature is most wild, are often subjected to the hand of man. And thus the rule over them exists, God having provided this to them.

But it is necessary to know that the manner of rule exists in different ways. One rule is a legal supervision of both the ruler and the ruled; for the law gives authority and rule to the ruler and to the subject, so that in the same way the ruler rules and the subject is subjected, the law directing that it should be done thus. Otherwise, a teacher rules over students, and differently, a master over slaves, and a general over an army. Thus, man rules over irrational animals in different ways, as has been said: in some ways as domestic, in others according to their wild nature; for not all are edible, but some are already for medicinal use and for another contributing need, which the physiologist will find.

Furthermore, to these belongs the [word]: 'And God said, Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant spreading seed, which is upon the face of all the earth' (Gen 1:29). For God gave authority and knowledge, so that man might know which of those upon the earth is useful for food, and which for medicine, and which for another need. But there is a different nature to these: some are trees, some are vegetables, and some are grasses, and above all, some are edible and some are good for another use.

The need of these should not be ignored according to the command before this—when God said, 'Let the earth sprout herb-bearing seed-bearing plant according to its kind' (Gen 1:11), He adds, 'and a fruitful tree producing fruit' (Gen 1:12), because the trees differ from the herb, calling them 'fruitful trees'—not only does man exercise authority over those resulting from agriculture, but also over their materials which he neither sows nor cultivates, as he has different needs from these; for He does not make these things portable throughout the inhabited places, but it is evident that for the necessity of men, every plant has become a sprout; for all things are made for their use.

The providential character of God over all things is signaled by His declaration: "It shall be for food to you, and to all the beasts of the earth, and to all the fowls of the heaven" (Genesis 9:3). For it is fitting that He who cares for men should also provide for the animals that have become necessary and useful to them, and for other things useful to them; for indeed, not according to the prior logic of irrational things, but indeed through man, He has fashioned His providence. God saw all things again to be good, for they bring forth [fruit]: "And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Before this, however, the word had praised each of the things coming into being by saying, "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:25, 1:31) or "good"; but now it is stated with certainty, "very good," because of the harmony and concord of all things.

Let what is said be clear through an example. One who wishes to assemble a dance selects the best dancers for each part, so that nothing is lacking for their specific task; if, moreover, these are brought together for that which has prepared them, he will find the work resulting from their concord to be exceedingly and superlatively beautiful, which is not possible to result from a single person alone. One might also find this in a military camp: for it is necessary that there be a best spearman, a best archer, a best general, and a best counselor, so that when the time comes, the work of all being joined together may show the magnitude of praise, being referred to a single purpose. The word teaches that all things are "very good" (Genesis 1:31) by showing their interconnectedness, their proportion, their harmony, and their ordered state, and even the unshakable stability of opposites; which, as was said before, is not perceived by the senses, but is judged by the Word. But also the one who leads those being driven out into daylight demonstrates the greatness of the rule. And the one who, lifting up his own movements according to the mind and marveling at them in thought, overcomes the struggles, demonstrates the rule given by God, ruling 'and all the earth' (Ps 89:11), which is all the bodily passions, dead 'the members upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire' (Rom 8:13), speaking of those that creep.

english: It has been completed, rather than being filled; it lies there. For it is not their existence that has been completed, but their making, just as we say also concerning the poetic arts, which bring the end through their activities, saying that the ship or the house has been completed.

Thus the heaven has been completed, having received its proper harmony, which received its fullness from both the firmament and the luminaries and also from the stars, and the earth from both the animals and the various plants. And when each of them had become, the 'has been completed' did not fit; but now, having received the concord and the harmony of all things, the 'The heaven and the earth and all their world were completed' follows.

And it is said that the world of the earth and its fullness according to what is said: 'The earth is the Lord's and its fullness' (Ps 24:1). Because even the variety of the heaven is called a world, Moses himself says concerning them in his words: 'Not looking up to the heaven and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, all the world of the heaven, being led astray, you shall worship them' (Deut 4:19), who through the position which was set by God, demonstrate beauty, some by moving in these circulations, others to be with these, some making their motion in a straight line, and others in an arc.

An army of heaven, therefore, because of the arrangement, has been said according to what has been said: 'Whose hands made all the host of heaven' (Job 38:7). Concerning which, those who have not understood well have erred, introducing fate and setting all things by necessity, defining the stars to be determining the poetic lives of men and the things happening to others, who, for a sign, if not for the doing, have been set according to also... concerning those having happened on the fourth day, we demonstrated the 'Let them be for signs and for seasons and for months and for years' (Gen 1:14), setting forth as if human life has not been compelled by the stars. For those escaping life through war and universal accidents are not under one formation. And moreover, the argument of fate is more strongly overturned.

From the laws: all Jews, having reached the eighth day from birth, are circumcised, and they receive the trial of iron even from the sprouts [infants], and no one could say how all at once they cast [the foreskin] off within a single hour, almost everywhere on earth and every day as Jews are born; but they say that even certain Ethiopians have the membranes of the genitals removed at the same time as birth, and even these do not all have their birth at once; and altogether the various customs and laws according to the nations negate fate. If this does not fit according to fate, much more do the things of choice. For if fate leads the happening by necessity, and choice has power over the possible things, fate will not be about these things. For virtue and vice have benefited or harmed the one possessing them, and each of those doing [actions] is blamed because of the bad habits, or praised for acting rightly; but the things happening by necessity [omitted]... no one accepts or blames the one doing something by necessity. Furthermore, if the laws are from fate, and those not obeying these are not from fate, it seems to negate and overturn fate itself. Significant, then, are the stars, not as makers, but signifying the weather or pestilential occurrences or something else that seems to the one foreseeing, and these things are about this.

Let us return to the thing set forth from the beginning: 'And God finished on the sixth day his works, which he made' (Gen 2:2), which indicates as if the completion is about the only ones which he has made. For there are works which have not yet happened, which were foretold as being to come, such as the resurrection of the dead and entirely those things which are to be according to providence, which happen in their own sequence from God. So the addition 'of the works which he made' is appropriately placed. It is also necessary to contemplate this, that God did not 'rest' (Gen 2:2) in the seventh without having acted, for already all things were completed; but he 'blessed' (Gen 2:3) only the seventh day and sanctified it, and the saying leads to this: 'That in it he rested from all his works, which God began to make' (Gen 2:2). 'Which he began'—for it is not the beginning of all the works...

english: During one of the six days, angels and archangels and all the spiritual essence did not receive a beginning. And because this is so, God himself says in Job: 'When the stars were created, all my angels shouted to me with a great voice' (Job 38:7). Therefore, having been created. Because of this, the saying is confirmed, saying: 'If the spirit of the ruler rises upon you, do not leave your place' (Luke 10:19). For this pretext becomes the cause of many evils, with the devil having cast down something even greater, which now works by introducing a slander against God, as if because of the command not to take hold of only the known good and evil, but also to prevent them from becoming gods, as if he saw them about to become gods.

Indeed, from this deception, the whole heresy called Ophite was established, which exalts the serpent greatly concerning him, as they think, saying: in whom, they say, God intended man to be in wickedness, calling wickedness to be the not-knowing of good and evil; thus they say this craftily: He, they say, made man in good things; and they mythologize other things about the serpent, slandering him whom they have raised up as a god to themselves. However, the serpent performs his deception well, persuading them only to have an opening not for good, just as the apostle said: 'I wish you to be wise unto good, blameless unto evil' (Romans 16:19).

But the serpent, wanting them to be wise unto evil, wished to open those eyes running toward this, who, while virtue is at work, are not opened but happen to be closed, remaining blind, which Jesus says he works in the Gospel, saying: 'I came that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind' (John 9:39). But Jesus, according to history, has made no one blind, but has granted sight to the blind. It is therefore evident that he makes those who see badly blind, and makes those who are useful to see again with the useful eyes, who, being the inner man, saving the ability to see clearly not sensually but intellectually, before knowing and imposing reason upon the sense, they hide...

Regarding what was said in the 82nd [section]: 'The wise will hide perception.' And so that what is said may become clear through an example: perception is the tactile sense of hot and cold, hard and soft, rough and smooth; and to the irrational and the child, these things are manifest through touch. But when the physician comes to feel the pulse, he hides the perception, providing a reason through the movement of the throbbing vessels. In the same way, the laypeople perceive images by sense alone, but the scribes contemplate them with the logic of the eye.

Thus the man, before the transgression, was looking at things with a mind that was scientifically applying understanding to things, as is necessary. As long as he had these eyes directing themselves toward appropriate spectacles, he did not know evil; instead of testing it, he did not accept it. But when these eyes grew dim, and those leaning toward evil were opened, then he also became cast out.

The devil, having this will, seeks to make the woman wise, introducing envy to conceive of God, and promising great things, so that by these things he might entice, saying: 'You shall become like gods, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:5), while also subverting her intention with more views, lest the idolatry through images be joined, all while flattering the angels who are with him.

3, 6–7. And she saw that the tree was good for food and that it was pleasing to the eyes and beautiful for understanding, and having taken of its fruit she ate, and she gave also to her husband with her, and they ate, and the eyes of the two were opened and they knew that they were naked. Holding fast to the deception of the serpent, she made for him a trial that was the opposite of it; for that which lies out for food is not tested by sight, except that once the deception has begun, it works a certain pleasure and enjoyment, even if it thus rouses the deceived to action.

After having perceived according to the deceptions of the serpent spoken of, she took it through consent and ate, performing the act of a finished work, and she receives the man as a partner, doing and distributing the things toward deception; for such is perception, of which we thought the woman possessed a reason.

english: Once the eyes were opened, they knew that they were naked (Gen 2:25). For this happens to those being deceived. For after the activity of their wickedness is made manifest, they come to realize that they were stripped of virtue; this is granted again by the pitiless God, so that he who works wickedness might not remain entirely insensate and stay completely outside of virtue.

This is the deception of the devil: that he makes the things seen according to the true logic by the eye of the pure soul to be seen conversely, supposing the pleasant instead of the good, and showing the good as something harmful. Thus also eyes are opened which previously were usefully closed. For there is in the soul an eye which imposes itself upon the intelligible through itself, but there is that which follows from instruction by another, which the serpent having perverted, filled the things of deception, so that both sensation and the mind would undergo harm; for when sensation suffers perversion, then also the opinions of the mind become diverted.

It has been said concerning those who have used things contrary: 'Woe to those saying the evil is good and the good is evil' (1 Tim 5:22). Thus, pleasures were raised up as the cause of errors; for even those in wisdom say they prefer the pleasant. For many prefer the easy way over virtue, not accepting the strenuous, and they are stripped because of it. Therefore, the pleasant things must be despised, since they become a hypothesis for sins.

There are some who say that 'Adam ate with it' (Gen 3:6) indicates his consent, so that he might not be utterly destroyed, agreeing with what was said by Paul: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, came into transgression' (1 Tim 2:14), as if he were able to turn away from the wickedness through her also. And they sewed fig leaves and made themselves girdles. And they heard the voice of the Lord walking in the garden, the cowardly ones, and both Adam and his wife fled from the face of God amidst the tree of the paradise (Gen 3:8). Remaining with the things previously viewed concerning the paradise and Adam and the woman, we connect these things. Since they knew that they were naked...

Ἀκολούθως οὖν, παραδείσου μνήμης γεγενημένης, διὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως φύλλων ἐμνημόνευσεν, ἃ συνέρραψαν οἱ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐκπεσόντες 87 κατὰ τὴν εἰρημένην διάνοιαν. Τοῦ γὰρ τηροῦντος τὴν ἀρετὴν καὶ ἐν αυ᾿̣τῇ ὄντος οἰκεῖον τοῦτο, ὡς λέγειν· "6Προορώμην τὸν Κύριον ἐνώπιόν μου διὰ παντός, ὅτι ἐκ δεξιῶν μού ἐστιν, ἵνα μὴ σαλευθῶ"6, καὶ "6Ἐγὼ δὲ διὰ παντὸς μετὰ σοῦ."6 Τοῦ δὲ ἀνθρώπου μετὰ Θεοῦ ὄντος, καὶ ὁ Θεὸς μετ' αὐτοῦ ἐστιν· εἴρηται γάρ· "6Ἐγγίσατε τῷ Θεῷ καὶ ἐγγίσ̣ει ὑμῖν"6· ἐπειδὰν δὲ ἀποστῶσιν αὐτοῦ τινες, ἀκούουσιν· "6Ἐπορεύθη[σ]αν πρὸς ἐμὲ πλάγιοι κἀγὼ πορεύσομαι πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἐν θυμῷ πλαγίῳ."6 Καὶ ὥσπερ ὁ τὸν ἥλιον καταλείπων καὶ βύων̣ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς οὐ ποιεῖ τινα τῷ ἡλίῳ ἐλάττωσιν– μένει γὰρ ὅπερ [ἦ]ν φωτίζων–, οὕτως ὁ καταλείπων Θεὸν ἑαυτοῦ βλάβην ἐργάζεται, καταλείπει δὲ αὐτὸν οὐχ ὡς ἐν τόπῳ, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἀρετὴν ἀποστρεφόμενος ὡς ἐκεῖνοι περὶ ὧν εἴρηται· "6Ἀπώσεται αὐτοὺς ὁ Θεός, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσήκουσαν αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἔσονται πλανῆται ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν"6· ἐπεὶ γὰρ αὐτοὶ οὐκ ἤκουσαν, αὐτὸς αὐτοὺς ἀπώσατο. Ἐπεὶ οὖν καὶ οὗτοι διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως ἀπέστησαν αὐτοῦ, καὶ αὐτὸς αὐτῶν μεμάκρυνται μέν, διὰ δὲ τὴν ἰδίαν ἀγαθότητα περιπατεῖ, αἴσθησιν παρέχων,
english: Having used the fifty-fold, he rose up and spoke of other things, but they did not understand that they had achieved such a thing not by using sword or any defense, but having called upon God himself and having received him leaning toward help through prayer; to whom, if they had made the prayer from anger, God would not have attended through his own exhortation, as it is fitting for the one praying to lift up holy hands without anger or disputations.

Therefore, from the virtue of the saints, the pretenders, desiring to hide their own faults by scattering leaves, think they are making a defense, just as it happened even regarding the first humans. To those using such a purpose, the Lord symbolically rebukes through the fig tree in the Gospels, having come to it and finding nothing but leaves, saying, 'No more shall fruit come from you for an age' (Matthew 21:19). And we do not say that the rebuke was spoken to the fig tree itself; for the sensible fig tree did not bear fruit not because of its own cause. But it is also said regarding Israel having fallen into impiety: 'There is no cluster in the vines, nor figs in the fig trees.' They therefore scattered fig leaves as a plausible defense, as has been said, providing it, but the word is not following the form of the history.

For since paradise was introduced and nakedness and, after this persuasion, knowledge, the word, using the cover from leaves, says it is being made for the subject of the narration according to the custom of the God-breathed Scripture. For often the soul is called at times a vine, at times a sheep, at times a bride in the divine instruction, and the word proceeds accordingly to each one after the other. For when he posits her as a vine, saying, 'A vine flourishing in Israel' (Song of Solomon 6:4), then he calls the teacher-farmers and the attackers foxes; for 'catch for us foxes, even the little foxes that spoil the vineyards' (Song of Solomon 2:15); but when [she is] a sheep...

He names the teachers shepherds and those who turn away wolves and lions; it has been said: 'Israel, a wandering sheep, lions drove him away' (cf. Ps 54:1/55:23). But also when he calls her a bride, he names the one leading into the truth a bridegroom and the one harming an adulterer; and all these things, even if they are different names, regarding the soul, are considered appropriate and fitting to the Divine Spirit in thought, not because this is a sheep or a bride or a vine.

Consequently, therefore, a memory of paradise having occurred, through the form of the word, he mentioned leaves, which those having fallen from virtue scattered according to the aforementioned understanding. And these themselves also heard the Lord God walking in the paradise. And before the transgression, he was not walking around them outside of them, but was with them.

For of the one guarding virtue and being in it, this is appropriate, as to say: 'I have set the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken' (Ps 16:8), and 'But I am with you always' (Mt 28:20). And of the man being with God, and God being with him: it has been said: 'Draw near to God and he will draw near to you' (Jas 4:8); but when some turn away from him, they hear: 'They went astray from me, and I will go to them in angry wrath' (Hos 8:1).

And just as the one leaving the sun and closing his eyes does not do anything to make the sun less—for it remains as it was, shining—so the one leaving God works harm upon himself; and he leaves him not as if in a place, but turning away from virtue, as those about whom it has been said: 'God will cast them off, because they did not listen to him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Dt 32:19); for because they themselves did not listen, he cast them off. Since therefore even these through the transgression turned away from him, and he himself has become distant from them, yet because he walks through his own goodness, providing perception...

source_text: ὡς εἴρηται, κατὰ τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας, ὁπῶς ἐπιστράφωσιν. Τοῦτο δὲ γίνεται̣ τὸ δειλινὸν καταλλήλως τοῖς παραβεβηκόσιν. Τῷ μὲν γὰρ ἐν ἀρετῇ ὄντι ἀκμάζει τὸ τῆς ἀληθείας φῶς, οὐδέπο̣τε γινομένῳ ἐν σκοτεινῇ καταστάσει–ἀκοῦσαι γοῦν ἔστιν λέγοντος τοῦ ἁγίου· "6Ἐκ νυκτὸς ὀρθρίζει τὸ πνεῦμά μου πρὸς σ̣ὲ ὁ Θεός"6, καὶ "6Ὁ Θεός, ὁ Θεός μου πρὸς σὲ ὀρθρίζω"6, καὶ "6Τὸ πρωῒ παρ[α̣]σ̣τήσομαί 88 σοι καὶ ἐπόψομαι"6–τότε δὲ γίνεται δειλινὴ καὶ σκοτώδης ἡ ὥρα ἐπὶ τὴν ἑσπέραν 34 ἐλαύνουσα, ὅτε τις ἑαυτὸν ἔξω τοῦ φωτὸς καθίστησιν ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ καὶ κακίᾳ γινόμενος, ὡς λέγειν τὸν Θεὸν πρὸς τὴν ἁμαρτάνουσαν ψυχήν· "6Νυκτὶ ὡμοίωσα τὴν μητέρα σου"6. Καὶ υἱοὶ δὲ νυκτὸς γίνονταί τινες καὶ σκότους, ὥστε τῷ ἁμαρτάνοντι τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγνοίας καὶ ἀσεβείας καὶ κακίας σκότος πάρεστιν. ∆είκνυται δὲ ὡς οὐκ ἀθρόως ἀφῆκεν αὐτοὺς τὸ φῶς ἐν τῷ λέγεσθαι ὡς τὸ δειλινὸν ἤκουσαν τοῦ Θεοῦ περιπα- τοῦντος. Οἱ γὰρ αὔραν αἰσθήσεως ἔχοντες ἀμαυράν τινα δέχονται κατάστασιν, οὔπω εἰς παντελῆ ἐλθόντες ἄγνοιαν, ἀλλὰ φιλανθρωπ[ί]ᾳ Θεοῦ διεγειρόμενοι ἔτι ἐμβοῶντος αὐτῶν τῷ κρυπτῷ, ἵν' ἐκ [τ]ούτου ἐν μεταγνώσει γένωνται, ὡς μαθε<ῖ>ν ὅτι "6Ψάντος ἑσπέρας αὐλισθήσεται κλαυ- θμός, καὶ εἰς τὸ πρωῒ ἀγαλλίωσις"6, ἵν' οὕτω καὶ περὶ τῶν τοιούτων λεχθῇ ὡς περί τινος αἰσθομένης οἷ κα[κ]ῶν ἐστιν· "6Ὀψὲ φωνὴ αὐτῆς ὠλόλυξεν"6· ἐκ τούτου γὰρ συμβήσεται μετανοοῦντας ἐλθεῖν ἐπὶ φῶς, ὡς εἰπεῖν· "6Αὕτη ἡ ἡμέρα ἣν ἐποίησεν ὁ Κύριος, ἀγαλλιασώμεθα καὶ εὐφρανθῶμεν ἐν αὐτῇ."6 Ἀκούσαντες οὖν τῆς φωνῆς Κυρίου περιπατοῦντος, ὡς εἴρηται, ἐκρύβησαν ἀπὸ προσώπου Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ. Πρόσωπον δὲ Κυρίου Θεοῦ οὐχ ὡς ἀνθρωπομόρφου λέγεται· εἴρηται γάρ· "6Πνεῦμα ὁ Θεός"6· πνεῦμα δὲ οὐκ ἐκ μερῶν συνέστηκεν, ὡς τὸ μέν τι αὐτῶν πρόσωπον καλεῖσθαι ἢ ἄλλο τι τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων μελῶν. Οὐ γὰρ προσήκει τὰς περὶ Θεοῦ φωνὰς ἀνθρωπίνως ἐκλαμβάνειν, διὰ τὸ ἡμῶν χρήσιμον οὕτως εἰρημένας. Καὶ οὐδὲν θαυμα- στόν, εἰ περὶ Θεοῦ ταῦτα λέγεται, ὁπότε καὶ περὶ αἰσθητῶν οὕτως διδασκόμεθα. Ἐν γοῦν Παροιμίαις γέγραπται· "6Θάνατος καὶ ζωὴ ἐν χειρὶ γλώσσης"6, καὶ οὐχ οὕτως νοοῦμεν ὡς τῆς γλώττης χεῖρα ἐχούσης, ἀλλ' ἐνέργειαν, ἥτις χεὶρ αὐτῆς ὠνομάσθη· καὶ ἐπεὶ εἴρηται· "6Ἐκ τῶν 89 ἑαυτοῦ τις λόγων δικαιοῦται καὶ ἐκ τῶν λόγων καταδικάζεται"6, διὰ τοῦτό φησιν ὡς ἐν χειρὶ γλώσσης, τοῦτ' ἔστιν τῷ λόγῳ, "6θάνατος καὶ ζωή"6 ἐστιν, ὅτε τις εὖ ἢ κακῶς αὐτῷ χρῆται. Ἐκρύβησαν οὖν ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀποστάντες τῆς περὶ Θεοῦ καθαρᾶς νοήσεως, οὐχ ὡς Κάιν· ἐκεῖνος γὰρ ἐξῆλθεν ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀφάνταστον ἑαυτὸν αὐτοῦ παρασκευάσας κατὰ ἐκεῖνον, περὶ οὗ εἴρηται. "6Εἶπεν ἄφρων ἐν καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ· οὐκ ἔστιν Θεός"6· πάντες δ' οἱ ἀπρονοησίαν εἰσάγοντες ταύτης εἰσὶ τῆς ἐννοίας. Οἱ δ' ἀποκρυπτόμενοι οὐκ ἀνεννόητοι μὲν τῆς θείας εἰσὶν ἐπιστασίας, διὰ δὲ τὴν ῥυπαρίαν τῆς ἁμαρτίας τὴν παρρησίαν οὐκ ἔχουσιν, καταφρονηταί τινες ὄντες, ἀλλ' οἱ ἅγιοι ἐλευθέραν ἔχο[ν]τες τὴν συνείδησιν ἐνώπιόν εἰσι τοῦ Κυρίου, ὡς λέγειν· "6Ζῇ Κύριος, ᾧ παρέστην ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ"6· περὶ δὲ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων λέγεται· "6Ἔστρεψαν ἐπ' ἐμὲ νῶτα καὶ οὐ πρόσωπα αὐτῶν"6, ὅπερ ἔδει ἵν' ὡς ἱερεῖς παραστᾶται τυγχάνωσιν καὶ ὡς ἄγγελοι διὰ παντὸς βλέποντες τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς Πατρός. ∆ύναται δὲ καθ' ἕτερον λόγον ἐκλαμβάνεσθαι τὸ "6Καὶ ἐκρύβησαν ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ Θεοῦ"6, πρόσωπον νοούντων ἡμῶν εἶναι τὸν μονογενὴ Υἱὸν αὐτοῦ ὄντα αὐτοῦ εἰκόνα καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως. Ὁ γὰρ τοῦτον ἰδὼν ἑώρακε τὸν Πατέρα. ∆έον οὖν αὐτοὺς πάντα πράττειν ἐπὶ τῷ τηρεῖν τὸ κατ' εἰκόνα, καθ' ὃ καὶ γεγένηνται. Παραβᾶται θελήσαντες εἶναι τῆς ἐντολῆς ἀπέστησαν τοῦ φωτίζεσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ εἰκόνος τοῦ Θεοῦ. Εἰκότως δὲ φεύγουσιν ὑπὸ τὸ ξύλον τὸ ἐμμέσῳ τῷ παραδείσῳ, ὃ ἦν τὸ γνωστὸν καλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ. Ὁ γὰρ κρυπτόμενος τὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόσωπον, ὡς μὴ ἐνεργεῖν τὴν ἀρετήν, ἀλλ' ἐπιμορφάζεσθαι, κρύπτεται ὑπὸ τὴν ὑπόκρισιν. Ὁ γὰρ γιγνώσκων καλὸν καὶ πονηρόν, ὡς μὴ διαστέλλειν καὶ αἱρεῖσθαι τὸ καλόν, οὕτως τῇ 90 ἐντρεχείᾳ οἴησιν ἔχων κ̣ρύπτεται Θεόν, τὴν ἀρετὴν ἐπι- μορφαζόμενος. ιιι, 9–12. Καὶ ἐκάλεσεν Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τὸν Ἀδὰμ καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ποῦ εἶ; Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Τὴν φωνήν σου ἤκουσα περιπατοῦντος ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ καὶ ἐφοβήθην, ὅτι γυμνός εἰμι, καὶ ἐκρύβην. Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Τίς ἀνήγγειλέν σοι ὅτι γυμνὸς εἶ, εἰ μὴ ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου, οὗ 35 ἐνετειλάμην σοι τούτου μόνου μὴ φαγεῖν, ἀπ' αὐτοῦ ἔφαγες. Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Ἀδάμ· Ἡ
english: As it has been said, according to common understandings, so that they might turn back. This fearful thing happens appropriately to those who have approached. For the light of truth flourishes in one existing in virtue, never occurring in a dark state—for indeed it is possible to hear the holy one saying: 'Out of the night my spirit breaks toward you, O God' (Ps 44:23), and 'God, my God, toward you I break toward the dawn' (Ps 57:8), and 'In the morning I will come to you and will see you' (Ps 43:4)—but then the hour becomes fearful and dark during the passing evening, when someone establishes himself outside the light, becoming in ignorance and wickedness, as the God says toward the sinning soul: 'I have made your mother like the night' (cf. Lam 1:2). And some become children of the night and of darkness, so that to the one sinning, the darkness from ignorance, impiety, and wickedness is present.

And it is shown how the light has not continuously abandoned them, in the saying that they heard the fearful [voice] of God walking. For those having the sense of perception receive a somewhat dim state, not having entered into complete ignorance, but being awakened by the philanthropy of God while the hidden [thing] still strikes them, so that from this they might come into knowledge, as to learn that 'weeping may tarry for the evening, but joy comes in the morning' (Ps 30:5), so that thus it might also be said concerning such people as if one were perceiving some evils: 'Late her voice cried out' (cf. Lam 2:19); for from this it will happen that the repentant come to the light, as to say: 'This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it' (Ps 118:24).

Having heard, therefore, the voice of the Lord walking, as it has been said, they fled from the face of the Lord God. But the face of the Lord God is not said to be anthropomorphic; for it has been said: 'God is Spirit' (John 4:24); and spirit is not composed of parts, such that one of them is called a face or something else of human members. For it is not proper to perceive the voices concerning God in a human way, because of our useful having said it thus. And it is nothing wonderful if these things are said concerning God, when we are thus taught even concerning sensible things. For in Proverbs it has been written: 'Death and life are in the power of the tongue' (Prov 18:21), and we do not understand it as the tongue having a hand, but as an energy, which was named its hand; and since it has been said: '...

Some of his own words justify him, and by his own words he is condemned; therefore he says that it is as if in the hand of the tongue—that is, by the word—'death and life' is, when one uses it well or badly. Thus they hid from the face of God, turning away from the pure thought concerning God, not as Cain did; for he went out from the face of God having prepared himself unseen, according to that which is said: 'The fool says in his heart, there is no God' (Ps 14:1). And all those entering into this thoughtlessness are of that concept.

But those hiding are not uncomprehending of the divine knowledge, yet because of the filthiness of sin they do not have boldness; some are being despised, but the holy, having a free conscience before the Lord, are as to say: 'The Lord lives, before whom he stood' (1 Sam 25:6); but concerning those sinning it is said: 'They turned their heads toward me and not their faces' (Ps 51:5), which it was necessary that they might happen to stand as priests and as angels, always seeing the face of the Father in the heavens. And it is possible by another sense to take 'And they hid from the face of God,' that our face is the Only-begotten Son, being his icon and character of the substance. For he having seen this one saw the Father. It is necessary therefore for them all to do things upon keeping the [image] according to the icon, according to which he was created. Wishing to transgress the commandment, they turned away from being enlightened from the icon of God. And rightly they flee under the tree, they who are in the midst of the paradise, which was the known good and evil. For he hiding the face of God, as to not work virtue but to be shaped, hides under hypocrisy. For he knowing good and evil, as to not distinguish and to choose the good, thus having a mind of indecision, hides God, shaping virtue.

And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: 'Where are you?' And he said to him: 'I heard the sound of you walking in the paradise and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid.' Πηγὴ ἀγαθότητος ὑπάρχων ὁ Θεὸς καὶ μετὰ τὰ σφάλματα πάλιν ἡμᾶς καλεῖ, τὴν παντελῆ γνῶσιν τοῦ καλοῦ μὴ ἀπαλείφων ἀπὸ τοῦ λογισμοῦ, κἂν ἡμεῖς διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τὴν ἀρετὴν ἀποστρεφώμεθα. Εἴσι δ' οἱ καὶ τὴν ἀσώματον οὐσίαν κατὰ τὸ πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον τῆς ψυχῆς ἐννοοῦντες καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐκτὸς παντὸς τόπου αὐτὴν εἶναι προσήκειν λογιζόμενοι, παρ' ἑαυτὴν δὲ σώματος πειραθεῖσαν ἐντρεπτικῶς ἀκούειν· Που εἶ; Ἐν τόπῳ ὑπάρχεις, ἡ ἀπὸ παντὸς τόπου ἐλευθέρα διὰ τὸ ἀσώματος, ὅπερ μὴ φυλάξασα, ἀλλὰ συναφθεῖσα σώματι, ἐν τόπῳ γέγονας; Ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ ἐν οὐρανῷ ἔχων τὸ πολίτευμα καὶ ἔχων τὴν καρδίαν ἐν οὐρανῷ διὰ τὸ ἐκεῖ τεθησαυρικέναι κἀκεῖ εἶναι οὐκ ἐν τόπῳ ἐστίν, ὑπερκόσμιο[ς γ]εγενημένος. Καὶ ἐπιτιμίας γὰρ̣ ἔδει, ἥτις οἰκείως ἀπὸ δεσπότου γίνεται, συγκεραν- νύντος ἀγαθό[τ]ητι τὴν ἐπιτιμίαν· διὰ γὰρ τοῦτο εἴρηται· "6Καὶ ἐκάλεσεν Κύριος ὁ Θεός"6. Τοῦτο καὶ ∆αυὶδ ψάλλει λέγων. "6Ἔλεος καὶ κρίσιν ᾄσομαί σοι, Κύριε"6· μετὰ γὰρ τοῦ ἐλεεῖν καὶ τὸ κρίνειν συναπτόμενον φιλανθρωπι´̣ας δεῖγμα ἐκφέρει. Καὶ γὰρ ἐπιτιμῶν ἐλέει· πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον γὰρ ἐπάγει τὰ κολαστήρια. Ὅταν γάρ τις ἐν ἁμαρτίᾳ γενόμενος αἰσθήσεως βραχεία̣ς δέηται τοῦ μόνως ἔννοιαν δέχεσθαι τοῦ Θεοῦ διὰ τῆς κτίσεως ἐν ᾗ ἐμπ̣εριπατεῖ τῶν ὅλων προνοούμενος τάξιν ἐπιθεὶς ἑκάστῳ τω῀̣ν ὄντων, τότε καὶ ἐπ̣ι̣σ̣τρέφει καὶ γιγνώσκει ὅτι ἐφορᾷ τὰ ὅλα καὶ διοικεῖ, οὕτω τε ἔξω καταφρονήσεως 92 γίνεται. Ὅταν γὰρ θεάσηται ἡλίου̣ μὲν τὴν τεταγμένην πορείαν, οὐρανῶν δὲ τὴν κίνησιν, σελήνης δὲ τὰς μεταβολάς, ἀστέρων δὲ τὰς κατὰ καιροὺς ἐπιτολάς, καὶ λογίσηται ὅτι ὁ τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς ἡνίοχος καὶ ταξίαρχος ὁ τῶν ὅλων ἐστὶν δημιουργός, ἐμπεριπατῶν ὅλοις φωνῆς ἀκούει Θεοῦ, οὐ κατὰ πρόσφορον γινομένης, ἀλλ' ἐν διανοίᾳ τυπουμένης, ὅτι Θεὸν οὐδὲν λανθάνει, ἀλλὰ πάντα ὑπὸ τὴν αὐτοῦ οἰκονομίαν ἐστίν. Καὶ οὕτω αἰσχυνθεὶς κρύπτεται· ὁ γὰρ ἁμαρτάνων, οὐκ ἔχων πρὸ ὀφθαλμῶν Θεὸν ἁμαρτάνει.
