english: They lead out their matters, bringing them as a thank-offering, doing it naturally; but those using it carelessly, as if to keep the precious things for themselves and to bring the cheap things, these have used a bad division. Since Israel does this very thing, the prophetic word says rebukingly and admonishingly: 'If you bring a blind man for sacrifice, is it not bad? And if you bring a lame or sick man, is it not bad? Bring him to your leader' (Malachi 1:8).

But also Ananias and Sapphira in the Acts of the Apostles, when many were offering for the needs of those in need, they themselves received the price of a field, from which, having decided upon it, they brought the half and the other half using a bad division, which the spokesman of the apostles, being moved by the Spirit, rebuking said: 'Did it not remain with you, and was it not under your authority when sold? Why did you dare in your heart to do this deed?' (Acts 5:3-4). This also was said to Cain by God: 'Why have you become exceedingly sorrowful, and why has your face fallen? If you had offered rightly, but had not offered rightly, you sinned' (Genesis 4:6).

For all sin as they bring to God as a needy person, ignoring what was said in the Psalms toward Him, the God: 'Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?' (Psalm 50:9) and also: 'Mine are all the beasts of the field, cattle on the mountains and oxen' (Psalm 50:10). For all that you have in abundance from me, I also have all things, so that one not in need did not command, but rather from these, using them symbolically, it is fitting to use virtue not carelessly, but perfectly and completely.

Furthermore, in order that the evil may not advance, it is exhorted to be at rest from it, so that by rubbing against it one might not work up a worse sorrow. In this way it is also said to Zion, being moved disorderly—for such is the name—'Stand up, you, Zion' (Isaiah 62:1). Since the rational animal is active, either working out evil or virtue, in a manner of speaking,

When one does evil, it is appropriate for him to stand against this, so that virtue may find the space that is becoming. This indeed David advises: 'Turn away from evil' (Psalm 34:14), saying, 'and do good' (Psalm 34:14). 'Be still' (1 Kings 19:12), therefore, he says, do not progress through evil; do not consider through negligence as if your sacrifice was not properly received. For many, often stumbling themselves and for this reason not having God as a co-worker, are displeased with providence, which God prevents in Cain, saying: 'Be still' (1 Kings 19:12).

And also the 'his turning toward you and you shall turn him back' (Psalm 94:7) comes, teaching that whatever is offered to God not according to what is becoming, these things are not offered to him, but belong to the Giver, turning back toward him because of not having found a place in God. So also those providing alms for the sake of being seen by men withhold their own reward, having nothing from God; for they did not do this with a divine purpose. The whole discourse of the word is most useful for character, and thus being taken simply, it teaches sincerely regarding offerings and not to do them carelessly; and since we lead the aforementioned into the modes of the soul in the instances of errors, it is necessary even now to do this.

The word of God, existing according to common concepts and being present to the conscience, paternally reproves those stumbling, which is also presented now. But 'Cain rose up against Abel' also shows the intention along with the act. These things are contained in the account of history; since we have judged Cain to be a hypocrite according to the account of the anagoge, such things would also be the case now. The secret man is a brother to the man appearing outwardly, and a man in thought; for it is proper to attend to both the serious matters, both in rightly calculating and in displaying an outward adornment suitable to the ways, which the Psalmist, instructing, says in the first Psalm: 'Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly' (Ps 1:1), and shortly after: 'He shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, which shall bring forth its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall' (Ps 1:3). By saying 'fruit' he means virtuous action from a disposition, but 'leaf' is the outward appearance, which is shown in form, adornment, and the smiling of teeth.

Therefore, whenever the hypocrite strives at these things, while his thought is found to be straying, he kills the brother, having a thought discordant with the outward. The plain is this: the mechanism against those being deceived, into which he brings himself previously to sin by means of them. Such also are the sophists, using the plain of words, through which they lead their own brothers into impiety. And the Lord God said to Cain: 'Where is Abel your brother?' (Gen 4:9). And he said: 'I do not know; am I not a keeper of my brother?'

The Philanthropic God also visits again those who have been entirely estranged from him through much goodness, and through the visitation raises them to perception, which he also does now toward Cain, first by bringing to him the words from conscience, and then also by saying 'Abel the brother,' as if weighing him down with the designation of nature and leading him to the perception of the stain. The magnitude of the deed is presented, that he killed both a brother and a righteous brother, whom God had made, having raised up, for help and assistance. english: It signifies this. For the divine providence, existing as a unifying force, does this through all things. Even while the fraternal disposition and the extreme proximity for union are sufficient in the law, it does not permit these to be joined by marriage, but allows others with sisters and near relatives, so that through them they may be gathered together and from others [text gapped] and a disposition, which Cain suffered. For one must see even his hypocrisy in saying with thoughtlessness: 'I do not know; am I a guardian of my brother?' (Gen 4:9). For through the 'I do not know' the audacity is shown, because he thought he could hide from God; and through the 'Am I a guardian?' the unprincipled, irrational, and therefore senseless thing is revealed; for he ought to have been a guardian of his brother. And God said: 'What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth' (Gen 4:10). And now you are cursed from the earth, which had the stomach of its earth to receive the blood of your brother from your hand, because you work the earth and it will not add its strength to give to you; you shall groan and tremble upon the earth (Gen 4:11-12).

And the Philanthropist teaches while he is shameless, and thinking he can hide from God, he instructs him as this is impossible: 'The voice' he says, 'of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth' (Gen 4:10), do not suppose that the sleepless eye of Providence has escaped the stain. But he reveals it as a voice of blood, just as also elsewhere: 'Behold, the wages of the laborers who laid hold on your fields, who deprived you, cry out' (Jas 5:4). And so it is to be struck, and it is also possible that the blood is said to be there instead of the soul. And if anyone says that he was reminded because of this blood, that the body hid it; he also remembers the pouring out and how the earth had the stomach of its earth to receive the blood of a brother continuously, so that, growing large, the thing done might cause the hot-tempered one to be struck with remorse. And he brings upon him also curses, fittingly for one who worked so much, I say: 'And now you are cursed from the earth, because you work the earth and it will not add its strength to give to you' (Gen 4:12). For often, because of the sin of men, the poverty of the earth happens, not yielding its fruits according to what was said: 'The earth shall mourn because of those who dwell...'

In it. For it has been given to her to bear fruits to those who maintain a right calculation, and to those falling, providing the necessary things through the philanthropy of God; and again, by His command, those fruits which are lacking from her are restored, so that a return may occur. It is for a leading back; if we follow the first principles, God blames the hypocrite because he perverts the life-giving power of the soul, making it like the man outside, as it has been said. Therefore, he will be accursed, no longer providing fruits, but wasting his opportunity on something useless, so that from this he may be cast down into the beginning of virtue. For it is useful even to be perverted by evil, when the results from it are not attained, so that having undergone toil, he may be imbued with the love of virtue according to what was said: 'Egypt has toiled, and the commerce of the Ethiopians and the Sabaeans, tall men, shall pass over you' (Ezekiel 30:16). And 'groaning' and 'trembling upon the earth' (Psalm 55:6) shall be, thus being judged, always being reproved by the conscience.

And Cain said to the Lord God: 'My guilt is too great to be forgiven; if you cast me out today from the face of the earth and from your face I will be hidden, I will be a wanderer and a trembler upon the earth, and it shall be that everyone who finds me will kill me' (Genesis 4:9, 12, 14). The word of God remains even for those who are strangers to themselves, through which they take Him to be a philanthropist and good regarding His own; and it is not possible to cut away this good concept, even if they are often dissatisfied through the depth of wickedness. Immediately, therefore, those who are altogether forgetful of God, being surrounded by necessity, flee to supplications and entreaties, as is seen also regarding Cain. For as [God] was moved to pity regarding the murder of the brother and, after acting with boldness, hypocritically asking him, 'Where is Abel your brother?' (Genesis 4:9), yet, lest more perversion exist in man, having known from the words of God—through which he learned from the reproof of what had happened in his conscience—that the eye of God is unavoidable, he must not turn this [eye] toward all foreign things, from which it will happen to groan and tremble and to expect refutation from everyone who finds him.

english: Having been struck, as if the protective power of God has departed from him, all other things are considered fearful by him, and he has no confidence in anything done by his own hand. These things are said to us regarding the whole scope of Cain's reply; but let us also see his mixed reply, which is faulty and does not partake of divine grace.

"Greater" he says, "is the cause for me to be forgiven," which would mean, according to a first understanding, that the evil upon me will be greater, if you, O God, do not pass over my injustice; for still, being under guardianship, the not-being-expelled is [a state]. This same thing is said regarding God in the prophet, concerning those of worthy consideration and those handed over to an unproven mind: "I will not visit their daughters when they play the harlot, nor their virgins when they commit adultery. For when they are sinning, those whom he wishes to train, he says: 'I will visit their lawlessness with a rod and their sins with whips, but my mercy I will not withdraw from them.'" (Ezekiel 16:25; Ezekiel 20:47).

What he says now, that is, that the reproach from you, Lord, will be greater than me, as has been said; and since he thinks himself having stumbled and having suffered a perversion, he thinks that having been cast out from the earth, he will be cast out from the face of God. According to another understanding, he might be saying these things, that the evil to me will be greater if I remain in the land, O God, lest you destroy me into non-existence; for if you cast me out from the earth, and from your face I will be hidden, no longer existing, which was possible for him, but since you do not cast me out from the earth—for this must be obeyed—I shall be in it groaning and trembling, from everyone finding me and killing me.

For many, when they know for themselves the immeasurableness of their errors, having some notion that God himself will visit them, they consider non-existence to be preferable, preferring to suffer insensibility to existing; this would be clear from what was said by the prophet concerning the traitors of Jesus: "They will wish it if they were consumed by fire." (2 Thessalonians 1:9). And in another way he might be imposing [this meaning] to his saying: "If you cast me out," and asking for a place of repentance today so that the present might be surpassed, "today"...
It was said. But he also desired that the one called 'his own' might fall into perfection toward God, so that he would not lie exposed to anyone finding him for destruction.

Cain might have wondered at any time, finding him and killing him, that nothing existed at all besides him and the mothers; to whom one might say that, having first the idea that a succession of men was to come, he feared that having worked such a great defilement, he might be destroyed as an abomination by those coming, the weight of which would pass upon the born ones as well; then, even if not this, he suspected that divine powers would be vengeful for the impious deed, which he was likely to have seen the pouring out of the evil.

But regarding the bringing back: And the Lord God said to him, 'Not thus' (Gen 4:15); everyone who kills Cain, seven avenges he will release. And the Lord God set a sign for Cain, not to kill him, everyone finding him. For a greater punishment, or according to the suspicion of Cain, that everyone finding him kills him, protecting the murderer of his own brother, God says, 'Not thus' (Gen 4:15); that is, this justice of the transgression is not suitable to you, to be destroyed by him. For this one will release seven avenging, which signifies perfect punishment.

For often the number seven in the Scripture is taken to mean perfection; this is shown by what is said: 'Seven eyes are watching over all the earth' (Zech 1:10); for God is not a body, so that his eyes might be by the number seven, but it teaches clearly that his watchful power is most complete and great.

Others have said that, just as the man of the Savior had seven resting spirits, 'spirit of wisdom and understanding, spirit of counsel and strength, spirit of knowledge and piety, spirit of the fear of God' (Isa 11:2), so each man, being a perfect man before sin, toward whom we are to arrive, the apostle teaching says, 'until we all arrive at a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ' (Eph 4:13), having these resting in him, if he should sin, will release them, for which vengeance ought to be most complete and appropriate. english: The phrase 'everyone who killed Cain' is said instead of a vocative, instead of 'O Cain, everyone who killed', or other ways about him, so that it might be 'everyone who killed Cain', which some say would not be a sin for certain powers. To these same things he gave a 'sign' 'not to let him be killed' (Gen 4:15), which would be the command of God for him; for no such judgments happen without forgiveness.

He set a sign, the momentum of repentance after the falls, by which he will not be easy to take away. For it is a great good not to fall; but to come after the falls into recognition would be a second chance, which God manages through teaching to rouse [one] so as not to fall to the deceiver. Such a mind is suggested by what is said in the Psalms: 'Light was signaled in the face of the Son, or the light of your face toward us, O Lord' (Ps 89:13), which you say properly, speaking of divine thought. For so also the fleeing from the face of the bow would happen, of the face of God in us, as it is said, while it exists; and what follows confirms it: 'So that your beloved ones may be delivered' (Ps 100:2). Therefore, through philanthropy and goodness, God gives a place of repentance even to those falling greatly, so that a recovery of virtue may happen again.

So Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Nod opposite Eden (Gen 4:16). We say that the going out of Cain from the face of God is not to be taken locally, but that everyone sinning becomes outside God, since we also understand entering toward God in this way, the Psalmist saying: 'Enter before Him in gladness' (Ps 100:2); for someone enters before God leaving all things outside, both sins and sensible things, and becoming another of the world, so that he might thus become a partaker of the knowledge concerning God. It is said here therefore: 'Cain went out from the face of God' (Gen 4:16), and we do not say that...

What kind of place is it in which God exists, and from which Cain, while existing, went out? For God is uncircumscribable and is not subject to places, even if a temple has later become a teaching for symbolic worship. Cain went out, having made himself unworthy of the face of God, having become otherwise thoughtless.

Concerning such things it is said, 'God is not before him' (Ps 31:9), and concerning the sons of Eli it is said, 'The sons of Eli did not know the Lord' (1 Sam 2:12); for if they drew near to the temple, it was in their disposition and works that he was found outside. That Cain went out in this way, the following shows: 'And he dwelt' (Gen 4:16) for he says 'in the land of Nod, opposite Eden.' For 'Nod' is interpreted as 'trembling'; for where was it necessary for the one departing from peaceful virtue to dwell, except in 'trembling,' in an unstable and uncertain thing, which is wickedness? And also 'opposite'; for wickedness is contrary to virtue.

We must remember, therefore, that when we were participating in the account of Adam's expulsion, we noted that He expelled him not as one having gone out of his own accord, but still possessing an impulse of longing for the enjoyment of the luxury of Paradise; therefore, opposite these things, He settled him, just as He himself had managed the dwelling. For to those who do not sin greatly, since virtue does not exist within them deeply, a certain quick opportunity is given, indicating a return, being given toward God, which was not said of Cain.

For neither has he been settled nor expelled, having perished through a willing longing for evil; therefore he dwells in 'trembling,' being incessantly disturbed, since he desired this, of the contrary stable thing, in order to have a strong standing, as if he could stand even with God, according to what was said: 'But you shall stand with me' (Ps 16:8), and by the Savior regarding those not tasting death: 'There are some standing here' (John 12:35), who were his acquaintances. Εἰ μὲν γάρ, ἀλλῶν οὐσῶν, ἐκέχρητο τῇ ἀδελφῇ, πιθανὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος· εἰ δέ, μηδένος ὑπάρχοντος, πρὸς σύστασιν τῆς διαδοχῆς τοῦτο γέγονεν, ποῦ χώραν ἔχει ἀδελφογαμία, <οὐχ> οἵου τε ὄντος ἑτέρωθεν δέξασθαι πρὸς συζυγίαν; Φέρεται καὶ λόγος παρὰ τοῖς Στωϊκοῖς ζητούμενος ὡς, εἰ συμβαίη ἐκπύρωσιν γενέσθαι τοῦ 56 κόσμου καὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ ζώπυρον παραμεῖναι τὸ τοῦ ἀνθρωπείου γένους μο´̣νος σοφὸς μείνοι μετὰ θυγατρὸς ἐπιστάμενος ὅτι διακοσμηθήσεται πάλιν κόσμος, δι' ὃ καὶ χρεία διαδοχῆς, εἰ καθηκόντως χρήσηται τῇ θυγατρί· καὶ φαίνεται αὐτοῖς ὁ λόγος οὐκ ἀνοίκειος τῷ μὴ εἶναι ἄλλην. Τοῦτο φαίνεται καὶ περὶ τῶν θυγατέρων τοῦ Λὼτ γεγενημένον, ὃ οἱ φιλαίτιοι μὲν αἰτιάσονται, τῶν δὲ συνετῶν οὐδείς. Μὴ γὰρ οἰόμεναι ἄλλον ἄνδρα εἶναι διὰ τὴν γεγενημένην καῦσιν τῶν πόλεων ἐκείνων, ἀλλὰ καὶ προσλαβοῦσαι ὡς κόραι ὅτι πᾶσα ἡ γῆ τοιαῦτα ὑπέστη ἐμπρησθεῖσα, λέγουσι γοῦν· "6Ἰδοὺ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν γεγήρακεν καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ὃς εἰσελεύσεται πρὸς ἡμᾶς, καθὼς καθήκει πάσῃ τῇ γῇ, δεῦτε καὶ ποτίσωμεν τὸν πατέρα ἑαυτῶν οἶνον"6· καὶ ὅτι οὐκ ἐμπαθῶς τοῦτο πεποιήκασιν, ἀλλὰ ζώπυρον ὑπολιποῦσαι, συνελθοῦσα ἡ 138 μία προετρέψατο καὶ τὴν ἄλλην τοῦτο ποιῆσαι, ὅπερ οὐκ ἂν ἐποίει ταχέως, εἰ πάθει ἐδούλευεν, ἀλλὰ τῷ αὐτῷ τρόπῳ ὡς ἡ πρώτη ᾠκονόμησεν καὶ ἡ δευτέρα πεποίηκεν διαδοχῆς ἕνεκεν πλείονος. english: It is written for every master of teaching to be carried forward: 'Stand fast therefore, and do not again be held by the yoke of slavery' (Gal 5:1). And the Psalmist says thankfully: 'You have set my feet upon a rock' (Ps 40:2). But concerning evils, as always rubbing against bad things, it has been said: 'The shaking of their feet shall not stand' (Ps 68:6). For it is a great sin to be always moving in evil, which the word says is not to be in Zion, wishing it: 'Set yourself, O Zion' (Ps 69:28).

This is what the blessed David, possessing this, sang so that he might not fall from it: 'And let not the hand of sinners shake me' (Ps 69:28), which is: the deeds of a sinner, of the devil, may not turn me away from virtue. And Cain knew his wife, and having conceived, she bore Enoch (Gen 4:17). And he was building a city, and he named the city after the name of his son Enoch.

Some seek from where Cain had a wife, since there were none other than Adam and Eve, from whom the evildoers introduce brother-marriage. It was necessary for them to realize that from this brother-marriage is not introduced. For if, while others existed, he used the relation to his sister, the word was probable; but if, of no one existing, it happened for the establishment of succession, where is there room for brother-marriage, such as being of another could be accepted for a yoke-mate? A word is also carried among the Stoics, seeking whether, if the conflagration of the world should happen and the one wise man of the human race should remain with his daughter to watch over the ember, knowing that the world will be decorated again, which is why there is a need for succession, if it is used properly for the daughter; and the word seems to them not unfamiliar regarding there not being another.

This also seems to have happened concerning the daughters of Lot, which the lovers blame, but none of the wise. For they do not suppose there was another man because of the having happened of the burning of those cities, but having also taken them as maidens, that all the land had undergone such things previously, they say: 'Behold, our father has grown old, and there is no man who shall come to us, as it is fitting for all the land; come, and let us give our father wine' (Gen 19:31). And that they did not do this through passion, but having left an ember, one came and turned the other to do this, which she would not have done quickly if she had served through passion, but by the same [means].

Τὰ μὲν οὖν πρὸς τὸ ῥητὸν οὕτως ἔχει· εἴη δὲ τὰ τῆς ἀναγωγῆς ταῦτα. Ὁ κτηνοτρόφος ἕτερός ἐστι τοῦ ποιμένος· ὁ μὲν γὰρ σὺν ἐπιστήμῃ νέμει, [ὁ] δὲ κτηνοτρόφος οὔ. Ἄβελ ὁ δίκαιος ποιμὴν ἐτύγχανεν, [τὰς] ἀλόγους ἑαυτοῦ δυνάμεις ἐπιθυμητικὴν ὀρεκτι[κὴ]ν θυμικὴν ἄγων κατὰ λόγον τὸν ὀρθόν· ὁ δὲ κτηνοτρό[φο]ς ἀμοιρῶν ἐπιστήμης, ἡδονικός τις ὤν, [μ]όνων ἐστὶ [τ]ῶν αἰσθήσεων, οὐ κρατῶν ἀλλὰ κρατούμενος ὑπ' αὐτῶν. Καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ παρα- δείγματος σαφὲς ἂν εἴη τὸ λεγόμενον τοῦτον τρόπον. Ὁ ἰατρὸς ἄλλως χρῆται τῇ ἁφῇ ἢ ὁ πρὸς 57 ἡδονὴν ὁρῶν· οὗτος οὖν κτηνοτρόφος τρόπον τινά ἐστι̣ν̣, ὁ δὲ ἰατρὸς ποιμήν· λόγῳ γὰρ χρῆται τῇ αἰσθήσει. Οὕτω καὶ περὶ ὀσφρήσεως καὶ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων ὁ λόγῳ αὐταῖς χρώμενος ἄριστος. Εἶπεν δὲ Λάμεχ ταῖς ἑαυτοῦ γυναιξὶν Ἀδὰ καὶ Σελλά· Ἀκούσατέ μου τῆς φωνῆς γυναῖκες Λάμεχ, ἐνωτίσασθέ μου τ̣ο̣υ`̣ς̣ λ̣ο´̣γ̣ο̣υ̣ς̣· ὁ´̣τι ἄνδρα ἀπέκτεινα εἰς τραῦμα ἐμοί, καὶ νεανίσκον εἰς μώλωπά μοι· ὅτι ἑπτάκις ἐκδεδίκηται ἐκ Κάιν, ἐκ δ[ὲ] Λάμεχ ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά. Τὸ ἐνωτίζεσθαι παρὰ τῇ θείᾳ παιδεύσει νομίζω μόνῃ 142 φέρεσθαι, διαφέρει δὲ τοῦ ἀκοῦσαι, ὅτε σὺν αὐτῷ συνάπτεται, ὅτι τὸ μὲν ἐνωτίζεσθαι τὴν ἐκ τοῦ σύνεγγυς ἀκοήν, τὸ δὲ ἀκοῦσαι τὸ ὁπωσοῦν ἀκοῦσαι, καὶ εἰ μὴ ἐγγὺς ὁ λόγος ἐστίν. english: Humans are animals of choice, participating in sciences; for they do not live by sensation alone like the irrational, but the virtue of the rational is already shown through being inventors of arts. The first point regarding the literal sense is this; the things regarding the ascent are these.

The cattle-tender is different from the shepherd; for the one grazes with science, but the cattle-tender does not. Abel was the righteous shepherd, governing his irrational powers—the desiring, the appetitive, and the spirited—according to the right reason; but the cattle-tender, lacking science and being a certain pleasure-seeker, is subject to the sensations alone, not ruling them but being ruled by them.

And as a clear example, it would be said in this way: The physician uses touch differently than one looking toward pleasure; this one, then, is a kind of cattle-tender, but the physician is a shepherd, for he uses reason with sensation. In the same way, regarding smell and the other sensations, the one using them with reason is best. For reasoning begins the sensation, and if the reasoning is held in check, the man receives the qualities according to the passions, such as being called a lion through the spirited part, a fox through the cunning, and a serpent through the earthly part, and also being called a horse through the pleasurable part; for they say, 'You have become like mares' (Psalm 55:19), and other men are called such because, being entirely of the sensations, they produce nothing divine, like us; for he says, 'Do not become like a horse and a similar creature, which have no understanding' (Psalm 49:20).

The cattle-tender is such, being a certain base person, not dwelling in a house but in tents, a precarious thing, not imitating those who dwell in tents for the sake of entering into the house, who also say as in the Psalm: 'How lovely are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts: my soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord' (Psalm 84:1-2); for the one progressing from tents desires the courts, singing: 'I will go in the way of a wonderful habitation until I reach the house of God' (Psalm 77:13). The other brother is 'he who showed the harp and the lyre' (Psalm 33:2), being his brother in righteousness; for he has neighbors for the enjoyment of pleasures and the deception through music being worked upon the ears; for 'woe' to 'those who rise up...'

Chasing the morning and the evening, remaining blind; for wine will intoxicate them; for they drink wine with lyres and psalteries, but they do not look upon the works of the Lord. And the other [one] crafts war-gear from bronze and iron, the bronze making its sound, just as Paul writes, 'I have become a sounding bronze' (1 Cor 13:1); and he himself is also a worker of iron, being a certain sophist and deceiving through seeming probabilities.

And Lamech said to his wives, Adam and Zillah: 'Hear my voice, women of Lamech; be instructed by my words; for I have killed a man for a wound, and a young man for a bruise' (Gen 4:23-24); for seventy times seven has been avenged from Cain, and from Lamech seventy times seven. I believe that being instructed is brought about only by divine instruction, and it differs from hearing, when it is joined with it; for the one, being instructed, is the hearing of that which is near, but the hearing is the hearing of that which is far off, and the word is not near. And in Isaiah, 'Hear, O heaven, and be instructed, O earth, for the Lord has spoken' (Isa 30:2), is not said in parallel, which is also 'Be instructed, O heaven, and I will speak' (Isa 40:9)—for instead of 'Pay attention,' other interpreters say 'Be instructed'—'and let the earth hear the words from my mouth' (Isa 30:2). And they say such an observation exists: when the law was being given by God, since it happened to be near the heavenly works, for this reason the heaven is commanded to be instructed; but when they departed from the upright citizenship, as to become far from the earth, then it is said, 'Hear, O heaven'—for they happened to be far—'and be instructed, O earth,' for this [earth] was near through its attachments. Therefore Lamech did not say 'Hear' and 'Be instructed' in parallel, but rather we have observed the difference between them in the Scripture not to be untimely; and what is it that we should learn, he says: 'Hear my voice, women of Lamech; be instructed by my words' (Gen 4:23). And someone might say that the voice and the words are in parallel; but he who seeks precision even regarding these would say that regarding the voice he ordered 'Hear,' but regarding the words he ordered the more precise thing, which is to be instructed.

Genesis 5:26. And to Seth there was born a son, and he named his name Enos; he hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God. The holy ones from the holy often possess both a physical descent from them and a descent according to the soul, in the same manner that Abraham became the father of Isaac, and Isaac of Jacob, and Jacob of Joseph; for these exist both by human succession from them and have become imitators of their virtue. But Esau became the son of Isaac according to the flesh alone, becoming a stranger to him through his own will; for he happened to be worthless. Seth, therefore, being placed instead of the righteous, begets Enos the righteous, who instead of the name of the Lord is called man; of such a nature, his soul's virtue declaring the 'according to the image' and the state of a truly existing man; for Enos is a 'man' among the Hebrews.

One must also add what is proper to man: 'He' says, 'hoped to call upon the name of the Lord'; and this is a virtuous practice for such a man. The hope that this truly is, is to become like God as much as possible; and to hope to call upon the name of the Lord God while simultaneously subjecting oneself to authority and to divine teaching is the hope.

english: After Methuselah was born, Enoch found favor with God after two hundred and thirty years, and he fathered sons and daughters. And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. And Enoch found favor with God, and he was not found, because God transferred him.

The Apostle, having received the word concerning Enoch, says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: 'By faith Enoch was transferred so as not to see death' (Heb 11:5). His life is described in a number of days, and having completed a year and a remainder, he was transferred, which one would logically consider to be a translation into better things, since he was promised the virtue which ought to exist in humans according to perfection and fullness. But his translation did not happen like that of other men; for the bodies of the others, remaining here and being dissolved, were separated from the souls; concerning this it is said that he was transferred, about which we understand that either he was taken up like Elijah or by some other way he was snatched into a divine place.

It is proper to observe here how what is said by Paul, 'And just as it is appointed for men to die once' (Heb 9:27), is made true. For if these, I say Elijah and Enoch, having been taken up, are to be with their thickest bodies even now and throughout the whole age, then the word of the wise and holy Paul concerning the necessity of all men dying is false. But it is not false. Therefore, what is set forth requires a theory, even if not in the way accustomed, that although other men have shared in death now, it must be understood that their mortal part is to be set aside according to the secret word of God, so that they might possess the fleshy life. For if the Savior is the 'firstborn from the dead' (Col 1:18), He would be the firstborn of these.

For it is undignified for such a word to be outside of them; furthermore, if they did not lay aside the fleshy life, as we have said, they would not have shared in the divine resurrection, by which from the dishonorable we shall all receive the body as honorable, from the glory as splendid, from the weak as powerful, from the psychic as spiritual. If one also reads the book of the Testament to a friend, he will know that he is said to be snatched into Paradise; and to know this, even if it is not from an irreproachable book, is not absurd. And there are those who [speak of] the translation by way of way...

They say it is so, according to which the Savior said to the disciples, 'You are no longer of this world, but I have chosen you' (John 15:19), effecting a transfer of election from the worldly things; and they receive another explicit thing constructed by this: 'We know that we have passed from death into life' (1 John 3:14). For those having passed from the death which follows through wickedness, we have been transferred unto the life which is from virtue.

This repayment suits not only Enoch, but all the saints; therefore, examine whether it is fitting to approve the former. And Noah was 500 years old, and Noah fathered three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. It is to be observed that he did not say at this point from how many years he began to father, but by chance he had three sons, not born at once. And it is also good that it is written that he had not fathered daughters, but sons, as a symbol showing that the righteous man is not a female-bearer, just as it has been written concerning Moses and Abraham; for these also did not have daughters.

For indeed someone is blessed, according to the Psalm, a father of well-born offspring, hearing: 'Blessed are you, and it shall be well with you. Your children like olive shoots around your table; thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord' (Psalm 128:3-4). But the daughters are perceived as symbols. Immediately also the tyrant Pharaoh, being fond of the males born by the Hebrews, destroys them, taking possession of the females. For those offspring of the soul that are well-born, those turning toward the things below strive to destroy, rejoicing in wealth and human things.

Immediately also the following explicitly teaches this: as a multitude became, daughters were born to them (Genesis 6:1). And it happened when men began to multiply on the earth, and daughters were born to them. The 'many' can also be applied to a multitude, over which especially it is most dominant, even regarding the Egyptians. For in the Exodus it is said: 'And the sons of Israel were fruitful and became Egyptians' (Exodus 1:7). But also the 'Many say to my soul' (Psalm 51:5) instead of 'Egyptians'; for words do not bring serious matters. english: To say these are earthly is appropriate, for thinking of earthly things, they were of little value and more suited to the many; for these are not in heaven, but upon the earth. It is fitting that 'and daughters were born to them' (Gen 6:2); for the foolish man neglects the female.

Indeed, the angels of God, seeing the daughters of men <that they were beautiful>, took wives for themselves from all those whom they chose. A wife is joined to a man by the Lord; therefore, he who uses marriage without hope toward God for himself and does not receive it from God—since God also brought the woman to Adam—is in error. It is therefore useful even the word [to avoid] doing anything without God. For he who strives for a marriage of honor does not look toward wealth, nor toward nobility, nor toward beauty, if he be uncontrolled.

So also the holy Abraham sends his own servant for a marriage, commanded to receive [the one] chosen for Isaac. The written Spirit also says about her, neglecting [it]: 'She was a virgin; a man knew her not' (Matt 1:25), because through 'she was a virgin' he shows the purity of the soul, and through 'a man knew her not' this very incorruptibility of the body. And that not every marriage is from God, Paul writes: 'Do not become unequally yoked with unbelievers' (2 Cor 6:14), which he commanded naturally at the beginning of the proclamation, even if Paul seems [to say]: 'If anyone has an unbelieving wife' (1 Cor 7:13); for it is clear that they were joined before faith, whom he did not wish to be divided after the faith so that the word might not be hindered.

And toward allegory, God joins a wife to a man for purpose, piety, and wisdom, so that he might beget virtues; for 'Wisdom' (Prov 8:2) indeed 'bears prudence to a man,' and Solomon says concerning wisdom: 'I became a lover of her beauty' (Song 1:4) and led her to live with myself. God joins this wife; for 'the Lord gives wisdom' (Prov 2:6). These men, concerning whom the preceding [text says] they took wives, did not expect this to happen from God. For this reproves their irrational desire, because they looked toward beauty; for this 'beautiful' signifies. It is sought by many whether angels by nature mixed with women...

Regarding what is said: some say that pleasure-seeking demons, having been enamored of the bodies of women, have united with them, but the resulting conception prevents this from being understood, for it is not possible for a human succession to exist in such a way. Others say that angels, desiring the bodies, have been entangled in sensation by God's providence, so that having been satiated with longing, they might return to what they left behind, while warning women toward sensation, and they say this is how they produce thoughts and actions. Others say that demons use pleasure as an instrument for wicked men, through whom they enjoy themselves by means of the sin of those people, as if they could unite with women.

Indeed, the Lord God said: 'My Spirit shall never remain in men for ever because they are flesh' (Psalm 51:13). The Spirit of God remains in those higher beings who have surpassed the material, for those who approach them are called 'flesh' because they are understood as material and subject to passions. For He does not speak of the immediate flesh; otherwise, it would happen that no man could partake of the Spirit of God. But that there is another flesh besides this visible one in which we are surrounded, Paul writes: 'For the mind of the flesh is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can it be: for they that are in the flesh cannot please God' (Romans 8:7); for if someone were to take the visible flesh, many would have pleased God with it, all the saints. And again saying, 'But ye are not in the flesh, but in the spirit' (Romans 8:9), he signifies the false flesh; for they were still in the flesh, having this life.

Furthermore, it is called flesh that which surrounds us, and the irrational animal, and man: 'For I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28), instead of upon men, 'and all flesh shall see the salvation of God' (Joel 2:32). And the word of scripture is also called flesh: 'For the flesh' he says, 'profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life' (John 6:63). For the scripture, when taken purely, does not give life sensually, just as we might say that he who makes shapes according to geometry is useful, but he who does this without reason would be less than a painter.

english: Since therefore many men, having been born, were full of weakness, he says, 'My Spirit shall not abide in them.' For 'a holy spirit of discipline will flee from guile' (Ps 51:13); but guile is a more grievous passion, for it harms thoughtlessly. And 'unto the age' (Gen 6:3) signifies how such they are throughout their life. This is equivalent to 'I will not eat meat unto the age' (Ex 11:5). Whether therefore men are being driven by demons having taken daughters, or, as is previously rendered, the angels of desirable sensations, the Spirit does not remain in these. For whoever has come to this through passions and sins, it is evident that they have no part of the divine Spirit; for even those who have come for the help of the divine Spirit are deprived.

If anyone should be surprised at the saying that angels are souls, he ought not to marvel; for the spiritual is the same for both, even if an angel has a subtle body and the man a thick one; for to please God is common to both, since it is also common to the rational nature. And if anyone brings an objection as to how the pre-existing souls desired bodies, of which they did not know, it must be said to whom that desiring is often said not strictly as desiring that toward which their actions lead. Often indeed, also rebuking those living not well, saying, 'you desire to perish' (Matt 27:5), we do not say that 'you desire this very thing' (Acts 22:4), but 'you do such things which lead you to destruction' (Gal 6:7). If therefore anyone says that the souls desired bodies, it must be understood thus: that they were in such a state that they had need of the intercourse in the body, their being unworthy to be in a place not like this, after such actions.

Yes, 'and their days shall be a hundred and twenty years' (Gen 15:16). Everything that God does and says, He does and says by a true judgment. Since therefore 'their days shall be a hundred and twenty' is said as a necessity, but this does not appear [to be so], it is necessary to interpret the intention of the thing foretold differently. The numbers received in the Scriptures were not received haphazardly, but for the sake of a certain word; often they are not even introduced naturally to the history, being received for the sake of a certain word. For to say, 'I left with myself seven thousand men, who did not do...' (1 Kings 19:18).

Because the history of bowing the knee to Baal is not possessed—for the holy one did not know so much—he was troubled for the sake of showing the thought, that everyone who surpasses the sensible and the world having been made in six days, having been brought forth in the restorative seventh week, is left by God as a goal for others and a benefit.

Thus also the number six was taken in the generation of this world as perfect, just as it has been said in the passages. And 'six times he is delivered from necessities' is not said because of the number or because of being delivered from necessities so many times, but rather, as long as one is in the things of the one having been made in six, he is under necessities, thus it is said; of the cessation, which is shown through the seventh, they do not have purification, as it was said to the disciples by the Savior: 'You are not of this world' (John 15:19) having surpassed the necessities in it.

These things were prepared beforehand to show that the number one hundred twenty is not in vain taken here; and it is necessary also to note this, that the scripture, taking the numbers, connects them with their own properties as of the world having been made in six days (Genesis 1). Let us take an example. For it is not possible to say that God made the world in six angels or in six monads or in six men; for time was being shown. Therefore, being offered in six days, it is said because time falls to the generation, being appropriately synchronized with the day, so as not to be years or months or hours; for the former is worthy of God, but the latter is the name of the incomplete; for not knowing what a day is, we are ignorant of the hour. And there, since it was concerning life, he mentioned years.

And... the many will say that God, as cutting off their life, established it at one hundred twenty, with the former living many years; but this was not fitting; for they seem to have lived more years. Let us therefore see the characteristic of the number. It is said therefore that this number, having been composed of its own parts, is doubled; for if the half is composed, which is sixty, the third is [missing], the fourth is [missing], the fifth is twenty-four, the sixth is twenty, the eighth is eighty-five, the tenth is [missing], the twelfth is [missing], the fifteenth is eight, the twentieth is [missing], the twenty-fourth is five, the thirtieth is four...

english: Four hundred sixty-two, one hundred twenty-one, makes the total four hundred forty, being double the one hundred twenty, of which the parts are fifteen, just as fifteen increased by progression makes the one hundred twenty. That the fifteen was received into the most perfect degree is clear; for of that same number six degrees [are missing]. But also the 'giving a portion to the seven', which signifies the Old Testament, and 'also to the eight', which is a symbol of the Resurrection and the New Testament, joins the fifteen. For the Jews, receiving only the old, give a portion to the seven, not hearing that it also gives to the eight; but also the heretics, setting aside the old, giving a portion to the eight, refuse to have the seven provide; the ecclesiastical, receiving both covenants, gives a portion to both. Since therefore also the one hundred twenty number is doubled, there exists a symbol of teaching being awakened toward the true life according to both practice and contemplation, honored, so that having doubled the life, they may have this life, being made manifest through the number, in order that the said thing—that he who lives not also by practice and contemplation does not live, but just as the profligate has died—may be true.

4. And the giants were upon the earth in those days and after that, as the sons of God were approaching the daughters of men and they became to themselves (Gen 6:4). Those were the giants from of old, the men who are named. Those outside the faith, bringing this in from myths, bring it in; but in the Divine Scripture, instead of strong men, they are named. For in Isaiah, God threatening to take away the useful things of these, since they were worthy of this, joins both giant and strong among those being taken away. And Goliath he thus called, testifying...

english: They were acting, and they were being destroyed together with the man, through whom he also came to fulfill his own needs, a life-spark being left behind with Noah and from them.

Likewise, men were also perishing as wickedness increased upon the earth, because they sinned by thinking with the evil, not casually but through careful use of sins. Let us carefully examine what was said from the beginning: 'The Lord God having seen,' he says, 'that the wickednesses of men had been multiplied upon the earth' (Gen 6:5). For did he not previously see their wickednesses? But it is evident that now he has seen them for the purpose of vengeance. For when he does not wish to send punishments to those sinning, it is said he does not see them, which is to say when he is sleeping, while others are watching. It is indeed said by someone: 'I awoke to my impieties,' and after having tested the patience of God through many impieties, after those who reproach had passed by, he says: 'I awoke to my impieties.' And another saint said: 'He arose like one sleeping, like a strong man having roared from wine'; for having been very patient, he comes excessively and unceasingly with punishments to those in such need, which is why the unceasingness and the multitude is called an awakening and a roaring from wine. For it is like a good physician to use the sufferings at the right time, which is made evident by 'The Lord God having seen.'

And if it is about to be that 'everyone thinks in his heart toward evil things' (Ps 32:9), even though Noah did not have it so, we should not be surprised; for it is said regarding the majority in this way, just as 'every brother betrays and every friend acts deceitfully' (Prov 27:6). And it is possible, since Noah was not at all a man—for he had ascended beyond the human condition—that this was said as not being applicable to him at all among men, but happening to a god, as it is said: 'He called those gods to whom the word of God came.' Similar to this is also 'I said in my ecstasy: every man is a liar' (Ps 53:6); for he was a god, as we have demonstrated, the one saying these things. For if a man were not thus, if he were a liar, then 'every man' would no longer be true.

Not a liar, but speaking the truth, yet he is not a man himself, who is called a man through excellence beyond human measure, as it is said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy, are you not men, as these also walk?' (James 3:16). For their malice was not practiced by them by chance, but with care and deliberation; for this reveals what is in the heart (Luke 6:45).

Likewise, 'from youth' can be understood in two ways: either being smeared with evil from a small age, or that no one among those described as a man is an elder, even if the nature is so, setting forward the novelties and the instabilities. 'For old age is not an honorable thing measured by long life or by the number of years; for much is wisdom to men, and old age is a life without a cloud' (Sirach 4:10). And it is not unlikely that the 'youth of sin' and 'remember not my ignorance' (Psalm 25:11) carry interpretations saying: 'Remember not whatever evil things I have done.'

Having said these things, it is worthy to consider what is revealed from 'God remembered that he made man upon the earth' (Psalm 8:4) and 'I was grieved that I made them' (Psalm 8:5), which is equivalent to 'I repented that I made Saul king' (1 Samuel 15:11). It must be said, however, that things are said about God in a human manner, and not in the way the words and the thought possess. For if hands, feet, eyes, and ears are transferred in the Scripture, one must not think that God is formed in a human way, but it is clear that we shall call each of these things regarding the active powers of God, such as hands and the unretreating eyes, and likewise his discerning eyes and his practical hands, even if through another understanding.

For indeed, regarding sensible things, each of the named things signifies only one thing, such as wood; but regarding God, they are called by many names, which are to be understood by the word as preceding the various things about him. For so God is called both Spirit and Source, and again hands and feet are said to belong to him; yet nowhere, even if he had something sensible, were his names so many; for neither light nor Spirit nor Source have hands.

english: It was thought and regretted as if regarding an unchangeable mind. For just as men, wishing to present a confession to those being taught by themselves that they erred greatly and are unworthy of lessons, say: 'I regretted that I gave so much to you, leading you to the knowledge of the transgression,' so also God is said to not undergo a passion of regret, but rather to speak for the sake of the manifestation of the greatness of the sin. For He did not not know that such things would be, but through goodness He viewed whether perhaps from the laws written according to the intellect [they would follow]. We use an image toward it not being a passion of God, but of those who change in such a way.

Let someone be wise... [gaps]... and because of this an heir... [gaps]... he himself did not change according to the mind among those changed, when the property came to the righteous alone; for this one had the purpose from the beginning. And good is 'I will blot out the man whom I have made from the face of the earth' (Gen 1:28); for He does not lead him into non-existence, nor does He blot him out according to the soul, but from the earth. And this is not only the work of God, having been deceived by evil, to destroy men, but also through a sign to destroy the one dwelling in the earth being a lowly one; for the lowly one is a resident of the earth, the holy one being not a resident but a sojourner. Thus also it is said in Jeremiah: 'The evils shall be burned upon those dwelling on the earth' (Jer 5:31), those rooting themselves on the earth, which the holy one says he did not suffer, thanking: 'In a short time He has brought me to an end in the land' (Ps 116:7), and in the Revelation it is said: 'Woe to those dwelling on the earth' (Rev 6:10), not to those sojourning; but the purpose of God is to snatch the man from the earthlings, even if he himself holds to the earthlings.

'But Noah found grace in the sight of the Lord God' (Gen 6:8). It is great and heavenly to find grace in the sight of God, and this is accomplished through pleasing Him, which follows that to please men, the one pleasing to men not always pleasing to God. For see what the blessed Paul says: 'If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a Christ's slave' (Gal 1:10).

Then I would not have been, and the Psalmist says: 'The Lord scatters the bones of those who please men' (Ps 52:9). But those who have the grace from God say: 'He who has graced us along with the beloved' (Eph 1:6), just as Mary also hears from the angel: 'Rejoice, favored one, the Lord is with you' (Luke 1:28). For this is the grace, to have the Lord with oneself; and one has the Lord with oneself by being distinguished by virtue and good deeds, saying: 'If you seek the testing of the Christ speaking in me' (1 Cor 4:9).

For He himself gives grace and peace; for this is what the holy man prays for, saying: 'Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ' (2 Cor 13:13). And God gives this gift, having provided us the occasion to receive it. For it is said in Proverbs: 'Grace and friendship set free, which you have kept for yourself, so that you may not become despised' (Prov 28:14); for in the power of one's own choice is the ability to keep these and to succeed.

Thus also Noah found grace in the sight of the Lord God from his own domestic preparation, himself having graced himself through works of virtue and from this having received grace from God; for the God of all, working together with those succeeding and striving on our part, adds to, adorns, and leads into the greatness of good. The disciples of the Savior, knowing this, having already pre-succeeded in the faith toward him, were saying to him, knowing that faith is also God-given: 'Increase our faith' (Luke 22:32).

For just as a word of wisdom is given through the Spirit and a word of knowledge according to the Spirit (1 Cor 12:8), so also faith is in the same Spirit. For it is impossible to receive the faith given from God according to grace without having that which is established from our own part. For this is made clear from 'increase our faith' (Luke 22:32); but even Isaiah says, from the person of the Lord's man, or even from himself: 'He has added to me an ear for hearing, and the instruction of the Lord opens my ears' (Isa 50:4); for the hearing and instruction given toward God opens even these ears to hear the intellect more divinely.

Thus also let us understand 'grace for grace' (John 1:16), understanding the one from God approaching through our own part. And also let us understand the 'found' [which was] said, so that it might be shown that having sought...

english: He found it rightly, those who do not seek in the way they ought, not finding; for they say, 'They shall seek me,' yet 'evil men and they shall not find' (John 14:20). From this it is known that he sought well from the judgment and gift of God, when, as if sealing the grace himself, he gives: 'Not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of the merciful God' (Romans 3:27), and 'If the Lord builds a house, in vain the builders labored for it' (Psalm 127:1).

Yes, 9. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God (Genesis 6:9). The genealogy of the righteous is not so much of men as of virtues; for these are his preceding offspring. This indeed teaches the written Spirit; for it being the case to say the generations of Noah, it brought forward: 'Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God' (Genesis 6:9).

Let us see what is signified by 'perfect in his generation.' According to a first interpretation, one might say that, compared to the men of his own time who had endowed themselves with immeasurable evil, he was perfect; this is not a great thing, if he were compared to the unknown, for it might perhaps be possible to say that of those entering the ark with him, he was called perfect because he was different; for it is indeed likely that they were such from the holy habit.

It might also be said thus: the generation of the righteous is similarity, and this is signified from 'This is the generation of those seeking him' (Psalm 14:3); for having said, 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who has innocent hands and is pure in heart' (Psalm 24:3-4) and the following, he brought forward: 'This is the generation of those seeking him,' having spoken of one generation of those adorned with the same virtue. By this, in the opposite way, similarly, it is the thing said: 'Sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their own generation'; for the generation of such things is the similar state and way of life.

And it is necessary to hear 'perfect' as it is in men, which Paul said to know perfectly in part, saying concerning the perfect: 'When the perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away' (1 Corinthians 13:10); all the perfection being accomplished in men is as towards that in the future.

An age is complete only in part. Let what is said be clear by way of an example: he who is in the first letters is complete, yet as far as the one listening to grammatical discourse, he is incomplete. And the Apostle himself, saying, 'We know in part and we prophesy in part' (1 Cor 13:9), speaks this concerning himself and those like him: 'As for those who are perfect, we think this,' and 'But we speak wisdom among the perfect' (1 Cor 1:6); for just as the citizenship existing there is incomplete, as we have said, as far as the knowledge that is to come, being 'face to face' (1 Cor 13:12), even if it has reached its utmost limit.

And the things said about Noah—that he was righteous, and perfect, and pleasing to God—must be taken all at once, even if the words have an order; for he was 'righteous' and 'being perfect' he had a pleasingness toward God. But the perfect and the righteous are anticipated by the pleasingness; for it is not that because he pleased, he became righteous and perfect, but because he appeared righteous and perfect, he has been shown to be pleasing to God. And if Noah is said to be a man of such a state, it is not necessary to be surprised, since we have often observed that the name 'man' signifies more; for it is not regarding mere dust alone, as it is said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not acting as men and walking according to man?' (Gal 1:7), and concerning the devil sowing evil thoughts, it is said: 'A man has done this' (John 6:70); here, in addition to declaring the nature, it also signifies the 'man' as the one who saves according to the 'image' (Gen 1:26). And also, that he 'being perfect pleased God' (Gen 6:8); for he pleased God having already been promised perfection, not pleasing God by pleasing in everything, but by being [pleasing] to both righteous men and in other ways to men; for he is praised not only for pleasing the righteous, but after [that] for pleasing God.

10. And Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. He fathered three sons, and Noah became a father of such a number; for nothing was said before this of having had another child. The explicit part is clear; but if one looks toward an upward leading, he might say that one fathering two of a certain physical sex would be casting symbols; for the two are kindred in matter, for this is divisible; but the one who fathered three is called perfect, being first to bear a complete image.

Τοσαύτη δὲ ἡ κακία τῶν ἀνθρώπων γεγένηται, οἵτινες γῆκαλοῦνται, ὡς Θεὸν ἰδεῖν αὐτὴν τὸν διὰ πολλὴν ἀγαθότητα παρορῶντα καὶ τὰ μεγάλα τῶν πταισμάτων· 167 εἴρηται γάρ· "6Ἐὰν ἀνομίας παρατηρήσῃ Κύριε, Κύριε τίς ὑποστήσεται;"6 Οὐκ ὀργὴν οὖν ἐπάγει καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, ἐπειδὰν δὲ τὰ μέτρια τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων γένηται, ὡς λεχθῆναι καθάπερ ἐν τῷ προφήτῃ Ἰωνᾴ· "6Ἀνέβη ἡ κραυγὴ τῆς κακίας πρὸς τὸν Θεόν"6, καὶ περὶ Σοδόμων· "6Κραυγὴ Σοδόμων καὶ Γομόρων πεπλήθυνται, καὶ αἱ ἁμαρτίαι αὐτῶν μεγάλαι σφόδρα"6, ὡς καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὸ ὅμοιον· "6Καὶ ἐπλήσθη ἡ γῆ ἀδικίας"6 τό τε λοιπόν. Ὁρᾷ οὐ πρότερον ἀγνοῶν, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐπὶ ἐκδικίας ἐποπτικὴν δύναμιν δηλῶν, καθὰ ἐν τῷ "6Καὶ εἶδεν ὁ Θεὸς τὴν γῆν, καὶ ἦν κατεφθαρμένη"6. Φθορὰ δέ ἐστιν καὶ τὸ εἰς ἀδόκιμον παραδοθῆναι νοῦν· ἐσχάτη γὰρ αὕτη τιμωρία. Οὐ δεῖ δὲ κατὰ τοὺς Μανιχαίους οἴεσθαι ὅτι ἡ ἄποιος ὕλη περιλειφθεῖσα ἐν τῷ περιπολεῖν
english: Of the Creator, for He is a support; and still, the removal of a number from Him makes a dyad, as it is evident that the three came by addition. But to humans, those things which are signified by the two, if a calculation were added, no longer remain material or human, partaking of rectitude; for it is not necessary merely to act, but also with right reason, so that it may receive praise.

And one is able, by changing the mode of speech, to take these things toward the perfection of the soul; for first a passion must come to the soul, then thus a disposition must become, and thus to impel toward action. And we say a passion is not the thing being denied, but the impulse of the soul as it would imprint upon the virtuous; and these things also happen from the opposite.

Three, therefore, are these offspring of the diligent; let the pre-passion now be as a weight toward the indifferent things. And if one, imposing [them] even upon interpretations, might find something useful, let him observe. Shem, indeed, is interpreted perfect, Japheth breadth or beauty, but Ham is daring or impetuous or heat or excess.

And what other offspring would have been fitting for the righteous, such as perfection, breadth and beauty, which are all the marks of virtue? For beauty, joined with breadth, makes the wide road go outward, which leads to destruction; but if it is that Ham is interpreted daring or impetuous or heat or excess, let these be taken as domestic to his manner, as if toward the worthless son for a reproach, but toward the perfect, let them be received with diligent use; for the virtuous is most unforced, since even the violent seize the kingdom; but such a one is also daring against the opposing powers, according to Paul the blessed saying, 'Our struggle is not against blood and flesh' (Eph 6:12), and the following: this impetuous one, just as he is daring, is not acquiring impetuousness toward evil, but happening upon virtue, being hot and zealous in the Spirit, from which he also stands apart from human [things] (Eph 1:11–12).
But the earth was against the Lord, and the earth was filled with injustice. And the Lord God saw the earth, and it was corrupted, because all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth.

The corruption of the earth does not signify the loss of the so-beautiful element into non-existence, but rather the excess of the sins of men; the earth calls men by a metonymic manner, just as the psalmist says: 'Let all the earth worship you and sing to you' (Ps 66:5), and again 'Sing to the Lord, all the earth' (Ps 96:1); for when it is said 'The heavens and the earth were finished' (Gen 2:4), this element is signified, and 'Let the earth blossom' (Isa 45:18). Such has become the wickedness of men, who are called earth, as to see God, that element which incites them through much goodness and the great things of the wings. For it has been said: 'If, Lord, you observe iniquity, Lord, who will stand?' (Job 35:12). It does not bring wrath day by day, but when the moderate measures of sins occur, as it was said just as in the prophet Jonah: 'The cry of wickedness ascended to God' (Jon 2:2), and concerning Sodom: 'The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has filled [the heavens], and their sins are exceedingly great' (Gen 18:20), just as here the similar is said: 'And the earth was filled with injustice' (Gen 6:11), and the rest.

See that [God] is not previously ignorant, but is manifesting the watchful power toward vengeance, just as in 'And God saw the earth, and it was corrupted' (Gen 6:11). And he calls the corruption the wickedness and the punishment upon it, just as the Scripture often declares in that which was said by Paul: 'If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him' (1 Cor 3:17); for he who, sinning through lawlessness, works the corruption of the temple of God, is found under punishment and is destroyed, the punishment being now signified by the corruption. And it is a corruption also to be delivered over to an unproven mind; for this is the most extreme punishment. And it is not necessary, according to the Manichaeans, to suppose that useless matter remaining in the wandering...

Θαυμασιώτερα δὲ ταῦτα καὶ μείζονα τῆς σωμάτων ἰάσεως, ὅσῳ καὶ ἡ ψυχῆς οὐσία τιμιωτέρα σώματος, ἀλλ' ὅπερ οἱ πολλοὶ ἀγνοοῦσιν. Ὁ οὖν τὰ παράδοξα οὕτως αὐτοῖς διηγούμενος ὠφελιμώτερον ποιεῖ, καὶ ἐν τοῖς νῦν συνεκτεθεῖσιν τὰ τῆς 169 ἱστορίας πολλὴν καὶ εὐσυνοπτοτέραν τοῖς πολλοῖς ἔχει τὴν ὠφελίαν. Προδεδήλωται γὰρ ὅτι ἐν ἑκατὸν ἔτεσιν ἐγίνετο τὸ τῆς κιβωτοῦ κατασκεύασμα, ἵνα ὁρῶντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι καὶ πυνθανόμενοι τὴν αἰτίαν λάβωσιν καιρὸν μετανοίας. Καιρὸν δὲ ἐνταῦθα οὐ δεῖ νομίζειν τὸν παρά τισιν ὡροσκόπον καλούμενον· οὐδὲ γὰρ εἱμαρμένη κρατεῖ τῶν πραγμάτων, ἀλλὰ ψήφῳ Θεοῦ πάντα γίνεται. ∆ιόπερ ἡγητέον τὸ "6Καιρὸς παντὸς ἀνθρώπου ἥκει ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"6 σημαίνειν τὴν ὡσανεὶ συμπλήρωσιν τῶν ἡμαρτημένων ἀνθρώποις, καθ' ἣν ἡ τῆς ἐκδικίας ἐπαγωγὴ προσάγεσθαι ὀφείλει, καθὸ λέγεται· "6Οὔπω γὰρ ἀναπεπληρῶνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι τῶν Ἀμαρραίων ἕως τοῦ νῦν"6 ἀντὶ τοῦ οὔπω τοσαῦτα ἥμαρτον ὡς ἀπογνωσθῆναι αὐτῶν τὴν μετάνοιαν. Καὶ γὰρ οὐκ ὀργὴν ἐπάγει ὁ Θεὸς καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, καίτοι ἁμαρτημάτων γινομένων, τοῦτο δὲ ποιεῖ τόπον μετανοίας παρέχων καὶ διδοὺς καιρὸν τοῦ καταγνῶναι ἑαυτῶν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας· ὅταν δὲ οὕτω συνετελεσθῇ τὰ κατ' αὐτοὺς ὡς μηκέτι ἔχειν καιρὸν τοῦ μεταγνῶναι, καιρὸς ἦλθεν τοῦ παθεῖν αὐτούς. Πάσας μὲν γὰρ ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ τὰς ἀρετὰς εἶναι δυνατόν, ἀλλήλαις γὰρ ἀντακολουθοῦσιν, τὰς δὲ κακίας οὐχ οἷόν τε διὰ τὰ προειρημένα. Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ὡς παρεκβάσει, ἐπανελθῶμεν δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς· "6Καιρὸς παντὸς ἀνθρώπου ἥκει"6. Οὐδεὶς τοιαῦτα ἁμαρτήματα ἔχει ὡς συγχωρηθῆναι αὐτῷ· καὶ ὥσπερ ἄριστος ἰατρὸς καιρὸν τοῦ τροφὴν δέξασθαι τὸν κάμνοντα, κἂν ἐν νυκτὶ γίνηται, κατὰ τὴν τοῦ νοσήματος τοιάνδε κατάστασιν τίθεται, οὕτω καὶ τὸ νῦν λεγόμενον. Τοιῶσδε γὰρ ἐχόντων τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὡς εἰς ἔσχατον ἁμαρτίας ἥκειν, δι' ἃς ὁ κατακλυσμὸς ἐπάγεται, γίνεται τοῦτο
english: He works the corruption of the earth. For this made men blameless, if the inability to be adorned toward God worked a sorrow; but the hardship of ways is shown through the corruption of the earth, just as it was foretold, of men corrupting the way of God, which had taken hold to prosper toward blessedness. Such are those having heard the words of Jesus and not doing them.

And if it also shows the flesh of man, as is often said, one should observe whether 'all flesh corrupted his way' (Ps 145:17) shows how each man has strayed from his own opinion. But that flesh is said instead of man is clear from 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh' (Isa 44:3), and 'He will judge all flesh' (Isa 40:6). Therefore all those of the generation of Noah, having become earthly and fleshy, each strayed from 'his way' (Gen 6:11) which he had received; for the way is called to be received of him and to be given to God. Thus they corrupted their own way or the way of God; for both are possible.

And God said to Noah: 'The time of every man comes against me, because the earth was filled with injustice from them' (Gen 6:11). Many of the written things have a more useful history for the many. For these, living by sensation and glory, do not reach the truly great and profitable things. And let the said thing be upon an example.

Jesus healed a blind man from birth, and Lazarus, having had four days in the tomb, he brought out by command alone, and again the one in the cave, remaining in much decay, he raised. These things were for the sensible fulfillment and were symbolic: the one [healing] the blind from birth showing the sight of a soul that had never seen, because it had been overturned in sin and ignorance from soft nails, and again the one already pathless and having lost hope, having fallen from the blessed life, was shown symbolically coming back to it through Jesus, and the one seized by decay, then having been saved, testified to the return of a soul falling into insensibility. But these are more wonderful and greater than the healing of bodies, since the essence of the soul is more precious than the body, but which the many do not know. He, therefore, explaining the paradoxes thus to them, makes it more useful, and in the things now set forth of the history...

It also has a more useful benefit for the many. For what does he say? 'The opportunity for every man has come upon the earth' (Luke 19:44). And Peter also says that by the patience of God the deluge was delayed, so that repentance might be given.

For it has been revealed that the construction of the ark took place in a hundred years, so that seeing men and inquiring about the cause might take the opportunity for repentance. But opportunity here must not be thought of as being called by someone a time-keeper; for not fate holds sway over things, but everything happens by the will of God.

Therefore, it should be understood that 'the opportunity for every man has come upon the earth' means the almost-fullness of the sinning men, by which the bringing on of vengeance must be approached, as it is said: 'For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet full unto this time' (Gen 15:16), instead of saying 'they have not sinned so much that their repentance be known.' For God does not bring wrath upon every single day, even though sins are being committed; rather, He does this by providing a place for repentance and giving the opportunity to recognize their own sinning; but when thus the things concerning them are completed so that they no longer have opportunity to recognize [their sin], the time has come for them to suffer.

And once the mention of the filling up of sin has occurred, this is to be noted: that it is not the same to fill up sins in one man and in a whole nation. For among the many, all sins are found to be present, such as one being unmanageable and another being spared, one being bold and another cowardly, and again one being licentious and another being foolish; but for one man, it is impossible to find these opposing vices in excess and deficiency. For it is possible for all virtues to be in a man, for they follow one another, but the vices are not so, because of the things previously mentioned.

And these things being a digression, let us return to the beginning: 'The opportunity for every man has come.' No one has such sins that they might be forgiven him; and just as an excellent physician, even if it happens at night, sets a time for the sick to receive nourishment according to the state of the disease, so also is the present thing being said. For when men have reached the extremity of sin, through which the deluge is brought, this happens.

english: They act without being recognized. It is not necessary to suppose it is a lie that the time of every man has come, even if eight were saved in the ark; for here the general has been taken instead of 'for the most part'.

If, however, the 'every man' says, 'For where are strife and jealousy among you, are you not men?' (James 3:16), Noah is not subject to this by surpassing the human condition; and thus it is true that the time of every man has come, according to that which is called to sin in this way. Nor is 'against me' added in vain; for no mortal possesses the knowing of the time, by which one might have worthily acted so that the rest might have been made known. For this indeed no mortal truly knows; for if he were knowing the hearts, he would not even have helped by quickly turning back those who had come into sin.

For the only thing belonging to the unexceedable goodness, the goodness of essence which is not diminished, is to see the hidden and to know the time. If even someone of mortals participates in goodness from God by disposition, yet he is ignorant of the impositions of sins and the causes, just as God, knowing all, knows the time of the reprimand, therefore it is said 'against me' and 'because the earth was filled with injustice from them'. It is fitting that this too is said; for punishment does not come upon them because of the sins of others. It is also evident from this that such a death did not come upon them by fate; for since he says 'the earth was filled with injustice from them', the time has come, which would not have been established, unless they were sinning.

Yes, and behold, 'I will destroy them and the earth' (Jonah 3:4). The philanthropy and goodness of God are shown through these by foretelling what is to come, so that by the fear of what is expected, he might restrain the evil, which also happened to the Ninevites upon hearing the prophet Jonah: 'In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown' (Jonah 3:4). Consequently, too, to the righteous man he foretells these things and pre-arranges the making of the ark, putting forward this construction more clearly for the sake of every proclamation toward repentance, and he promises to destroy them and the earth, since it was necessary for this. For there are many reprimands given by God for the sake of the recognition of sins occurring; he wants...

For he says that he wished to gather all men into the knowledge of truth, as a bird gathers its young under its wings, but you did not wish to (Matt 23:37). For necessity does not force the good to become so, nor is it possible; for such a thing is no longer good. But when God, knowing all things, after many admonitions finds those whom he admonishes not obeying, he destroys them, according to what is profitable for his judgment. And the earth is also destroyed—that is, the things in the earth—for this is what 'the earth' signifies appropriately; for the things of men perishing, it was necessary for the things standing through them to pass away also. Just as the birds were left behind through Noah and those with him, and likewise the birds of all other animals were left behind.

Make for yourself an ark of squared timber; you shall make an ark for the sick; and you shall make it secure inside and outside with pitch (Gen 6:14). And so you shall make the ark: three hundred cubits the length of the ark, and fifty cubits the breadth, and thirty cubits its height. You shall make the ark by gathering [pieces] together, and you shall complete it one cubit by one cubit upward; and you shall make the door of the ark on the side. Make for it two or three decks. And I, behold, I bring the flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh, in which is the spirit of life under heaven; and whatever is on the earth shall perish (Gen 6:17).

The phrase 'of squared timber' has the greater following, being commanded to make Noah's ark, first so that much time would not be consumed in dividing them, and secondly, which is more truthful, so that being made from whole timbers it might be more secure; for it was going to encounter storms and not a small gale, against which it would not have withstood if it had not been constructed from whole timbers. And 'the sick' is also useful, which are divided places, because of these two things: first, so that the habitation of the animals, which he was going to bring with him, would not be mixed, and second, for the joining of the construction; [it is] weaker...

english: For it was—if fifty in width, three hundred in length, and thirty cubits in height—existing as an unconnected thing. It was well-sealed both outside and inside to prevent water from entering toward nothingness.

And indeed, the fact that the length was greater than the width was good; for in this way it was easy to move, since even the boats are in proportion to this shape. And if someone were to say that it became square underneath, this is not without truth; for it was made not for sailing previously, but for guarding, and for this reason it became so; otherwise it would have been quickly worn down, if it were not square. And it was joined together appropriately, so that the influx of the waters might have a sliding effect and not, as if against rock, throw the waves upward everywhere by its height. And the making of the door on the sides was appropriately arranged.

The dwellings were constructed appropriately so as to endure all the animals being brought in, both those and those for food. And the passage, 'But I, even I, bring a flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven; whatever is on the earth shall perish' (Genesis 6:17), is indeed awakening, as previously stated, and shows that both those on the earth and those in the air shall perish; for perhaps the aquatic ones were saved. And 'I establish my covenant with you' (Genesis 9:9). The covenant made by God with Noah does not appear to be an alliance, as Symmachus and Aquila interpreted. Perhaps so that He might not despise the words, the future was revealed to Noah, so that he might be hopeful concerning the things to come and might instruct, and his own generation, as 'God brought these things upon them because of sins; and you are being saved through righteousness' (Genesis 6:13), so that the shame of wickedness might be shown and the attraction of virtue; not as virtue exists as a pleasant wage, but because the diligent one, not being subject to the manner of punishment, does not rest from it. And 'I establish' shows the stability here. If you, your sons, your wife, and the wives of your sons enter into the ark (Genesis 7:7). The Savior in the Gospel said—

Regarding every idle word, men will give an account on the day of judgment; but an idle word is useless and having nothing beneficial. If this is not presented as a burden to men, much more do the divine words not contain such a thing, but everything is brought forth usefully in them, and we have seen this from the things set forth.

When entering the ark, Noah arranged the sons, and to the wife the wives of his sons; and when the time for going out into the earth remained, the flooding having ceased, the saying is noted thus: 'And God said to Noah: You and your wife and your sons and the wives of your sons come out of the ark' (Gen 7:7). For it was proper, since the corruption of men was about to happen, that the righteous should not be without companions, so as to use the married ones. Therefore he separated the wives of the men, saying: 'Let in you and your sons and your wife and the wives of your sons' (Gen 8:18); but when it was received that the succession was about to be restored again, he gave to Noah the wife, saying: 'Come out, you and your wife and your sons and the wives of your sons' (Gen 8:18).

And that because of custom it was not spoken appropriately, but with observation, it is possible to say, and to believe the Gospel, it having been said by the Savior: 'No one is able to serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other; you cannot serve God and mammon' (Matt 6:24). And it is clear that the love of money is the slavery of mammon, and [it is] upon every evil. For it is in no way possible to serve both evil and virtue; for the one doing sin is a slave of sin, and everyone who does [sin] hates the evil things. For those who love [God] hate the evil things. 'For either he will hate the one and love the other'—for the virtuous one loves God and hates evil—'or he will hold to the one and despise the other,' which is precisely said; for he said 'to hold against' the evil, not 'to love' it. For no one with love toward...
