english: He does not act, but having slipped, he holds on; and he is not said to hate God, but to despise Him. Therefore, the dwelling place of the word is this: for the diligent, to be loved by God; for wickedness, to be hated; and again, for wickedness, to hold on to the worthless person, and for God, to be despised by such a person.

For no one is ever said to despise someone of sin or to hate God, even if the worthless ones, having leaned toward wickedness for a moment, are said to hate God according to: 'Lord, did I not hate those whom you hate?' (Psalm 43:22). But the Lord does not do this, but, having slipped, as it was said, he is said to hate. And to despise is the most important of such precision and observation, according to what is said again by the Savior: 'Whoever confesses me before men, I will confess him also' (Matthew 10:32)—not 'in me' he said, 'but I will deny him' (Matthew 10:33). For the one confessing God in Christ does this, but the one denying does not do this in Christ. Therefore, the confession must be in Him.

It has been said that confession is to those who are not such, but only to those saying it with words: 'They profess God, but their works deny Him' (Titus 1:16), and 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me' (Isaiah 29:13). For in the one confessing, the one being confessed is present, and the one confessing is in the one being confessed. But let no one think the same regarding 'I am in the Father and the Father is in me' (John 14:10); for the one signifies [union], the other signifies being in the one being confessed, as is shown in 'whoever confesses in me,' where 'I will confess him also' is not changed—for God does not partake of man—but [it signifies] a judgment from God.

Not of the one confessing. Thus also it has been said concerning the sons of Noah and him and his wife and his sons, but as we have well observed: 'Enter, you and your sons with you' (Gen 7:1). For not he through them, but they through him and the benefit from him were saved. And this is confirmed by what is coming in the next, the saying of God to Noah: 'Because I saw you righteous before me in this generation' (Gen 6:9). For the greatness of his soul is shown by the 'righteous,' since it is not simply testified, but before God.

Regarding verse 19: And from all animals and from all flesh, two by two from all (Gen 7:2). If someone, aiming at the natures of numbers and knowing that the seven in the Scriptures has many prefigurations remembered, and the two is appropriate to the matter, as was said before, will understand how he arranged the number seven among the clean in the following, but the two among the unclean even now; and he will also seek how, even before the law was given concerning clean and unclean, the two is said, lest someone might argue that to the righteous was fore-seen the scientific arrangement of the law. And he also will provide how one man is so powerful over such animals as to even bring them into the ark; let him hear that it is given to the righteous to fulfill the command through God's cooperation, and nothing is improbable regarding what is said by God and the wild animals. And if even to the foremost of the apostles, Peter, in the vessel like a mirror of all animals, the images were made manifest, what is improbable if [God] brought together [them] because a world is to be made again, when he commands the righteous the bringing in of these, so that from them also a succession of generations might come after these things.

english: And female; there shall be from the winged ones according to kind, and from the cattle according to kind, and from all creeping things of the earth according to their kind. Two by two from all shall come in to you to be fed with you, male and female. And let one note that here 'kind' is used instead of 'species', it being said sometimes 'species' and 'kind'. [Gap] And you shall take to yourself from all the foods that you eat, and you shall gather to yourself, and there shall be for you and for them to eat.

It is to be supposed for the righteous man not only to think of himself and those with him, but also of the speechless, for he justly pities the souls of his cattle. Regarding 'gathering to yourself', it has a remark that in the places where you live, and other animals do not approach, gather the foods; for if they lay in those places, they were working out their need by greedily attacking the foods.

And Noah did all that the Lord God commanded him, so he did. Great is the praise when, having done it with understanding, a reliable one capable of judging rightly says, 'that he did thus as the one who commanded had instructed him'; for this is the virtue of the action. For there was once [gap] not indeed thus as he was commanded; for [gap] to the showing of the action [gap] of the disposition, not the manner which is [gap]. Every action not occurring with the proper calculation is incomplete, even if the result becomes perfect; and the righteous is testified to as having also done [gap].

For this also the Savior instructs, saying, 'Have mercy and you shall be shown mercy' (Luke 6:36), but he intends that mercy should not come through pitying, which is not to be a merchant or to play with the needs of the suffering; for they say, 'Become perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect' (Matthew 5:48); for God is giving of Himself and not receiving from another; so also you, zeal for the giving, just as the blessed Paul also leaves [it]: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive' (Acts 20:35). God is not one who receives anything from anyone, but is the provider of all good things. Thus, the imitator of God gives. As it is written, 'And the Lord God said to Noah: Enter, you and all your household, into the ark, because I have seen you righteous before me in this generation' (Gen 7:1).

In this way it appears that the whole house consisted of only the eight; for they did not bring a healer unless it was to prevent men from being lost or because of the being of such people. Therefore, a house is called here the kinship within the eight, for often such a name is shared by those who are of the same kind, especially regarding the one having been built. The same thing you would find regarding a city.

For it is said in the Gospel, 'And he led him' (meaning Jesus), 'to the brow of the mountain, where their city was built' (Matt 13:52), signifying now the name of the city that was constructed and built; and in 'And when Jesus entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred' (Matt 21:10), the gathering of the people is signified by the city. And again, in 'Jesus began to upbraid the cities in which most of his powers had come to pass, because they did not repent' (Luke 19:43), this signifies: for repentance does not happen in non-living things or material things; whereas the name of the house signifies the building in 'This is this house...' ...the assembly, the gathering, if it is said... the royal, and the jailer, and the house. He says the reason for entering the ark was 'because I saw you righteous before me' (Gen 7:1). He did not say simply 'because I saw you'—for Abel was righteous and Enoch, whose hope was 'to call upon the name of the Lord God' (Heb 11:6)—but 'because I saw you righteous before me in this generation,' making it clear. It is not merely presented that because of his virtue and his children participating in it they were saved, but, as previously foretold, the generation signifies the likeness, just as we have set forth also in the cases of those who perished. english: In the generation of the righteous, so that we might take the righteous with him, he himself was found righteous against [the world], not being entirely righteous against God being righteous; for only sons and women were found righteous against Noah. But it is great thus to be the opposite of God to be called righteous, as it is said: 'And the stars are not pure before him' (Job 9:21) and the other lights; but also in the psalms it is said: 'No living thing shall be justified before you' (Psalm 5:4), and again another saying he says: 'All our righteousness was as a garment laid aside' (Isaiah 64:6) from the presence of all the righteous.

From the clean animals he brought into the ark seven seven male and female, and from the animals not being clean two two male and female, and from the birds of the heaven the clean seven seven male and female, and from the birds not being clean two two male and female, to breed seed upon all the earth. Consequently, 'seven seven' (Genesis 7:2) he commands to be brought in from the clean. Since they were for food and for religious services for men, and they themselves who remained in the ark had need, therefore more are taken, so that from them and a greater generation might arise a succession suitable for their needs; but concerning the others, having brought in this many, he commanded 'two two' (Genesis 7:2) to be brought in.

And if it is necessary also to bring in natural philosophy by the word, one might say, as before, that since the two are divided, and this is characteristic of matter, the number two is characteristic of the unclean. english: Eighty-six and sixty-four, a cube, for four times four is sixty-four. But also, being tripled up to seven from the unit, the seven hundred twenty-nine is formed, and being both a square and a cube: one, three, nine, twenty-seven, eighty-one, two hundred forty-three, seven hundred twenty-nine, as it has been said, completes both a cube and a square; thus the square: seventy-two times twenty-seven is seven hundred twenty-nine; thus the cube: nine times ninety-nine is seven hundred twenty-nine. The square signifies stability, but the cube [signifies something else].

Therefore, what has been spoken concerning the numbers would not be unrepresentative, having been proven by not involving the divine letters in nothing. And to those things spoken, it is appropriate to add that a porthole was appropriately left in the ark, so that, lest another origin arise, a heresy concerning two creators be introduced. For if, even with such security made, the heretics find differences, introducing divinities, how much more would they find plausible arguments for their own evil hypothesis.

For, 'And in seven days I will cause rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and I will destroy all the living things which I have made upon the face of the earth' (Genesis 7:4, 17). And this is foretold by the philanthropy of God for correction, in order to hear about the destruction that shall be after seven days, just as in the [disasters] we have set aside the preaching according to Jonah, which also happened through the repentance of the Ninevites, as it occurred. And forty days and forty nights of rain from above and below has happened in this way, so that the mountains were overwhelmed by fifty cubits.

If even the number according to which the destruction occurred has a reason, consider how 'I will destroy all the living things which I have made upon the face of the earth.' Some, having taken the [matter] of the destruction, thought that a previous world had endured a conflagration according to the Stoics, with the same [elements] existing in the matter which is unchangeable from this world. The blessed David was also worthy of such an acceptance, concerning whom God said to find 'David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my will' (Acts 13:22).

Genesis 6:3: 'And Noah was five hundred years old, and the flood of water came upon the earth.' ... [regarding] the goodness of God, how in a hundred percent of years he allowed the ark to be made; for this is evident from the five hundred years from when Noah began to ... it became wise toward the assembling of all things, so that seeing the strangeness of the construction, men might hear, learn the reason, and cease from wickedness. english: He planted a vine, which is the chosen one; for he planted the people to be a kingdom and a chosen priesthood. He built a tower to provide refuge for the approaching enemies (Isa 5:2); the tower is a pedagogical thing, guarding and at the same time mocking the enemy's onset. Having built, he hears: 'If a spirit of the prevailing one ascends upon you, do not leave your place' (Luke 17:5). He also made a hedge and placed a fence around it, which signifies the safety from the angels. And despite all these things having happened, he remained in the same fruitlessness; therefore he says: 'What more shall I do to my vine when I have done nothing for it?' (Isa 5:4).

I have done all things without fail; therefore, since they themselves do not have the power to say what must happen, I will say, 'I will announce to you what I shall do to my vine' (Isa 5:5-6); I will take away what I gave it, 'I will pull down its wall and it shall be a pavement, and I will take away the fence and it shall be a plunder' (Isa 5:5-6). For it is useful to provide this help, which they received from the angels, to those who are useless, so that seeing what evils they are, they may desire to turn back; therefore he also rebukes, saying: 'And I will command the clouds not to rain upon it' (Isa 5:6), which signify the prophets and the messengers of the spiritual rain, concerning which it was said: 'The clouds rained down righteousness' (Job 36:28).

For with this rain, instead of grapes, he would have had to bear thorns; therefore the ruin of Israel has become such a loss by not receiving it. Thus it was; the deluge was brought upon them, with no one among the men desiring to be benefited by their own inclination. There will be a total destruction of the virtue that stands as a whole, just as the Savior says: 'Will the Son of Man, when he comes, find faith upon the earth?' (Luke 18:8). And Noah entered, and his sons, and his wife, and the wives of his sons with...

[He entered] into the ark because of the water of the flood. And from the winged ones and from the livestock the clean and from the livestock the not clean and from all the creeping things of the earth, two by two, they entered toward Noah into the ark, male and female, according to what God commanded him (Genesis 7:2). It is evident that, since certain signs of the flood existed and were made manifest to Noah, such as the moisture of the earth or the similarities, Noah entered into the ark, not after much time had passed.

And the things concerning the sons after Noah and the wives of the sons having entered, having been observed previously, have been said: for it was not fitting, such a punishment coming upon all, for them to perform the things of weddings; therefore, in order to have leisure from these, he divided the pairs, giving them out at the exit from the ark. And generally also he says that the animals had entered, having mentioned the clean ones first because of their preciousness; and the things previously mentioned—when Noah was being arranged toward God to bring in from the animals into the ark, and you cast them in here, so that we may not always say the same things.

And it happened after the seven days, and the water of the flood became upon the earth in the six hundredth year in the life of Noah, of the second month, the seventh and twentieth of the month (Genesis 7:11). Some observed because the flood happened in such a number, saying that, since for the perfection of a work [gaps] they emerged, because of this, it was remembered, a perfect inundation occurring, which for the salvation of the world came to be. For the removing of the sinners from the earth and the taking of the human race at the beginning to live with virtue is perfect; and just as it is of an excellent physician not only to excise a corruption having happened in bodies, but also to grow the flesh instead of the corruptions that remained, so is the work of God.

It is said that three days and three nights were spent in the heart of the earth, from the interval of the night of Friday and that of Sunday, through the whole night of the Sabbath. These things are said to us as a digression, for those wishing to show that the Scripture, when touching the ends of times, usually uses such methods.

On that day all the fountains of the deep burst forth, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened, and rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights (Gen 7:11–12). This number is an ill-omened one. For the sons of Israel also completed so many years in their journey, and Moses himself did not eat bread for forty days; and the Savior also fasted with this number of days, which provides a following understanding to the divine letters for those not passing over them as trivial. Therefore also the duration of the water occurred in so many days in number.

If anyone should seek, setting aside those things concerning the floodgates of the heavens, why the deluge occurred—since God, calling upon the water of the sea, sends the rain—how the deluge happened, as if by some mechanical way of the sea becoming rain and then returning upon it; to which it might be said that first the fountains of the deep burst forth to provide the supply—and indeed, it is written that when it was willed to overflow, 'the fountains of the great deep burst forth' (Gen 7:11)—and then nothing could stop the quantity of water from stopping God, just as in the Gospels the five loaves were increased for five thousand (Matt 14:17-21).

On that day Noah, Shem, Ham, Japheth, the sons of Noah, and the wife of Noah and the three wives of his sons entered into the ark with him, and all the animals according to kind, and all the cattle according to kind, and every creeping thing moving upon the earth according to kind, and every winged thing according to kind (Gen 7:13–16). They entered with Noah into the ark, two by two of all flesh, in which is the spirit of life. And the males and females entering from all flesh entered, just as God commanded Noah. It is evident that the deluge did not happen suddenly, but provided a sign, as previously said, so that the process might be leadingly...

english: The animals entered the ark not in a confused mass, so that the ark would not be damaged by the sudden rushing of the waters through their joining together. The entry occurred in order, first Noah, through whom the others were saved, and then the others following him; thus the animals entered, which should be noted as having happened by divine power, for the numbering and bringing in was not by human endeavor, but had become a cooperation with God. Also, 'according to kind' is well-stated; for it was not possible for them to have the same sustenance, being divided by their natures. And he added 'in which is the spirit of life' for contrast with the dead. If anyone were to note how, then, the pure were not mentioned but the impure: 'two [two]' they say 'entered into the ark' (Gen 7:9), and it is clear that these were the impure; to which someone says that it is evident that, since the impure entered and the pure also entered, if the lesser entered, it is clear that the greater also entered. Furthermore, the 'two two' could also be taken to refer to the pure, the word indicating that all entered in pairs.

And the Lord God closed the ark from the outside, and the deluge happened for forty days and forty nights upon the earth, and the water multiplied and lifted up the ark, and it was raised from the earth, and the water prevailed and multiplied greatly upon the earth, and the ark was carried upon the water (Gen 7:17-20). And following this history, the ark is closed 'from the outside' by the power of God, with no man being outside. Since he succeeded in making it secure both inside and outside, and since it was not possible to secure it from the outside if the door had not been closed, so as not to say that entry was made for the water through the door, he added the security from God; and this is both varied and convenient. And 'lifted up the ark' is also well-stated, uniformly and not suddenly, just as we previously set forth the reason. And the water prevailed greatly, greatly upon the earth and covered all the high mountains which were under the heaven; the water was raised fifteen cubits above. The commentators excessively...

They say [men are called] to ascend to the high mountains. And indeed he signaled as fifteen cubits the water rose above the high mountains, from which it is clear, as that has been rightly said, especially since it also happens contrary to the will of God; for to Noah, on account of righteousness, God commanded to construct an ark, saying that he would destroy all flesh, so that no one was saved outside of the ark (Gen 6:17).

And concerning the rising of the water above fifteen cubits, if anyone wishes to be expert in the number, he will see that it is taken from many places in the Scripture: the steps of the temple were fifteen, and the word commands to give a portion to the seven and also to the eight, meaning this: that those approaching provide the old [covenant] along with the new part to the seven and to the eight. One might perhaps say that those who became contemptuous of the mystery signified by the number had become [ripe] for the wickedness of the flood.

For it is signaled again in the Scriptures by the multitude of the water, as in: 'What do you think against the Lord? A completion...' (Job 40:21-23). For if anyone thought that the fluid things of life, instead of being taken as a flood when they multiply, with the failing of the love of many, would be a completion, he would understand it properly in the word.

And all flesh moved upon the earth, the winged, and the cattle, and the beasts; and every creeping thing moving upon the earth, and every man, and all things that have the breath of life, and everyone who was upon the dry land died (Gen 7:21-23). The spoken [word] is manifest; for it declares the destruction of all living things except those in the ark; but for those reasoning, it implies that even the irrational perished because of having become [subject to] necessity. english: Dogs, according to what was said: 'Watch out for the dogs'; and having fully received the craftiness of wickedness, they were dissolved in a manner fitting the destruction caused by wickedness, this being a symbolic indication of the water. These themselves are also earthly, as having lost the heavenly image; and they themselves perished 'upon the dry land,' of a wickedness possessing nothing life-giving (Gen 7:23–24).

And Noah alone was left remaining, and those with him in the ark, and the water rose upon the earth for one hundred and fifty days. Fittingly Noah is saved without participating in wickedness, along with those who were with him and being instructed by him, having surpassed the burden of the allegorically understood water by fifteen cubits, reaching the temple through the steps, and having fulfilled the things foretold through the number: for 'water' 'will not be able to much extinguish love' (Gen 8:1–3).

And God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock and all the winged creatures, as many as were with him inside the ark. And God brought a wind upon the earth, and the water subsided; and the fountains of the abyss were covered and the cataracts of the heaven, and the rain was restrained from the heaven. And the water was receding as it went from the earth, the water was receding and retreating after fifty and one hundred days.

And the 'remembered' is to be heard in a God-befitting way, not as from forgetfulness, but just as he says concerning the ungodly: 'I do not know where you are from; depart, workers of iniquity; never did I know you' (Matt 25:12), the 'never' here indicating knowledge, 'never as having had you as our own'; 'remembered' is not having been overlooked—for the holy is before God always—but rather to make the memory of him a beginning of a race to lead him to the beginning, and similarly for the others. Some seek where the water of the deluge has retreated, through the coming of a wind, by which the water was subsided, whether this be the will of God or a divine power being at work; and in addition to this, it became a co-worker for the subsiding of the abysses and the upper downpour being hindered (Gen 8:4).
And the ark rested in the seventh month, and the following. The spoken is manifest; let us look at the thing toward understanding.

Yes, the ark is the church saving those who are clinging to it through prudence and works of virtue, which also sits in highness. For it never becomes in lowliness, therefore nor do the gates of Hades prevail against it; it stands before Christ glorious, having neither wrinkle nor line or anything of that kind, since even Christ is in highness, which is shown in 'Behold, this one comes leaping upon the mountains' (Song of Solomon 2:8), the prophets and Moses and the invisible powers. It sits, therefore, upon the rock, by the word of the cleavage of piety. For 'the foundations' (Psalm 127:1) of God are 'in the holy mountains' (Psalm 127:1), which also are the city of God; for 'God' (Psalm 89:2) 'established it for all eternity' (Psalm 89:2). 'For they received' (Isaiah 26:2) it says 'the city having the foundations' (Isaiah 26:2), of which God is the craftsman and creator. Let the mountains also have driven away 1380 sheep that did not fall by the plan. And if anyone through the number wishes to speak technically, he might say that the stability of the divine church is shown through it; for this is square, and the same is also a cube; for three times three is twenty-seven. And 'Arariad' is interpreted as a testimony of descent; but God testifies to that which is upon the church through a descending polity, which is unseasonable; for it has been said: 'If you pass through water, rivers shall not overwhelm you' (Isaiah 43:2), and again: 'We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out to refreshment' (Isaiah 43:2). And it is also good that the deluge be fulfilled in a year; for when the true sun shines and illuminates our intellect, then every disturbance of the soul shall be driven away.

english: It has been shut according to the saying, 'Do not throw the holy things to the dogs' (Matt 7:6); for whenever someone rightly shuts or opens, he is an imitator of Noah.

And he sent the raven (Gen 8:7), and the following. Not all who are under the same guidance of the church exist, but some are doves and others are ravens, being symbols of manners and characters. And the dove is a sign of pure life, for it has been arranged among the pure and is brought up for sacrifice, but the raven has nothing of this. According to this understanding, the history concerning Elijah (1 Kings 17) is also to be interpreted, how ravens nourished him; for when a teacher removes the unclean from uncleanness as if to change his manner, the one being helped has food.

This one himself, whom I say also has the manner of the raven, even if he seems to be under the righteous, having gone out as if in a contest toward temptation, does not turn back. And do not marvel if the righteous sends such a one into the gymnasium, where he also says a divine word: 'Child, if you approach to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation' (Sir 24:2); therefore he does not turn back, being someone uncertain and being ready to fall into temptation, not having been established.

And he sent the dove (Gen 8:8), and the following. Being ready for temptations is a prelude and a foundation of the true citizenship; for this reason also the one living according to the dove is sent to the 81st stadium. Regarding the important word, he says to them: 'If you sleep...'

english: Between the lots, the wings of a dove are moving, and their feathers are in the greenness of gold. Toward such a soul the word says: 'My good one, my dove' (Song of Solomon 2:14).

Because such a soul is certainly such that, even if it is born into trials and is sent away from the helpers, it returns immediately to the helper, especially when it does not yet realize that the end of the trial is to take hold of the land. For it is not proper to oppose the immeasurable; therefore also the righteous man extends his hand helping and stretching out aid. We lead this up through the clear [text].

And having waited yet seven other days, he sent her away again. He sends the dove away again in the same manner, and she returns having olive fruit in her mouth (Genesis 8:11). For the diligent person does all things by word; so he led the light-bearing actions toward the righteous man, a sign of not acting on his own, but rather moving toward the teacher, 'toward evening,' near the end. And having been sent away a third time, she no longer returns; for after so many progresses, to be without a teacher has become self-sufficient. And the upward leading is thus; but the spoken words are not obscure.
And it happened in the one hundred and sixty-first, and the following. Since the spoken word is clear, let the things of the intellect be spoken of.

english: No one being harmed. And Noah built an altar. Even if he did indeed act in concert with something for salvation, having constructed the ark and having safely sealed it and having done the other things, he did not set it upon himself; rather, as one giving thanks, he builds an altar.

And previously we said properly that he brought more fittingly clean animals into the ark than [unspecified] animals; for it was intended to perform sacred rites from them. And even if it was not commanded by law to perform sacred rites, but being righteous—just as Abel from the beginning did and had and was receiving from God (Gen 4:4)—he considered it just to receive from the Giver thankfully.

And the 'from all' must be heard as him having presented to the altar with prudence. For there are three things brought up for sacrifice: among the animals of the livestock, a calf, a sheep, and of these [missing text], and a dove. These therefore are the 'all'.

And it is possible to find this from the Scriptures, that, regarding what is said in the general, it is proper to take it according to what follows; for the 'And all flesh shall see the salvation of God' (Isa 49:6) must not simply be understood as all, but the livestock are clean except for the living thing, which is the human nature. This was previously spoken because of those things said in the law.

english: And the Lord said to Abram: 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house into the land which I will show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed, and I will bless those blessing you, and those cursing you I will curse; and all the families of the earth shall be blessed in you' (Gen 12:1-3).

Not as a total exclusion does God command Abraham to depart from his land and his kindred, but seeing in him something worthy to be remaining arranged under his guardianship, which was the faith in him; for the one having faith in God was not bound to remain with the foolish, since his father was an idolater. For often the company of the evil harms the diligent, and especially when they are fresh. Because of this also the Savior preaches: 'If anyone wants to come after me and does not hate his father and his brothers and sisters and also his wife and children, he cannot be my disciple' (Luke 14:26).

It was not hatred of the kin being worked by this that the Lord said, but if something of these things became an obstacle toward virtue, it is to be hated for the sake of virtue, which the disciples, having done, said: 'Behold, we have left all and have followed you' (Matt 19:27).

This therefore also now is commanded to the patriarch, God promising to show him a land so that he may live there, to make him into a great nation, and to bless him and to magnify his name and to show him blessed, so that those blessing him find blessing from him, and those cursing him receive a curse from him. And in addition to these, it is promised to him that all the families of the earth shall be blessed in him, which all things are not human, as we are entering from the lifting up, beginning from those from above. For the devil is the father of every sinner according to the...

It has been said: 'Everyone who does sin is of the devil' (1 John 3:8). For just as he who does the will of God becomes his offspring—for he says, 'Everyone who does righteousness is born of God' (1 John 3:7)—so 'the one doing sin is of the devil' (1 John 3:8) and of his father. And there is also a kinship through the composition of this father.

Therefore, God exhorts him to explain this, calling it earth, for it is nothing heavenly but all earthly in the opposing devil, so that, casting off the image of the swine, he might take up the image of the heavenly. Such a thing is brought forth in a psalm regarding the Church from among the Gentiles, saying: 'Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house, for the king of your beauty has desired you, and he is your Lord' (Psalm 45:10).

For already, having existed, the word, with a prophetic eye, was awakening the daughter to move away from idolatry, exhorting her to hear and to see, having a pure heart both to hear and to see the Word of God; and for this purpose also to incline the ear, so that from these she might forget 'your people' (Psalm 45:10) of the household 'and your father' (Psalm 45:10) so as to renounce him, adding also the reason, which we also agreed exists in the patriarch: the beauty of the soul; for nothing beautifies the soul like virtue. It is therefore necessary to forget all earthly things, which are divided into the things previously mentioned.

And he says to the earnest one that he has come to an earth which, if God shows it to him, is not visible, even though he followed this also for the sake of a symbol, but is invisible; 'for hope that is seen is not hope' (Romans 8:24). And what is it that he will do 'into a great nation' (Acts 15:5) after taking [it] according to the spoken word? For it is clear that this also existed according to history. english: When things are becoming in the soul, there is not a human magnitude established, but a heavenly one, which is a blessing, not merely spoken out, but truly manifested, through the becoming of a great and famous name from the accompanying virtue and the world following from the spiritual blessing; for a good name is more desirable than wealth and 'good reputation sustains the bones' (Sirach 7:36). Nor is it sufficient to bless, but he goes further saying: 'And you shall be blessed' (Gen 12:2), becoming worthy of blessing because of the magnitude and the progress of perfected virtue; and he blesses also those who bless [him], not by mere utterance, but by the choice and election of those whom he himself is chosen by. Likewise, those standing in opposition to him will fall under a curse.

And this appears to the one reading the histories, in which it is made clear that as many as received him poorly were blessed, but as many as did not use him properly have become under a curse, such as Abimelech. And these things can also be said concerning invisible powers, where holy angels bless the diligent one and are blessed by him, but the devil and the demons curse him and fall under a curse. Furthermore, there will be another achievement: to be blessed in him all the tribes of the earth, being delivered from being tribes of the earth through the imitation of him according to holiness, no longer thinking of their earthly things. And the diligent one is destined for this, to be blessed in him through imitation by all the tribes of the earth, even if not all approach, separating themselves from this by their own will.

And Abram went, just as the Lord spoke to him (Gen 12:4), and Lot went with him. And Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran. And Abram took his wife Sarai and Lot the son of his brother, and all their possessions which they had gathered, and every soul whom they had gathered from Haran, and they went to journey to the land of Canaan, and they came to the land of Canaan (Gen 12:5). This is a great testimony to the patriarch, that he thus traveled just as God spoke to him, and of the acceptance of Lot following along with Abram. And the saying testifies also to the time in which he went out and how he led out all that they had gathered from Haran and every soul whom they had gathered, and thus they came to the land of C[anaan].

And this would indeed have the greatest reception in itself: that he did not remain, not being overcome by the familiarity of kinship, nor of friends, nor of others, whatever enticements there were toward not departing from the fatherland, but he saw all things aside, becoming obedient to the divine command. An addition, as we have previously said, is that he also journeyed thus just as God spoke to him. For it often happens to do the commanded thing, but not to carry it out as the one who commanded had set forth. Here it happened thus, that God commanded, and the cause of the deed was divine, and the result was according to the purpose of the commander.

Not thus do those practicing almsgiving act for the sake of being seen by men, completing the deed, but being secured [in their merit] by the manner of the acting. But the blessed Paul does not act thus, but saying, 'Become imitators of me' (1 Cor 11:1), he did not simply command this, but further brought it forth, 'just as I [am] of Christ' (1 Cor 11:1), not in appearance but in truth. Again the Savior, saying, 'Learn from me that I am gentle and humble in heart' (Matt 11:29), leads the hearers to understand toward learning both the manner and the energy and the causes of gentleness and humility.

And the patriarch also leads his possessions, not as one enslaved to them, as if he were not enslaved to his only begotten son, but having taken them for the needs. And these things, having been said for the sake of the history, are sufficient for benefit, to which one must also add the leading out from Haran and the souls which they acquired, to show that he acquired the household in his own manner; for no one, according to what has been said, is slow in the house of a wise man. And the word of the leading out also has much benefit for being able to level all things.

Haran, therefore, is interpreted as 'wheels,' which is a symbol of the senses; for the places of the senses are like wheels. Thus God wills to turn him away from the sensible things. And the possessions, having become established in these things, the saint leads along to be useful to him for the entrance into the intelligible perfections; for does not the perfect one among the great also lack the decorated adornment, the grinding of teeth and the stepping of the foot? english: "My beginning" is interpreted opportunistically; for the wise man is with wisdom, either being led by her or having the rule from her, and having her as a spouse according to the Song of Solomon: "I brought her into my life to live with me" (Song of Solomon 1:2, 1:4), making wisdom clear, "and I became a lover of her beauty" (Song of Solomon 1:4); and she also bears prudence to a man.

This also leads on Lot the brother, concerning whom we would understand thus: Abram is a son of God through righteousness, for "everyone who does righteousness is born of God" (1 John 5:3), and because of this he is a participant in the mysteries of the divine, the invisible, and the superlative; and such a one has a brother who wisely transforms the sensible. For such a thing contributes to the perfect one; and Lot is his son, interpreted as "a turning away, having been liberated"; for since he is not a son of the wise but of one possessing the sensible, he is a turning away, being slightly shaken from the sensible, but since he is under the holy one and follows him, he exists as having been liberated, receiving this beginning of the divine and superlative understanding.

This indeed, Abram was leading both in man and in manner, wisely receiving the sensible things as well; for it is beautiful even for a turning away to flow toward the beautiful and be shaken from the opposites; such also is a prayer sent up, saying by the Psalmist: "Let the whole earth be shaken from before his face" (Psalm 104:7); for this happening, the earth no longer remains earth, because the Face has seized those upon the earth to become heavenly. Of the same thought is also "He who sits upon the cherubim, let the earth be shaken" (Psalm 97:5), so that a change may occur around him.

Thus also those with him, the patriarch, went out, changing toward the better; for they came into Canaan, which is interpreted as "prepared"; for it is proper for the one now being brought in to have begun to leave the sensible things to be turned toward the reception of more divine things. "And Abram traveled through the land as far as the place of Shechem, at the high oak; and the Canaanites were living in the land then" (Genesis 12:6). The word introduces that, having been moved as a newcomer into this land, he necessarily understands its form by traveling its length, and likely its breadth as well, learning its territory; for the saying "as far as the place of Shechem" signifies...

And that the Canaanites dwelt upon the land. Necessarily, therefore, one must move toward the ascent. The holy [one], having been transferred from the sensible things, which he also rightly divides, toward a more divine progress, and having passed on, perceived the length, which they say provides as it were the height, and he perceived the height of the divine things. This very thing also the blessed Paul says: 'what breadth and length and depth to know the surpassing grace of God' (Ephesians 3:18). All these things, therefore, he perceived from the greater [thing] and is testifying concerning the others.

And he comes 'as far as the place of Sychar' (John 4:5), where the spring happened to be, upon which Jesus sat down having labored, because he had a body conformed to our flesh, which it is probable they suggest is because of the greater and theological occupation, which is indicated by the length; he came also to the discourse concerning the incarnation according to that which was said by Jesus: 'Abraham desired to see my day, and he saw and rejoiced' (John 8:56). And he comes to Sychar, being worthy of being interpreted as a 'shoulder' through the diverse actions of all these things; for the shoulder, from which the 'shoulder' [support] comes, is a symbol of work, as it has been said: 'Give your heart unto your shoulders' (Proverbs 4:23), and concerning one of the patriarchs: 'He set his shoulder to toil' (Genesis 49:24).

So also it is said concerning the man whom the Savior took up: 'His beginning was upon his shoulder' (Acts 1:11); having worked, he had the beginning, but the work was not from evil unto virtue—for 'sin he did not do' (Hebrews 4:15)—but the guarding of perfection; so also regarding the man who was king, having the eternal, innate, and essential kingdom of the God Word, not by work or by toil. And he comes 'to the high oak,' and since many of the trees and plants signify something intelligible, as those saying in Isaiah: 'In joy you shall go forth and in gladness you shall be taught; for the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you in joy, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands' (Isaiah 55:13), which signifies nothing sensible, but the exodus of the blessed, who do not depart with weeping, but with joy.

english: Therefore, when the righteous depart from life, the mountains and the hills, the angels and the righteous ones, will receive them with joy, rejoicing because of the one sheep. Along with this, even all the woods of the field will strike rejoicing, which are the intelligible things in paradise.

Then he says: 'Instead of a stack, a cypress shall rise up' (Gen 49:11), instead of being fruitless and thorny, useful and fragrant—for this is what the one repenting becomes—'and instead of boxwood, myrtle shall rise up' (Gen 49:11), changing from a foul odor to a fragrance. Since we have trees taken up intellectually, it is necessary also to contemplate the oak, to which Abraham comes, upon which sitting he was worthy of a vision when he also received the promise concerning Isaac. Through works and labors, advancing toward the heights, one is presented with the participation in the fragrance and the contemplation of the high and divine notions.

You shall also observe what was signaled, that 'the Canaanites still dwelt in the land' (Gen 48:11), lest we might think that to the one advancing everything is immediately set free, but he still has some of the old habit—for this is what 'still' signifies—which might be understood concerning those following the saint who have not yet attained perfection.

And the Lord appeared to Abraham and said to him: 'To your seed I will give this land' (Gen 28:13). And Abraham built there an altar to the Lord who appeared to him. Accordingly, to the one who has obeyed the commands given by God Himself, He appears, making the good hope of those expecting Him more certain; for He also promises to give the land to his seed. Accordingly also the saint, being thankful, builds an altar to the one who proposed the promise. And let these things be spoken in a manner of interpretation.

It is worthy to contemplate regarding 'God appeared to Abraham,' for the invisible God, as is demonstrated in the Gospel, it being said 'No one has seen God ever' (John 1:18), and 'Not that anyone has seen the Father' (John 6:46), but also Paul saying concerning God: 'Whom no man of men has seen nor is able to see' (1 Tim 6:16), which signifies that which is invisible by nature. For some of the visible things we do not see, but we are able to see, even if this does not follow; such is the nature of the visible things. But the invisible is not such that it cannot be seen...

Not something, but because of being invisible, it is not seen. It is therefore clear that seeing is twofold: one according to sense, the other according to intellect; the one is perceptive of visible things, the other of invisible things, which is a pure mind, through which God appeared to Abraham (Gen 15:1). The word also has another observation. For it has not been said, 'Abraham saw God,' but 'God appeared to Abraham' (Gen 15:1). Since we are toward created nature and its weakness, the thing is not possible; but as toward the philanthropy of God, it becomes possible, through His goodness granting Himself to His own comprehension.

And if ever 'saw' is placed instead of 'appeared' as in Isaiah (Isa 6:1): 'I saw the Lord sitting,' and the following, let us be instructed from what happened to Abraham: that, God granting Himself, this happens. That seeing is sometimes also applied to the intellect, as Paul writing to the Romans says: 'For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are perceived in the works, being clearly seen' (Rom 1:20). And Moses, regarding God, of whom he had a concept, that He is invisible, was saying: 'Show me yourself; that I may know you clearly' (Ex 33:18), and again: 'For He appears to those who do not believe in Him' (Heb 11:6); for if the thing seen were of a visible nature and it were possible to appear to the unbelieving, now it is said: 'He appears to those who do not believe in Him' (Heb 11:6), having had the intellect illumined by divine light. Again the matter applies to the sensible things: for first we see them, then, of the type coming from the sense into the intellect, we perceive them; and the intelligible things provide themselves for being known, not by the intellect preceding beforehand, if not only by turning itself toward comprehension, but also by following that which appeared. And sometimes the thought about God happens also from the comprehension of the creation, according to 'For from the beauty of the things, analogously, the Creator of them is perceived' and just as God appeared to Abraham. For the name 'God' is joined to creation as in 'In the beginning God made the heaven' (Gen 1:1), and: 'God said, Let there be light' (Gen 1:3), the appellation of 'Lord' being spoken then when the law was provided. Thus, having beheld through the all-harmonious order of the all...

english: God turned away from the many-wandering error which he learned from the father, and subsequently God presents himself to the holy one for understanding after the instruction from hearing, which happened in the 'Go out from your land and from your kindred' (Gen 12:1). But the hearing of the soul should be considered the persuasive assent of those being brought under, and the eye the imposition after progress and the most certain grasp of the instructions. For it is to be understood that to know the same things differently is more introductory, progressing, and intimately having progressed from the understanding of God.

It is also promised to the seed that he will give the land, that land about which the Savior said, 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth' (Matt 5:5), and in the Psalms, 'Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land' (Ps 37:35), and it is clear that not this [land] which we plow and sow—of which he was king—but the heavenly one, which is the most perfect knowledge of God; this 'the righteous shall inherit and dwell upon it for an age of ages' (Ps 37:34), but it shall not be upon the sensible [land]. This, therefore, God promises to give to the seed of the holy one, and 'seed' in this place he calls the child. For a difference is often found between seed and child; for if someone has become a child of someone, to him he has also become seed, but not, because it is seed, does a child become; for it happens not to be formed or to be completed or to be made like, as the Scripture says. Just as in bodily things there is seed not becoming a child, and a child being and seed, so also in the things according to soul and intellect. The Savior therefore says to those saying, 'We have Abraham as father' (Matt 3:9): 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham' (Matt 3:9); for from these one becomes a child. These whom he said are not children of Abraham, he says are his seed, claiming: 'I know that seed...'

You are the seed of Abraham, so it is clear that it is not both seed and child, but rather they have received seed according to the succession from Abraham and have borne fruit from his nourishment, but they did not imitate his practice, though it was possible for them, using the appropriate means, to become children. Therefore here, since a promise is given to the seed, we take the seed to mean child. In the Psalms, indeed, it is said: 'The seed of Abraham are his servants, the sons of Jacob his chosen ones' (Ps 105:44). But as for that which is sometimes declared as not both seed and child, Paul writes: 'not all are children' (Rom 9:7); for not all those of Israel are Israel (Rom 9:6), but rather that one about whom the Savior said: 'Behold a man Israelite in whom there is no deceit' (Rom 7:7); but not these about whom it has been said: 'See Israel according to the flesh' (2 Cor 1:3). These things are regarding the difference between seed and child; let us return to what was explicitly set forth.

Abraham, therefore, builds an altar, moving in a thankful manner, spiritually offering sacrifices, even though he was making the symbol regarding those about whom it has been said: 'offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God' (2 Cor 8:13), and 'sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise' (Heb 13:15), and 'sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord' (Ps 37:3). 'It is necessary, indeed, that the patterns in the heavens be purified by these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves are superior to these sacrifices' (Heb 9:23). Such an altar is built by the one making progress and having followed the one who called him, having become as a remnant outside the land and the kindred and the house of the father, as to be worthy to see God, him having made him worthy to appear to the saint. [Genesis] 12:8. And he departed from there to the mountain toward the east of Bethel, and he set up his tent there, toward the sea, and the Annaites toward the south. What the explicit word signifies is not unclear; but for instruction, it signifies that he crossed over to a higher progress and state. It is signified through the mountain, and not simply 'into...

english: Not a mountain, but the house of God; for this is interpreted as Bethel, which is not only [a house] but also with other things according to what was said in Aisma: 'My brother is like a deer or a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel' (Gen 25:9). For many mountains and hills are in the house of God, as from 'Behold, this one comes leaping upon the mountains, fleeing upon the hills' (Ps 42:6); and with each progress there is to ascend to a hill, and from the hill to a mountain, and from lower mountains to higher ones; for this is known both in the introductions of virtues and in the virtues themselves.

But there is one mountain above all, the Savior and Lord of us, concerning whom it is said: 'The mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest at the latter end of the days' (Zech 14:4), which is another thing compared to the other mountains, so as to speak for the sake of the holy teaching, lest some should misunderstand: 'Why do you suppose [it is] fortified mountains?' Then, teaching the most excellent mountain, he says: 'The mountain of God, a fertile mountain, a fortified mountain, a fertile mountain. Why do you suppose [it is] fortified mountains, the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell?' which signifies the Lord having become man. For the incarnation is shown through this word, just as also with Job: 'Did you not care for me like milk, and did you not curdle me like cheese?' (Job 10:10). For the Savior alone [comes] from a virgin; therefore it is said. Is this said concerning others? For no one else had such a constitution. Therefore Job did not say 'I was curdled,' but 'You curdled me like cheese'; for what the Spirit has done, that the casting of the seed in others works, at the command of God. And the same 'fertile' exists from the presence of the Spirit and from the power of the Most High.

And in the common sense, all and even the temple of the Savior are by creation from God, but [the Savior is] exceptional through the Lord; for He has used it as an instrument toward the incarnation. And just as all the earth of God is a creation, but the temple had [it] exceptional because of the God being honored there, so also regarding the things previously mentioned. And since, wherever God honors, that place is called His house, Jacob testifies saying: 'How fearful is this place! This is nothing else but the house of God, and this is a gate of heaven' (Gen 28:17). Therefore one must not pay attention, if [he] says...

Many will call themselves Christs according to what is said: 'Many will come in my name, saying, I am the Christ' (John 8:56). For there is a mountain in which God pleased to dwell; for the pleasure of the dwelling was not made by any man. Therefore, Abram, advancing through the intellect, burns toward this mountain.

Indeed, coming without neglect, he testified to him, saying: 'Your father Abraham rejoiced in order to see my day, and he saw and rejoiced' (John 8:56), having been enlightened by the true light being presented to him from the preceding advancements. And it is also good to say that this mountain is 'toward the east'; for it has lights from every side. Whatever conception of this mountain you take, it is luminous; for it is called wisdom, word, life, truth, justice, sanctification, and redemption. All these things, while rising, are lights—not many lights according to their essence, for they have one underlying subject, the Son of God—but diverse according to their energies.

Therefore, 'toward the east' of the house of God, which shines through all, the holy man came, being led by virtues; and it is also possible to call the various doctrines of piety 'eastings,' through which Abraham had arrived at the tent, which he used for the advancements—for this tent signifies the house of God being permanent; for 'I will pass through a place of wondrous habitation until the house of God' (Psalm 84:10). Having passed through the tent, he presses into the house that remains forever, with which there is no other ascent. This is also said in another psalm: 'How beloved are your habitations, Lord of powers! My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord' (Psalm 84:2).

For he who has not yet reached the courts, while in the tents, has love advancing and expects completion in saying: 'My heart and my flesh shall rejoice in a living God' (Psalm 36:9), when it occurs in that establishment, with which there is no other, into which those who have reached are called blessed, the psalmist saying: 'Blessed are all those dwelling in your house' (Psalm 84:4), not as sojourners but as dwellers; for this belongs to those in tents and advancements, but to dwell is to come into the house of God, in which they are blessed, as it were 'unto the ages of ages,' praising him.

english: Above all things the end is evident: that for which the tent has been pitched, having advanced through progress and remaining toward perfection, and for which the one persuaded by the word, despite being dissuaded, will arrive: 'Watch your foot, lest when you go into the house of God and draw near, you hear' (Ps 119:10). For thus he will be able to dwell in the house, saying, 'That I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days' (Ps 27:4). It must be known that through these things the divine citizenship is symbolically shown, even if the persona of Abraham is not yet fully completed, for he has not yet been called away.

And he pitches the tent 'by the sea,' being firm and unshakeable because of holding fast to virtue perfectly, so as to say: 'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?' (Rom 8:35) and the following, regarding which he says 'sea,' would not be sins. For whenever a saint is, even in perfection, he has a dizziness pressing upon him and the instability of created nature, which the perfect man, as a charioteer, prevents from the activity of evil by remaining in its power, which is blessed; for this is good even while existing in virtue, since even the evil man exists in the power of virtue, having turned to this by his own intention, though he did not guard himself as one who has become good.

And he himself also pitches the tent 'in winds from the south' in a way suitable to reaching the mountain of the house of God and being illuminated through all things from the east, which are the virtues according to their kind, and making no care for any of the opposing things—for even the waves from the sea do not overturn his well-established structure—which transforms the words of Jesus into works by becoming a feast; for this is interpreted as 'winds.' For the great feast is the perfection of virtue. For this is also what the psalmist says: 'Hear the voice of rejoicing and confession of those celebrating' (Ps 100:1); for he who rejoices at the presence of the Spirit and confesses, not as one sinning and repenting, but as one giving thanks, celebrates—for the name of confession lies in place of thanksgiving, as in 'We confess to You, O Lord Father of the heavens...'

For they say, 'the thought of a man' [Eccl 2:2], which makes it clear that of the one rejoicing, 'he shall confess to you and a treasure of thought shall celebrate for you.' And he built there an altar to the Lord and called upon the name of the Lord.

Appropriately, the one who crossed over and upon the given mountain built the house of God; and having been illumined by the rising suns and having struck down the opposing things in such a way that no one would stir up indignation, he raised up an altar, upon which he completes the sacrifice of pleasingness and righteousness according to what was said before concerning the spiritual sacrifice, which is the system of virtues. 'And he called upon the name of the Lord,' which someone taking hastily might say means that the altar, which he built, he named 'of the Lord'; but it is possible to say it more mystically and more sublimely, that he called upon the name of the Lord not by a mere word, but truly, the mind making its petition to God, not performing the virtues through something else, but through the good itself. For according to this understanding, even the Savior, while teaching, instructed to pray and to say, 'Our Father,' not to do this by mere utterance, but so that they might present themselves as sons and no longer call upon God the Father in vain; thus we hear: 'No one says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit' [1 Cor 12:3], and this does not apply to those who say this by mere utterance and in vain.

Therefore, Abraham was doing the building of the altar of virtues for the Lord, through it and not through something else. And Abram took [it] and having gone, he campaigned in the wilderness. Since the spoken word is not manifest, it must be spoken toward the understanding. For even if someone is perfect, he is not released from those who fight, even if he is a child, just as to the Corinthians, to whom Paul writes: 'You have not received a temptation which is not human; but God is faithful, who will not let you be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will make the way of the escape to endure' [1 Cor 10:13]. And to the Ephesians, as if already perfect, he writes and counts himself: 'For our struggle is not against blood and flesh' [Eph 6:12]; he does not say 'not...

english: It has happened, but it is not our wrestling match. For it once happened, when he set himself to be a fleshly thing having been brought under sin, signifying those in such a state, to whom it is also necessary to say as he himself writes: 'I beat my body and make it my slave, lest after preaching to others I myself become disqualified' (1 Cor 9:27). He has the battle using heavenly weapons as against spiritual heavenly things.

It is therefore perfect to fight just as Abraham stood at the house of God according to what was assigned, and by becoming like that himself, as it has been said: 'Those who have trusted in the Lord are like Mount Zion' (Ps 125:1). Having become thus, standing knowing that the opposing phalanx would not let go of him, he encamped, just as Jacob, when he was about to encounter Esau, a great war being present and envying him, 'saw the camp of God' (Gen 32:2); for it was necessary for God to be preparing for the athlete's courage to show him that he has allies.

And Elisha, when he was about to go out from the king of Syria, had a divine camp around himself, which the little boy of the prophet had been terrified by, later having become courageous from the uncovering of his eyes. And likewise it is to have encamped 'in the wilderness.' So also the Savior is tested in the wilderness; and in Isaiah you have: 'As a storm through a wilderness, coming out of the wilderness from the earth' (Isa 34:10), which signifies a trial.

Therefore Abraham encamped 'in the wilderness'; for mostly the trials happened outside of cities because they were found without help from similar men: 'For brother helped by brother is like a strong city' (Prov 18:19). And the Savior, as foretold, is tested in the wilderness, so that what is called such may be: a soul coming into trial sees itself as a wilderness without allies, God doing this providentially; for if he had pre-revealed to them the outcome and that they would conquer the trial, the effort would not have been great; nor did he send a prayer or do anything else. It is shown to them again that God also allies with them, so that they might not thus become evil. And so indeed for men, but for the Savior after the trial, angels appear, and these are for service, so that the ill-willed, before these angels appeared, might not say...

that victory belongs to angels. What is the service of the angels, or the placement of the souls who are persuaded by God? For they did not come for the sake of helping. And indeed he rebukes Peter because he wanted to fight excessively, saying: 'Do you think that I was not able to entreat my Father, and he would have given to me more than twelve legions of angels?' (Matt 26:53). Thus, an alliance is not necessary.

And there was a famine upon the earth; and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there, because a famine had grown strong upon the earth (Gen 12:10). The literal sense is clear; but this is the meaning for the intellect. The wise of God are above the earth, not being of it; therefore, in this way, a famine has occurred. For to those who think of earthly things, a famine of hearing the word of the Lord often happens, if they are worthy of it, and later they again receive it. In this way, too, Abram comes to 'sojourn' (not to dwell) in Egypt, descending in sympathy with those suffering the famine, not to live there; for those around Daniel did not come to Babylon because of sins, but so that they might help those deported there because of sins. For God has pity on those sinning to the extent that it is possible for them to repent. And just as doctors are sent where there is much harm or disease, not so that they themselves might share in the disease, but so that they might heal those who are sick, so the saints became present in the confusion and in Babylon, not being residents; for they had possessed nothing worthy of it, which is the property of those dwelling there.

And it happened, as Abram approached entering Egypt, that Abram said to Sarai his wife (Gen 12:11-13): 'I know that you are a woman of beautiful countenance; so it will be, when the Egyptians see you, they will say, "She is his wife," and they will kill me, and they will take you to themselves; so say then that you are my sister, so that it may go well for me because of you, and my soul may live because of you.' Regarding the spoken word, it is fitting with prudence, believing that God, having brought him out of his own land, will not neglect his marriage; he suggests to her to say to them that she is his sister, so that, this being said first and alone, they might not receive the notion that she is his wife, deceiving them through this. english: Brotherhood and in his own land, as he later says: 'For truly she is my sister' (Gen 12:13). Therefore, this alone deceives them with a false wisdom, and he says it first as a subordinate matter. For since it was likely that those according to the laws of adultery among the Egyptians would kill him so that they would not allow it to be known that they were adulterers, Abram was reckoned as such.

These things, then, are for the sake of the spoken word; but regarding the intellect, those coming from virtue into vice are said to descend into Egypt; for it has been said many times: 'Woe to those descending into Egypt' (Hos 7:14). Here it is not 'he descended' that is intended, but 'he entered'; for his descent is an entrance. For every diligent person descends with those who stumble, not stumbling himself but leading them along from the stumbling block; and just as one becomes a Jew to the Jews without being a Jew, and lawless to the lawless without being lawless, so one becomes into Egypt without becoming Egyptian. Therefore, let others descend there, but he enters; for it was not their wickedness that brought him there, but a certain economy being carried out.

The virtuous man enters into Egypt often using foreign instruction, so that he may construct something useful from it, just as blessed Paul has done, asserting from Aratus 'For we are also of the same race' (Acts 17:28), in order to do the following: and the 'To an Unknown God' (Acts 17:23) and the 'Cretans are always liars' (Titus 1:12); so also every intellect exhorts to be taken captive into the obedience of Christ.

Having entered, as we have said, into Egypt, he subjects something to virtue, so that he may say that she is his wife; for the diligent and perfect man does not say that his virtue is his own exclusively to those inferior to him, lest he provoke them to envy, but says that she is his sister, giving the secondary things toward a unity toward his own virtue, so that he might descend together with the weak, so that they might desire her as one set forth to be received. For often, when we have learned something desiring to make it common, we make the contemplations common, such as those concerning providence, so that with...

so that he might also receive her to himself. For the evangelical teaching is a celestial spouse of the perfect; yet this is not snatched away, even if it is spoken among the perfect, but it is shared with all, just as Paul says, 'But I desire all men to be as I am myself' (1 Cor 4:6). For having become such, they will know that this instruction is a spouse of the perfect. For 'Wisdom' 'bears prudence to a man' (Prov 8:12), and I, says the perfect one, 'became a lover of her beauty' (Prov 8:26), clearly meaning Wisdom; for the wise man wishes to impart his own to all, so that they will not envy.

And it happened, when Abram entered into Egypt (Gen 12), the Egyptians seeing the woman that she was exceedingly beautiful, and the princes of Pharaoh saw her, and they commended her to Pharaoh, and they brought her into the house of Pharaoh; and they dealt well with Abram because of her, and there came to him sheep and oxen and donkeys and boys and girls and mules and camels. The wise intention of the patriarch did not miss the mark; for he did not plot, but rather a way becomes available so that the marriage of the holy one might not be corrupted; for the Egyptians did not rush upon her as if toward one neglected; but rather the princes, having seen her, presenting her as a favor to the king, brought her, and thus it happened that they dealt well with them because of her.

Abram therefore enters into Egypt according to the allegorical manner as a perfect toward the imperfect, so that he might be benefited, fitting himself, possessing the virtue, as previously foretold, not as one approaching him as an exclusive possession, but showing it to all as a sister to share with, so that they might be able, having seen, to love her. And observe that the princes saw her; for even in the rank of the Egyptians according to allegory, there are certain purer ones who also have much inclination toward seeing the virtue. "6Ἔκστασις"6 οὖν ἐπι<πί>πτει αὐτῷ, ἔκ<σ>τασις δὲ οὐχ ἡ παραφροσύνῃ ὁμοία, ἀλλ' ὁ θαυμασμὸς καὶ τὸ μεταστῆναι ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρατῶν ἐπὶ τὰ ἀόρατα. Λέγει γοῦν ὁ ἀπόστολος· "6Εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν Θεῷ, εἴτε σωφρο- νοῦμεν ὑμῖν"6, οὐ τόδε δηλῶν ὅτι Θεῷ ἐμάνημεν, ἀλλ' ὅτι, κἂν ἔξω τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων διὰ θεωρίαν γενώμεθα, Θεῷ τοῦτο ποιοῦμεν, καθὰ καὶ ∆αυίδ φησιν· "6Ἐγὼ εἶπα ἐν τῇ ἐκστάσει μου· Πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ψεύστης"6· ἐκστὰς γὰρ καὶ γενόμενος θεὸς λέγει περὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὅτι ψεῦσταί εἰσιν, αὐτὸς οὐκέτι ἄνθρωπος ὑπάρχων διὰ τὴν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος κοινωνίαν, ἀλλ' ἄλλος ἐκείνων τυγχάνων, περὶ ὧν εἴρηται· "6Ὅπου γὰρ ἔρις καὶ ζῆλος ἐν ὑμῖν, οὐχὶ ἄνθρωποί ἐστε καὶ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον περιπατεῖτε;"6 Ἐκστάντος οὖν τοῦ Ἀβράμ, σκοτεινὸς φόβος 92 ἐπι- <πί>πτει αὐτῷ, οὐ σκότους μετέχων ἀλλ' ἀσαφείας καὶ μὴ γιγνωσκόμενος προχείρως· οὗτος μέγας ὑπάρχων φόβος οὐ μικροῖς συμβαίνει. Ὅτι δὲ ἀντὶ ἀσαφείας πολλάκις ὁ σκότος παραλαμβάνεται, εἴρηται· "6Καὶ ἔθετο σκότος ἀποκρυφὴν αὐτοῦ"6· καὶ τῷ ὄντι ἡ τῶν ὑπερφυῶν δογμάτων θεωρία καὶ κατάλημψις καὶ τοῖς μεγάλοις εἴλιγγον ἐμποιεῖ καὶ φόβον θεῖον μετ' εὐλαβείας τοῖς τοιούτοις ἐπιβάλλουσιν. χῃ, 13–14. Καὶ ἐρρέθη πρὸς Ἀβράμ· Γιγνώσκων γνώσῃ ὅτι πάροικον ἔσται τὸ σπέρμα σου ἐν γῇ οὐκ ἰδίᾳ, καὶ δουλώσουσιν αὐτοὺς καὶ κακώσουσιν αὐτοὺς τετρακόσια ἔτη· τὸ δὲ ἔθνος, ᾧ ἂν δουλεύσουσιν, κρινῶ ἐγώ· μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ἐλεύσονται ὧδε μετὰ ἀποσκευῆς πολλῆς. 231 Τὴν εἰς Αἴγυπτον παροίκησιντοῦ λαοῦ τὸ λόγιον προαναφωνεῖ· οὐκ ἰδίαν γὰρ οὖσαν παρῴκησαν δουλεύ- σαντες τῷ Φαραὼ καὶ πολλὰ ὑπ' αὐτοῦ καὶ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων κακωθέντες. Οὐ μάχεται δὲ τοῖς ἐνταῦθα τὰ ἐν τῇ Ἐξόδῳ γεγραμμένα· ἐκεῖ γὰρ εἴρηται· "6Μετὰ τετρακόσια καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη ἐξῆλθεν ἡ δύναμις Κυρίου ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου"6, ἐνταῦθα "6μετὰ τετρακόσιά"6 φησιν· ἀλλ' ἐπιστῆσαι δεῖ ὅτι οὐκ ἐρρέθη ὡς πληρωθέντων τῶν τετρακοσίων ἐτῶν ἐξῆλθον ἀλλὰ μετὰ τετρακόσια ἔτη, ὅπερ ἐμφαίνει τὰ τριάκοντα. Καὶ τὸ "6κρινῶ δὲ ἐγὼ τὸ ἔθνος ᾧ ἂν δουλεύσωσιν"6 ἐκβάσεως τετύχηκεν κατὰ τὰ ἐν Ἐξόδῳ γεγραμμένα· δεκάπληγον γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἐπήγαγεν καὶ τελευταῖον ἔδυσαν ὡσεὶ μόλιβος ἐν ὕδατι πολλῷ. Ἀλλὰ καὶ "6μετὰ ἀποσκευῆς πολλῆς"6 ἐξεληλύθασιν, ὡς ἡ ἱστορία δηλοῖ, ἐξ ἧς παιδευόμεθα ὅτι, κἂν ἐν χρόνῳ Θεός τινα κακώσῃ, οὐκ ἀδιαφόρως τοῦτο ποιεῖ ἀλλ' ἐπ' ἀγαθῷ τέλει. Εἰ δὲ αἰνίττεται ὁ λόγος καὶ τὴν τῶν ἁγίων παροίκησιν, συνεπισκέψαι. χῃ, 15–16. Σὺ δὲ ἀπελεύσῃ πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας σου <μετ' εἰρήνης> τραφεὶς ἐν γήρει καλῷ· τετάρτῃ δὲ γενεᾷ ἀποστραφήσονται ὧδε· οὔπω γὰρ ἀναπεπλήρωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι τῶν Ἀμορραίων ἕως τοῦ νῦν. Φαίνεται ἐκ τοῦ προχείρου τὴν ἐκ τοῦ βίου ἀναχώρησιν αὐτῷ προαπαγγέλλων. Πρὸς δὲ ἀναγωγὴν ταῦτα ἂν λεχθείη. Ὁ σοφὸς ἐν εἰρήνῃ ἀπέρχεται τοῦ βίου, ὁ δ' ἁμαρτάνων συγκεχυμένους ἔχει λογισμούς, ταραττομένην ἔχει τὴν ψυχήν· καὶ ὡς παραλαμβάνεταί τις ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ, οὕτω καὶ κρίνεται. Ὁ εἰρήνην ἑαυτῷ ἀπ' ἐντεῦθεν κατασκευάσας ἐν εἰρήνῃ καὶ ἀπέρχεται, ὁ δὲ ταράχους ἔχων καὶ συγκεχυμένους λογισμοὺς πρὸς τοῦτο καὶ κρι- θήσεται. Τοῦτο δηλοῦται ἐκ τοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἐκκλησιαστῇ· "6Οὗ ἐὰν πέσῃ τὸ ξύλον, ἐκεῖ μενεῖ"6. Οὐκ ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχον ἐπὶ ἱστορίας· οὐ γὰρ πάντως ἔνθα πίπτει ξύλον, ἐκεῖ μενεῖ· πολλάκις γὰρ καὶ μετάγεται· ἀλλὰ δῆλον ὡς ὁ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν ὁ διὰ τοῦ ξύλου ἐν αἰνιγμῷ σημαινόμενος, οὕτω κριθησόμενος ὡς καὶ εὑρίσκεται. 232 Ἁρμοζόντως οὖν ἐν εἰρήνῃἈβραὰμ ἀπελεύσεται πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ε̣ὐάρεστος ὢν Θεῷ, τῆς αὐτῆς ἐπαγγελίας κοινωνῶν· "6Ἀπαρχὴ"6 γὰρ "6Χριστός, ἔπειτα οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ"6. Καὶ αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν δικαίων διάφορος ἡ ἐπαγγελία καὶ ἡ μονή· πολλαὶ γὰρ μοναὶ παρὰ τῷ Πατρί. Πρὸς οὖν τοὺς πατέρας τοὺς κατὰ πνεῦμα ἀπελεύσεται ὁ σπουδαῖος τῇ
english: And I have brought her to their ruler, that is, the Word ruling over them, in order to praise her; for this was the purpose of the holy Abraham, to bring them joyfully. [Genesis 12:12: And there fell upon Abram a dark and great fear concerning the suns.]

But Abram, beholding divine sights, was seized by a fear befitting perfection. Note that a dark ecstasy fell upon him concerning the suns, signifying the progress of the Word by the passing of the day of his present state, so that another progress of blessing might be received by him as it comes upon him, according to which it was said: 'I will fulfill him with length of days,' [Genesis 25:15] not necessarily promising him long life, but clearly progress in illuminations. Therefore 'ecstasy' falls upon him; and ecstasy is not like madness, but is wonder and the translation from the visible to the invisible. For the apostle says: 'Whether then we are beside ourselves, or whether we are in our right minds' [2 Cor 5:13], not declaring that we have learned from God, but that, even if we become outside of human things through contemplation, we do this through God, just as David says: 'I said in my ecstasy: Every man is a liar' [Ps 52:6]; for having become ecstatic, he says concerning men that they are liars, he himself no longer being a man because of the communion of the Holy Spirit, but being another of those concerning whom it was said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not humans and walking according to human ways?' [Gal 5:15]. While Abram is in ecstasy, a dark fear falls upon him, not participating in darkness but in uncertainty and not knowing readily; such a great fear does not happen to small men. And since instead of uncertainty darkness is often taken, it is said: 'And he set darkness in his hiding place' [Ps 18:11]; and in truth, the contemplation and comprehension of super-abundant dogmas instills a gloom upon the great, and falls upon such people a divine fear with reverence.

And it was said to Abram: 'Knowing you shall know that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years; and the nation, which they shall serve, I will judge; and after these things they shall come out this way with much spoil.' [Genesis 15:13-14] The sojourning into Egypt...

The word foretells it; for they did not dwell as strangers being their own, having served Pharaoh and having been much ill-treated by him and the Egyptians. It does not contend with what is written there in Exodus; for there it is said: 'After four hundred and thirty years the power of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt' (Exodus 12:40), here it says 'after forty'; but it must be understood that it was not said that they went out upon the completion of the four hundred years, but after four hundred years, which the thirty [years] make manifest. And the 'I will judge the nation whom they shall serve' (Exodus 12:3) has reached its outcome according to what is written in Exodus; for He brought upon them ten-fold plagues, and they sank at last like lead in much water. But also 'with much baggage' (Exodus 12:36) they have gone out, as history shows, from which we are instructed that, even if God ill-treats someone in time, He does not do this differently, but for a good end.

If the word also alludes to the sojourning of the saints, consider this. 'And you shall go to your fathers in peace, having been nourished in a good old age; but in the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full' (Genesis 15:15-16). It is apparent from the immediate text that he is foretelling to him the departure from life. And for edification, these things might be said. The wise man departs from life in peace, but the one sinning has confused thoughts and has a troubled soul; and just as one is received in death, so he will be judged. The one having prepared peace for himself from this place, he departs in peace, but the one having trouble and confused thoughts toward this, he will be judged. This is shown from what is in Ecclesiastes: 'Wherever the wood falls, there it remains' (Ecclesiastes 9:7). This does not have this meaning in history; for it is not always that wherever wood falls, there it remains; for often it is moved; but it is clear that the man is what is signified in enigma through the wood, so he will be judged as he is found.

Therefore, fittingly, Abraham will depart to the fathers being pleasing to God, sharing the same promise; for 'the firstfruits' [are] 'Christ, then those of Christ.' And even for the righteous, the promise and the dwelling are different; for there are many dwellings with the Father.
