source_text: ὁμοιότητι τῶν τρόπων υἱὸς ὑπάρχων αὐτῶν, κἂν κατὰ σάρκα φαύλους ἔχῃ πατέρας. Ταῦτα περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ἀβρὰμ εἰπὼν περὶ τῶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ λέγει ὅτι "6τετάρτῃ γενεᾷ ἀποστραφήσονται ὧδε"6, τὴν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν τῆς κληρονομίας δηλῶν. ∆ιὰ δὲ τοῦτο μετὰ "6τετρακόσια ἔτη"6 φησὶν τὴν ἀποστροφὴν ἔσεσθαι, διότι̣ ο̣ὔπω ἐξεπλήρωσαν οἱ Ἀμορραῖοι ἑαυτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας, δι' ἃς λοιπὸν πείσονται καταστροφήν, ἵν' ἐκείνων δικασθέντων αὐτοὶ οἰκήτορες τῆς γῆς ἐκείνων γένωνται. Καὶ τὰς τιμωρίας γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς μέτρῳ καὶ καιρῷ ἐπιφέρει μακροθυμῶν ἕως ὁ καιρὸς ἐνστῇ τῆς ἀνταποδόσεως. Τούτῳ ὅμοιον καὶ κατασκευαστικὸν ὑπάρχει τὸ ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ λεγόμενον· "6Τότε Ἰησοῦς ἤρξατο ὀνειδίζειν τὰς πόλεις ἐν αἷς ἐγένοντο αἱ πλεῖσται δυνάμεις αὐτοῦ, ὅτι οὐ μετενόησαν· Οὐαί σοι, Χοραζίν· οὐα<ί> σοι Βηθσαϊδάν, ὅτι εἰ ἐν Τύρῳ καὶ Σιδόνι ἐγένοντο αἱ δυνάμεις αἱ γενόμεναι ἐν σοί, πάλαι ἂν ἐν σάκκῳ 93 καὶ σποδῷ μετε- νόησαν"6. Πρὸς ὃ λέγοι τις ἄν· Πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἐγένοντο, εἴ γε μετενόουν, ἀλλ' ἐκεῖ ἐπετελέσθησαν ἔνθα οὐ μετενόη- σαν; Καὶ λέγοιμεν ὅτι σοφία ἐστὶν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὃς καὶ ταῦτα ἐποίησεν· ἐπεὶ γὰρ τὰ κρυπτὰ ἐπιστάμενος ἐγίνωσκεν ὅτι μετανοήσαντες οὐ γνησ̣ίαν ἐποιοῦντο μετά- νοιαν, διὰ τοῦτο ἐκεῖ οὐκ ἐγένοντο αἱ δυνάμεις. Καὶ ἔστιν περὶ αὐτῶν οἰκεῖον εἰπεῖν· κρεῖσσον γὰρ αὐτοῖς μὴ ἐπεγνωσκέναι τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἢ ἐπιγνοῦσιν ἀνακᾶμψαι εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω. Οὕτως οὐ πεποίηκεν Τύρῳ καὶ Σιδόνι τὰ παράδοξα· ἔμελλεν γὰρ αὐτοῖς εὐμετάπτωτος εἶναι ἡ μετάνοια. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὗτοι παρ' οἷς ἐγένοντο <τὸ> κίνη<μα> οὐ<κ> εἶχον ψυχῆς γνωριζόμενον τῷ κριτῇ, ὅπερ ἔχρῃζεν τῆς τῶν σημείων ἐπιδείξεως, διὰ τοῦτο 233 ἐποίησεν, ἵνα οὗτοι μὲν ἀναπολόγητοι ὦσιν, ἐκεῖνοι δὲ μὴ πλέον βλάβωσιν ἀκαίρως τινὸς ἀξιούμενοι. Εἰ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ὑπερβολικῶς εἴρηται πρὸς τοῦ Σωτῆρος πρὸς ἐντροπὴν τῶν θεασαμένων τὰ σημεῖα καὶ μὴ μετανοησάντων, –καὶ γὰρ οὗτος ὁ τρόπος διδασκαλικὸς ὑπάρχει, –συνεπι- σκέψαι. ῾Η̣ μακροθυμία οὖν καὶ ἀγαθότης τοῦ κριτοῦ δείκνυται τῷ ἀπεκδέχεσθαι τὴν ἀναπλήρωσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῶν Ἀμορραίων, μετὰ τὸ ἐλέγξαι καὶ προτρέψασθαι καὶ ὅσα συντελεῖ μετάγνωσιν ἐπάγοντος τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν κόλασιν, καθὰ καὶ τῷ Φαραὼ γεγένηται· πολλάκις γὰρ ἐπιτι- μώμενος καὶ συγχωρήσεως ἀξιούμενος ἐπήγαγεν ἑαυτῷ διὰ τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τὴν τελευταίαν κατάκρισιν. χῃ, 17. Ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐγένετο ὁ ἥλιος πρὸς δυσμαῖς, φλὸξ ἐγένετο, καὶ ἰδοὺ κλίβανος καπνιζόμενος καὶ λαμπάδες πυρός, αἳ διῆλθον ἀνάμεσον τῶν διχοτομημάτων τούτων. Τὸ σαφὲς τοῦ ῥητοῦ οὕτως ἂν παρασταίη. Περὶ δυσμὰς τοῦ ἡλίου ἤδη χωροῦντος "6φλὸξ ἐγένετο"6 καὶ "6κλίβανος καπνιζόμενος"6 ἐφαίνετο "6καὶ λαμπάδες πυρός, αἳ διῆλθον ἀνάμεσον τῶν διχοτομημάτων"6, ἀμφο- τέραι καίουσαι καὶ φωτίζουσαι τὸν τόπον πρὸς τὸ ὁρᾶν τὸν πατριάρχην τὰ γινόμενα καὶ σύμβολα ἐπιδεικνύναι θειότερον, ἅπερ ἀναγκαῖον διεραυνήσασθαι. Καὶ τοῦτο δὲ σημειωτέον, ὅτι οὐ νῦν μόνον διαθήκης γινομένης πῦρ ἐφάνη, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ Μωσέως ὁ νόμος ἐπὶ πυρὶ δίδοται· ἐώρων γὰρ τὸ πῦρ, τὸν λαλοῦντα οὐ θεωροῦντες ἤκουον τὰ νομοθετηθέντα. Ἃ δὲ ᾐνίττετο διὰ τούτων εἴη ἂν τοιαῦτα. Ἐπεὶ ὁ νόμος ἆθλα καὶ ἐπίτιμα ἔχει, ἐμμέσῳ τοῦ πυρὸς δοθεὶς ἐδήλου ὅτι τοῖς μὲν καῦσιν ἐπιφέρει, τοῖς δὲ φωτισμόν. ∆ιττὴν γὰρ ἔχει δύναμιν τὸ πῦρ, φωτίζον ἅμα καὶ καῖον· ὁ δοθεὶς οὖν νόμος τοὺς μὲν λιποτάκτας αὐτοῦ καίει, τοὺς δὲ φύλακας αὐτοῦ φωτίζει. Οὕτω καὶ ἐνταῦθα λαμπάδες καὶ καπνὸς̣ ἐφαίνοντο· ἔστι δὲ ὁ καπνὸς ἀπο- 234 τέλεσμα καὶ ὡς παρακολούθημα πυρὸς ἐξαφθέντος, ἀλλὰ καὶ φλὸξ προτέρα ἐγίνετο. Λέγομεν οὖν ὡς ἐν τοιαύτῃ δυσχωρίᾳ τῷ διαιροῦντι τὰ πρακτέα καὶ μὴ φωτισμοῦ δεῖ τοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ φόβου, ὅσπερ διὰ τοῦ κλιβάνου δηλοῦται, ἵνα ἅπαντα κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν ἐπιτελῆται λόγον. χῃ, 18– 19. Ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ διέθετο Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἀβρὰμ διαθήκην λέγων· Τῷ σπέρματί σου δώσω τὴν γῆν ταύτην ἀπὸ τοῦ ποταμοῦ Αι᾿̣γύπτου ἕως τοῦ ποταμοῦ τοῦ μεγάλου ποταμοῦ Εὐφράτου, τοὺς Καιναίους, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. Τῶν λαμπάδων διελθουσῶν τὰ διχοτομήματα, ἐβεβα̣ιοῦτο ἡ διαθήκη, λέγοντος τοῦ Θεοῦ· "6Τῷ σπέρματί σου δώσω τὴν γῆν ταύτην"6, διαγράφει δὲ καὶ τὸ διάστημα τῆς γῆς. ∆εῖ δὲ κατὰ τὰ προαποδοθέντα ἀνάγοντα̣ γ̣ῆν ἐννοεῖν τῷ σπέρματι διδομένην τῷ κατὰ πνεῦμα τοῦ ἁγίου. <Ταύ>την καὶ ὁ Σωτὴρ τοῖς πραότητα κατορθώσασιν κατεπαγγέλλεται. Αὕτη πρέπουσα ἐπαγγελία τοῖς τέκνοις τοῖς ἀληθέσι καὶ οὐ τοῖς
english: A son is like a father in manner, even if the father is weak in the flesh. Regarding Abraham, it is said concerning those from him that 'in the fourth generation they shall turn away from this place' (Gen 15:16), signifying the inheritance of the land. Because of this, it is said that after 'four hundred years' (Gen 15:16) the turning away shall be, because the Amorites had not yet filled up their sins, by which they would afterward be judged, so that after they are judged, they might become inhabitants of that land.

For God brings punishments with measure and timing, being long-suffering until the time of retribution arrives. Similar and constructive to this is what is said in the Gospel: 'Then Jesus began to upbraid the cities in which most of his powers had come to pass, because they did not repent: Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida, for if in Tyre and Sidon the powers that happened in you had happened, long ago they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes' (Matt 11:20-22). To this someone asks: How is it then that they did not repent, if indeed they were repenting, but rather they were completed there where they did not repent? And we say that the Son of God is wisdom, who also did these things; for knowing the hidden things, he knew that those repenting were not making a true repentance, and because of this the powers did not occur there.

And it is appropriate to say concerning them: it is better for them not to have known the truth than to have known and to have turned back to what is behind. Thus he did not do the extraordinary things for Tyre and Sidon; for it was to be easy for them to repent. Since those among whom the movement occurred did not have a soul recognizable to the judge, which required the demonstration of signs, he did this so that these might be without defense, and those [Amorites] might not cause more harm at an unseasonable time. And if this has been said excessively by the Savior to rebuke those who saw the signs and did not repent—and indeed this way is didactic—one should consider it. For the long-suffering and goodness of the Judge is shown in awaiting the fulfillment of the sins of the Amorites, after having reproved and exhorted and everything that leads to recognition, before God brings the punishment, just as it happened to Pharaoh.
For often, being subject to punishment and being deemed worthy of forgiveness, he brought upon himself through his own hardness of heart the final condemnation.

And when the sun had gone toward the west, a flame became, and behold, a smoking oven and torches of fire, which passed between the divided pieces. The clarity of the saying would be shown thus: concerning the sun already setting, 'a flame became' and 'a smoking oven' appeared, and 'also torches of fire, which passed between the divided pieces,' both burning and lighting the place so as to see the patriarch's actions and to show the symbols more divinely, which is necessary to investigate. And this is to be noted, that not only when a covenant is being made did fire appear, but also through Moses the law is given upon fire; for they saw the fire, but not seeing the one speaking, they heard the things having been legislated. But it was suggested through these things that such things might be. Since the law has struggle and punishment, having been given in the midst of the fire, it was evident that it brings burning to some and illumination to others. For the fire has a twofold power, lighting and burning at once; so the law having been given burns those who fall away from it, and illuminates its guardians. So also here torches and smoke appeared; and smoke is a completion and as a following-up of fire having appeared, but a flame became first. We say therefore that in such a difficulty for the one dividing the practical things, there must be illumination from God and fear, as is indicated by the oven, so that all things may be accomplished according to the right word.

On that day the Lord God established a covenant with Abram, saying: 'To your seed I will give this land from the river of Egypt even to the great river Euphrates, the Kenites, and the following.' Of the torches passing through the divided pieces, the covenant was being confirmed, the God saying: 'To your seed I will give this land,' and he also traces out the extent of the land. And it is necessary, according to the previously stated things, to understand the land being given to the seed as being given to the one according to the Holy Spirit. english: Through succession to all. For 'the children of the flesh are not these children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed' (Genesis 17:19). For he who does the works of it is his child. And also well [is] 'from river to river'; for the virtue which is the due promise to the seed is that which is in the middle of flowing things, not being parts of the flowing things, but their boundaries; for if any virtue should become external to it, these things immediately encounter it. And if this has been said to the virtuous one because of the lying in wait of trials, you will understand, it being in the middle of those distressing [things] and overcoming them.

But Sarah the wife of Abram did not bear him children. And she had an Egyptian handmaid, whose name was Hagar. And Sarah said to Abram: 'Behold, the Lord has closed up on me the not-to-bear-children; go therefore to my handmaid, so that I may make children from her.' And Abram obeyed the voice of Sarah. The apostle led these to the two covenants by the law of allegory; and since the literal has also come to pass, it is also worthy to be seen. The holy ones lived together thus, not to hunt pleasures but for the sake of children. For such a tradition is brought about concerning them, that they only had intercourse with women when they had a time of conception; neither while nursing nor while feeding the infant, nor while pregnant, did they have intercourse; for in none of these times did they consider union to be appropriate.

And Jacob also confirms the tradition; for having tested in much time that Rachel did not accept to bear children, he no longer approached her; and she, thinking that if he approached her, she would bear, was saying: 'Give me children, or if not, kill me.' For he did not know that Jacob was not a potter, but was seeking union as if the holy one had ceased for the said reason, so that he might not labor in vain. And he said to her: 'Am I instead God to you, who has deprived you of the fruit of the womb?' (Genesis 29:31). And Sarah, being wise and holy, knowing for much time that through intercourse she had not received according to the belly, abstained from the fellowship with him, and since she knew that he would have children following [him], she gave her handmaid to him as a wife concubine. The temperance and also the abundance of Sarah and of Abram are shown.
The lack of passion comes not from one's own impulse, but through offspring produced by a woman. The explicit teaching is indeed useful, as we have explained.

The logic of ascent is smoothed out by using the pattern of the blessed Paul, who led the two women toward the two covenants; using this method in other matters, he led Sarah toward perfect virtue and philosophy, she being a married woman, free and noble, and living according to the laws; and virtue lives with the wise according to the laws, so that she may bring forth divine offspring from herself. For 'Wisdom' 'bears prudence to a man' (Prov 31:10), and it is said toward the pious and holy: 'Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine, your children like olive shoots around your table' (Ps 128:3). Thus the man who fears the Lord shall be blessed toward perfect virtue.

Sarah is led toward the spiritual, while Hagar the handmaid, the Egypt, is signified by Philo as the preliminary exercises and by Paul as the shadow. For it is impossible to grasp any of the spiritual or high notions without the shadow according to the letter or the introductory training; for one must first produce offspring from the lesser things. According to the shadow, they were immersing themselves, performing Pascha sensuously and circumcising themselves physically, being led by these things toward 'offering a sacrifice of praise to God' (Heb 13:15), which is the property of the free.

Since it is a matter of diligence for the wise to make room for the greater things, virtue proposes to use the introductory things first with a divine aim and to bring forth offspring from them. For since he who is now approaching virtue is not able to grasp perfection and thus bring forth from it, it is assumed that he first clothes himself in the preliminary trainings, so that he may also make room for it perfectly, if he is able.

english: Ten years have not passed, and the impassibility of the wise man is because he aims to prepare [the soul] as it is suitable for the marriage. The matters of the upbringing have already been spoken of, that according to the aim of virtue, it is necessary to have first used the introductory things, so that through them he might first become a parent; and the children from the preliminary training are no less children of virtue because of the aim having done the same toward it. Having used this, therefore, he accomplished a better acquisition; for progress is most ready for the wise man.

"And he saw that she had conceived in the womb, and the lady was dishonored in her presence" (Gen 18:13). The aim, as has been spoken, is for the wise man to be trained in the preliminary training and in the shadow, so that having been trained in these things, he may proceed to the greater things; for as such a sequence is proper, so there is not a following return from the knowledge of the perfects into the smaller things. For the apostle neglects, writing to the Galatians, those who wish to live with the shadow of the law after the gospel (Gal 4:25). For the Jews, having the shadow as a companion, [are one thing], and the Galatians, after believing the gospel, wished to Judaize (Acts 15:5), having been deceived by a certain Ebion, who wished to Judaize after Christianizing and was persuading the others thus, since he had the epithet of this name among the apostles because of his making poverty manifest; for Ebion is interpreted as poor, because of his shallow and poor intellect, being called Ebion the poor; for that the Galatians were Greeks, Paul writes: "But at that time you did not know God, but served those which are by nature not gods; but now having known God, or rather having been known by God" (Gal 4:8). He therefore blames them, as has been said; for it is necessary to repay the promise of the Scriptures: "Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being perfected in the flesh?" (Gal 3:3); for having once been cast into a divine beginning, they were not appropriately seeking the types, for they were seeking them at an unseasonable time. For it is necessary to understand for what reason the sensory circumcision is given and until when...

For what period must he live as a citizen? If someone perceives this, he has fathered a child from a concubine, and after this he is able to perceive the circumcision being made in the heart by the Spirit (Rom 2:29). And this holy man, following the guidance of virtue, entered toward her to whom a maidservant had been handed to him, as we have shown, who also conceived, toward whom it is not fitting to remain thereafter exceeding what is necessary.

For many, having used preliminary exercises for the sake of complete instruction, having left behind them such things, are born in a slave-like manner and in a certain way dishonor virtue. But these things must not be referred to the person of Abraham, but to such a manner of those using this kind of way. And if, since we said that virtue... is the thing presupposing the things of the introduction, someone says that the offspring are a kind of part of it and such a person dwells with virtue primarily—for the underlying subject acts according to its postulates—it must be said therefore that of those things happening in time, some are prior to some and others are later, but when they are simultaneous, we take as understood that of those existing at once, one precedes and the other follows, as if regarding natural causes; virtue indeed is the cause of all things happening through it; therefore, even if such things precede it in time, it is by nature prior, just as marriage exists prior to child-rearing; for because of these things marriage... of virtue. And regarding the other sciences, the same...

Therefore, he who prefers other things to virtue dishonors virtue; for if someone were to choose it not for its own sake but for the sake of some other praise or glory, he in a certain way dishonors the good, it not receiving dishonor in itself. english: Noticing that the word was being made certain as something to happen, he was implying that it is not proper to remain in the things before it, thereby dishonoring virtue.

Sarah said: 'I am wronged by you; I gave my maidservant of mine into your bosom; but seeing that she has conception in her womb, I have been dishonored in opposition to her; may God judge between me and you.' (Gen 16:2). The 'from you' is twofold, that is, either 'from you' or 'from whom'; so that regarding the 'from you' it is thus: when anyone, desiring to use the preliminary exercises for the sake of virtue and the perfection of wisdom, remains in these in some way dishonoring the virtue by not using them for what is necessary, and the 'from whom' will receive the same intellect, the only difference being that he truly dishonors the virtue by hastening to give birth from the introduction alone and setting this as the end.

Pay attention also to 'in opposition to her'; for the virtue was not simply dishonored, but 'in opposition to her'; for when anyone, having used the preliminary exercises because of the perfection of wisdom, goes beyond the need, he dishonors the virtue in himself. As for 'may God judge between me and you', one might say it literally as having been spoken because of some movement from a human being in her, but following the intention of those who have understood, it is said toward the one remaining in the introductory character: that you did not bear perfect children from me, but rather allowed them to remain still in those things.

Abram said to Sarah: 'Behold, your maidservant is in your hands; use her as it is pleasing to you.' (Gen 16:6). Regarding the literal sense, the word of the patriarch introduces an indifference, as he receives the maidservant from the woman without desiring pleasure and now being content with her and withdrawing when he wishes; but toward an elevation, the diligent one, even if remaining in the introduction and being alienated from the perfection of virtue, receives the rebuke from her unpleasantly, and then, having moved from the smaller things, as if subjecting himself to her, uses her instructions to restore authority. For whenever he is eager to say, do, and think all things toward the goal of virtue, he most readily receives the corrections from her.

And Sarah mistreated her and drove her away from her presence. This mistreatment of the handmaid, whom we lead into the preliminary exercises, turns out to be a kind of dismissal of them. For those who are pressing toward perfection no longer need them. Because of this, she rightly departs; for she no longer endures the introductory elements of having attained progress and perfection.

And an angel of the Lord of God found her at the water spring in the desert, at the spring on the road to Shur (Gen 16:7). And the angel of the Lord said to her, 'Hagar, handmaid of Sarah, whence do you come and whither are you going?' And she said, 'I am fleeing from the presence of Sarah, my mistress' (Gen 16:8). From these things, one can see and know the virtue of Hagar and that she was not ungrateful, as an angel was conversing with her and placing care for her not as a trivial matter; for it is evident that it was according to the will of God. It was not unlikely that she was diligent, as she was chosen by the holy Sarah for the companionship of Abraham. And her thankfulness is shown by her saying, 'I am fleeing from the presence of Sarah, my mistress'; nothing trivial is said about her. In the things previously mentioned, Sarah's virtue and the spiritual understanding of the divine Scriptures were placed, while Hagar was the introductory and shadowy one.

Therefore, the one approaching the divine instruction ought to attend to her in this way, so as to understand him according to letter and spirit, in a manner and order that fits. Thus it is necessary for the child of Sarah's introduction, so that he may reach the more perfect things, just as it was said concerning the Israelites, 'that they were first entrusted with the words of God' (Rom 3:2), which are given until a time of correction. For no one remaining in the letter or in her introductory wisdom is being made an opponent. Therefore, this lover of wisdom, if he remains using only the introductory things, in a way dishonors virtue; and if he rises up, he will have lost the introductory guidance as having departed from it; once progress has been attained, the former things pass away, just as was the case with the Egyptian Hagar; for the things of the introduction are confirmed by earthly examples.

english: So she flees, and while fleeing, an angel finds her; for an angel does not become invisible. For this is what the addition of 'of the Lord' signifies. It has been said that the evil ones are called such, as it is said: 'An apostolate through evil angels... we shall judge angels' (Acts 13:46). The angel does not find her fleeing, but turns her back because of the greatness of virtue; for the didactic word and the lessons of the introduction turn back toward virtue.

And it is also good that, saying she was found in the desert and at the spring, she is said to be found on Your way, which is interpreted as continuity; for she did not become a fugitive outside the house, nor did she flee quickly. Just as when we began the introductions to virtue, she does not go outside the enclosure but remains in the introduction. Therefore, the didactic word also turns back, showing him the fitness of remaining by saying: 'Where do you come from and where are you going?' For the virtuous person must know both the beginnings and the goal. But he who uses the introduction, often boasting of the greatness of virtue, remains in it in a certain way, fleeing the tone of perfection; for this is shown by: 'I am fleeing from the presence of Sarah, my mistress' (Gen 16:6).

But even when the beauty of the spiritual law stands present, the shadowy things flee, those luminous sacrifices being handed over and brought in by the shadow; so also the partial is nullified when the perfect stands present. The one hearing toward the Savior fled from the presence, saying: 'You must be born again' (John 3:7), and saying: 'How can a man be born when he is old?' (John 3:4); for the divine thinks in a human way. And it is also good to be found at the spring of water; for the one being led into the pure things is found, which is what the water signifies, and into the desert of evils such a one is, having been removed from wickedness and possessing virtue.

And the angel of the Lord said to her: 'Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hands' (Gen 20:6). The literal sense is not obscure; but it is shown from the allegory that, even if each one is led by some reasonable action, which he thought to be among those surrounding the shadow of the law, and as if he were fleeing...

The teaching word turns such a spiritual vision back toward the preceding will. For the Lord indeed placed the things in the letters of the shadow to stand away by saying: 'What multitude of your sacrifices to me?' (Psalm 50:6) and 'Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving and pay to the Most High your vows' (Psalm 51:16). Great indeed is that which, being called master under the hands of spiritual teaching, is found and humbled by it, not being humble itself but as toward a master. english: Nevertheless, the promise of the teaching word happens in this way: it will prescribe; for often, through closeness, those teaching know the burdens of those being discipled and do not ignore their intelligence. But that the state of the stomach is unclear is learned from the Gospel, saying of the Savior: 'Woe to those with full bellies and to those nursing at that time' (Luke 10:23). For such conditions are unstable when a trial stands near. Because of this, the word says that such ones desire to be weaned: 'You who have been weaned from milk, who have been turned away from the breast, expect hope upon hope in tribulation upon tribulation'; for as a remainder, standing in stability, they receive tribulation upon tribulation.

But they are incomplete regarding what Paul says: 'I gave you milk, not food; for you were not able, and even now you are not able' (1 Cor 3:2). It is therefore foretold to her that she will bear a son, saying, 'You will call his name Ishmael' (Gen 16:12). This one will be a rustic man. In many ways, one who is not such is separated from the diligent, the wise, and the civilized. We say, therefore, as toward a citizen, and toward an expert, and toward an unlearned person, and toward a recently learned person, and toward a rustic.

Since, therefore, the offspring of virtue is lawful citizenship, he who is not according to citizenship, against the city of the living God, the heavenly, living the heavenly city, is a rustic, lacking that state, dwelling in a field and not yet in a city. And it is good even to say not only rustic but also a man; for participation in the Word of God does not happen to one just beginning, but after making progress—for regarding those, He said, toward whom the Word of God became—and thus he will be a citizen of the heavenly city; for concerning such things, these things are said by the wise Paul to the Hebrews: 'Zion, mountains and city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, being inscribed in it' (Heb 12:22). The Savior says, therefore: 'Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but that your names are inscribed in the heavens' (Luke 10:20). And it is not necessary anywhere to reason thus, that names are inscribed in the heavens by gathering them together, but names according to virtue; these things have the heavens in eternal memory.

Scripture. And these indeed are written in the heavens, but those conversely positioned, thinking of earthly things, called their names upon their own earths, fittingly of Jeremiah concerning them saying: 'Having been set down upon the earth they shall be written' (Jer 32:50). His hand is upon all and the hands of all are upon him, and according to the face of all his brothers he will dwell. And Hagar called the name of the Lord who was speaking to her: 'You are the God who sees me,' because he said: 'For indeed I have seen one who sees me' (Gen 16:13). Because of this she called the well 'The Well of him whom I saw between Kadesh and Beerlahai' (Gen 16:14).

In what was previously read, he was an angel of God speaking to her, but now he is named Lord and God; and he who does not distinguish himself from the matters says that the angel does not convey his own words but the words of God like the prophets; for in a certain way even the angels, when they minister the [divine]... and foretell the things to come, do the work of prophets... and the name of the angel is one of activity and not of essence, just as the name of the prophet is by designation... the angel spoke the things of God... [he] named [him] through the one dwelling, just as Isaiah, prophesying, at times indeed from his own person as one having the spiritual [thing] in himself speaking, and at times as one bearing the face of God, not beforehand saying 'the Lord says' as when he says: 'I made earth and man upon it' (Isa 45:7), but from the Lord he announces... 'Hear, O heaven, and be attentive, O earth, for the Lord has spoken' (Isa 40:9). We say this not as all the words are being borne through him, but as a participation is being granted and authority, and because of the indwelling of God, [they are] called gods, those who partake.

Indeed, it was also said of Moses that an angel was speaking: 'And the angel of the Lord called him and said: I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob' (Ex 3:2-6). These are words regarding the ministering of angels, but [they are also] regarding the power of God. And this is the first explanation...

The one making progress, when he brings forth toward the goal of the teacher, that which is being brought forth is not easy to misinterpret. Therefore, the appropriate word of the birth applies to the one rightly educating and sowing what is profitable; it said, 'Hagar bore a son to Abram' (Gen 16:15). Since this is so... providing what the Scripture says, it is brought forward: 'And Abram called the name of his son' (Gen 16:11), and it leads to 'whom she bore to him' (Gen 16:15); for if not for the meaning which he had, the phrase 'And Abram called the name of his son' would have sufficed, without adding 'whom she bore to him.'

english: And I will multiply your covenant through me and through you exceedingly. Let there be no blame found against me. He promised to multiply himself according to the word, and this is no wonder. For other nations have also become many. And Abraham fell upon his face. They are rejoicing and being multiplied just as the patriarch. And God spoke to him, saying: 'And behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be a father of a multitude of nations. And your name shall not be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, because a father of many nations I have made you. And I will multiply you exceedingly, exceedingly.' Again, the Lord, after the falling, confirms the promise, saying to him that He will make a covenant with him; and he shall be a father of a multitude.
